en: (B1) Second Pāda. (Section 1: (A.3, Pāda 2, Adhikaraṇa 1) The Denotation of Meaning.
Thus, the investigation concerning the application of direct statement (*śruti*) having been completed, the investigation concerning the application of indicative power (*liṅga*) is now introduced.

In this context, *liṅga* is the fitness residing in established words and word-meanings, which is conducive to the postulation of a word expressive of a case-role (*kāraka*) that constitutes the objective (*uddeśyatā*) of another [element], thereby forming part of its subsidiarity (*aṅgatva*).
For example, in the passage "he cuts with the *struva* ladle," there is a fitness residing in the *struva* that is conducive to the postulation of the word "liquid" (*drava*).

Thus, in the case of mantras, the indicative power (*liṅga*) consists in a fitness that is conducive to the postulation of words expressing the intendedness of their own meaning-function (*svārthavṛtti-uddeśyatā*) and conducive to the postulation of words expressing their own status as a grammatical factor (*kārakatva*). And because it brings about the assumption of a direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) in the form of a word, it serves as the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the application (*viniyoga*) of that [mantra] to that purpose through that [statement]. Since it is impossible to investigate the specific details of indicative power—which consists in the inherent capacity of things—what [is the nature] of the capacity of the mantra?

When there is a doubt as to whether the application [of a mantra] pertains only to a primary meaning or even to that which is conveyed by a secondary (jaghanya) function— regarding a mantra recited within the context of a sacrifice,

such as "I cut the grass, the seat of the gods" (*barhir devasadanaṃ dāmi*)— its application is common to both the primary and the secondary [objects], such as the *ulapa* grass and the clarified butter (*ājya*), because there is no difference in the causal complex consisting of the requirement for a reminder (*smāraka-ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth.

[The opponent argues: "Just as in the case of the command 'Bring the sacrificial posts,' when there exists an indicator of intention (*tātparya*) in the form of syntactic expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth, the sublation of the primary meaning is irrelevant. [To this we reply:

Since the cognition of a secondary meaning depends upon the apprehension of a relationship with the primary meaning, it is delayed; therefore, it is impossible for a mantra or similar element—which has already fulfilled its purpose through its application to the primary meaning cognized first—to serve as the applicator of a secondary meaning.
Therefore, when there is a desire for a reminder of that [meaning], its cessation occurs through other means such as meditation (adhyāna) and so forth.
For this very reason, in a context where the application of the primary meaning is not already established, its assumption arises solely by the force of the recitation of the mantra.

However, where there is an obstruction by another conflicting quality within the context (*prakaraṇa*), then, provided there exists a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that establishes a general connection, there is "extraction" (*utkarṣa*).

This is as in the case of the *pūṣānumantraṇa* mantra and others recited in the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices; for even though the name (*samākhyā*) "sacrifice-consecration" (*yāgānumantraṇa*) serves to establish a general connection, [the mantra is extracted from its context].
Even when excellence (utkarṣa) is impossible, there is application within the very context for a secondary meaning (jaghanyārtha), as in the case of the Manotā mantra and others.

When even that is impossible due to the lack of an unestablished indication (lakṣaṇā) and so forth, then the expression of that meaning serves a transcendental purpose (adṛṣṭārthatva), as in the case of muttering (japa) and the like. // 1.16 //
Thus ends the first section concerning the application of mantras according to their primary meaning.

(B2) Although it would be logical to examine the application by syntactical connection (*vākya*) and so forth immediately after examining the application by direct assertion (*śruti*), because they share the commonality of being verbal, nevertheless—since each subsequent means of proof (*pramāṇa*) functions as an applicator only by depending on the preceding one through the postulation of such dependence—it is necessary to first examine that which is useful for the application by indicative power (*liṅga*). For this very reason, since it depends upon direct assertion, its examination follows the examination of the latter; thus, there is a "contextual connection" (*avasara-saṅgati*) due to the sequence of the topics.

Intending that there is no flaw even though there is no immediate connection due to the difference between the sections (*pāda*), he declares the subject matter of the section as something to be investigated, beginning with the word "thus" (*evam*).

Although it is necessary for even *śruti* to imply *sāmarthya* (capacity), since it is impossible for *śruti* alone to effect an application when capacity is absent, nevertheless: "The application of *śruti* does not occur by placing the knowledge of *liṅga* (indicative power) at the forefront;
rather, it is *liṅga* that effects the application by placing the knowledge of *śruti* at the forefront."

According to this principle, since even that which lacks inherent capacity may be employed through a scriptural injunction (*śruti*) that is postulated, there is no requirement for intrinsic capacity; therefore, the occasion for this [scriptural injunction] arises only after that [intrinsic capacity], and not before it—this is indicated by the word "now" (*adhunā*).
Thus, it is said to be "utilizing the indicative power" (*liṅgopayogī*).
The meaning is that it is useful for the application of the *liṅga* (indicative mark).

Therefore, among the two kinds of *liṅga* to be described— namely, that which consists of the capacity of the thing (*vastu-sāmarthya*) and that which consists of the capacity of the mantra (*mantra-sāmarthya*)—

since a consideration of specific modes is impossible in the case of the first and the last [of those two], where only the capacity of the thing has been determined as the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, since in the section on Mantras it was established that the capacity of a mantra functions as a means of application (*viniyojaka*) by virtue of its purpose being the manifestation of meaning, it is possible to consider specific modes [of that capacity]; thus, the determination of what is useful for the application effected by the mantra’s capacity constitutes the subject matter (*padārtha*).
However, the determination of the capacity of things (*vastu-sāmarthya*) follows as a secondary topic (*prasaṅga*).

Therefore, even though this section concerning the application of the *aindra* mantra involves an investigation into scriptural application (*śruti-viniyoga*), there is no flaw; the sense is that it is appropriately connected by way of being an exception (*apavāda-saṅgati*) to the primary application established in the preceding section, as this section serves to set aside that primary application.
Regarding that investigation into the application of *liṅga* which is now being introduced, he states its definition: "In this context, *liṅga* [is as follows]."

In this context, it should be observed that in some instances one assumes a word expressive of either the objecthood (*uddeśyatā*) or the status of being a factor of action (*kārakatā*), while in others one assumes words expressive of both. Among these, he illustrates the first case with the example "yathā" (as follows).

Therefore, the point is that in cases where the application is postulated through the otherwise inexplicability of a purificatory injunction (*saṃskāravidhi*), one should understand that the semantic competency (*yogyatā*) must be conducive to the assumption of words expressive of both [the substance and the action] residing in the purificatory rite itself.

In this way, he demonstrates that even in the case of a word functioning as a *liṅga* within a mantra, it is conducive to the assumption of a term denoting both [the deity and the sacrificer], by stating "evam" (thus).

And here, although the injunction of the Viśvajit possesses the requisite capacity (yogyatā) favorable for the postulation of a word expressing heaven as the objective to be attained (bhāvya), the phrase "which constitutes the factor of subsidiarity" (aṅgatvaghaṭakībhūtā) was stated both to demonstrate the absence of its applicatory power (viniyojakatva) and to indicate that it serves as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for subsidiarity; and this [subsidiarity] is as follows.

The meaning is that, because it consists in the impossibility of [the mantra's purpose] being otherwise established, it serves as a means of proof for the application of its meaning by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyāpti*), through the postulation of a scriptural text (*śruti*) consisting of words such as the accusative case-ending. In that regard, when the connection of mantras recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices— though not applied by an explicit scriptural statement (*śruti*)— is understood through the context known as "qualification" (*adhikāra*), their specific application is then determined by indicative power (*liṅga*) regarding the particular means [of performance].

In that case as well, even though the mark (*liṅga*) consists of fitness, Devadatta’s fitness for cooking does not result in his application to the act of cooking if there is an absence of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*); therefore, expectancy is also a necessary auxiliary factor.
And this [expectancy] functions in the same way for both the mantra and the context (*prakaraṇa*), as it does for the means (*dvāra*);
for in its absence, a connection is logically untenable.

And thus, intending that just as the mantra "barhir devasadanaṃ dāmi" is enjoined as an auxiliary to the primary act of cutting kusha grass because it requires a reminder of that act, [the author] states the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) with the words "kratuprakaraṇe" etc.

Now, one might ask: since there is no impossibility of the primary meaning, how can there be an application [of the mantra] there by means of expressing a secondary sense? To this, he says: "As in the case of 'staffs'."

The meaning is as follows: in the case of the statement "bring in the sacrificial posts" (*yaṣṭīḥ praveśaya*), even though there is no sublation of the primary sense, we observe indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based solely on the speaker's intention (*tātparya*). Therefore, here too, since the factors that grasp the intention—such as expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth—are present, the occurrence of indication is justified. For, while the primary sense itself is quickly established through the indicative power (*liṅga*) aided by mere expectancy via the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the mantra, the assumption of a Vedic text (*śruti*) [for the secondary sense] would be delayed; furthermore, since the expectancy residing in the secondary sense is already established as a cause for recollection (*smṛti*)—just like the mantra—it can be fulfilled even by other means such as visualization (*dhyāna*) and the like.
Since the accomplishment of cessation [occurs through the primary sense], the application [of the term] does not apply to the secondary sense.

Nor is there a lack of a decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*) regarding whether the expectancy for the primary or the secondary meaning determines the application of the mantra; for, since the apprehension of the possible relationship (*śakyasaṃbandhagraha*) is the cause of the verbal cognition of the secondary meaning, the primary meaning is presented first. Consequently, once the mantra applied by the expectancy for that [primary] meaning has its own expectancy satisfied, it is impossible for a connection with the subsequently perceived secondary meaning to arise through the expectancy of only one of the two. This is the intended sense.
He states the established conclusion (siddhānta): "By means of a possible relation," and so forth.

By this [argument], the view that— since capacity exists even in the secondary sense (gauṇa) by way of conveying the primary meaning (mukhyārtha), and since there is no distinction in the postulation of a single injunctive scripture (śruti) common to both— the application occurs in both cases— is also refuted; because when a ritual act (padārtha) is understood as something to be performed and requires a reminder, the application of the mantra occurs through indicative power (liṅga), and since it is necessary to postulate an injunctive scripture for the application of the mantra for those [acts] which are mutually independent, the postulation of scripture must first occur with respect to the primary meaning.
Because there is no possibility of postulating a further scriptural statement due to the very fact that the requirement [of the injunction] has already been satisfied;
since the primary meaning, by virtue of being the first encountered, satisfies the requirement through the postulation of a scriptural statement right there,
for that very reason, even when an implied injunction is postulated in accordance with it, the application is determined to be right there, and not in the secondary sense.

Just as in the case of the mantra, "May I succeed through the arms of the Aśvins," although there is no explicit injunction for its recitation, its application to that very primary meaning will be explained by postulating such an injunction;
thus he says, "for this very reason."

Now, one might object: "How can there be an application of the *pūṣānumantraṇa* mantra and others to the meaning of Agni through secondary figurative indication (*gauṇī vṛtti*), when the deity Pūṣan is absent from the context and the primary meaning is thus sublated? He dispels this doubt by demonstrating the non-application in that case with the words: "But where... (*yatra tu*).
Since it is impossible for the weak *prakaraṇa* (context) to sublate the *liṅga* (indicative power), there is no application of the mantra to a secondary sense within that very *prakaraṇa*;
rather, its displacement (*utkarṣa*) occurs only where Pūṣan is the deity, as in the Cāturmāsya sacrifice.

To prevent the undesirable consequence of displacing the *yājyā* verses belonging to the Upāṃśuyāja—which have Viṣṇu and other deities—since such deities are absent from the *prakaraṇa*, the word "contradictory" (*virodhin*) was stated.

In that case, even though it is impossible for [the mantra] to be applied to the Āgneya and other sacrifices, its application is established by postulating a prescription of a deity for the Upāṃśuyāja, since no deity has been explicitly heard [in that context].

For this very reason, just as with the Vasantādi-anumantraṇa mantras, it is impossible to postulate a prescription of Pūṣan as the deity for the Upāṃśuyāja; rather, because there are other qualities present in the Āgneya and other sacrifices, the mantra must be displaced (utkarṣa).
And here, the *liṅga*—which consists of the inherent capacity of the thing itself—is the means of application independently of any authority that establishes a general connection.
Just as the knowledge of the object [of the mantra] constitutes an auxiliary element (*kratvaṅga*) of the sacrifice,

so too does the indicative power (*liṅga*) residing in the mantra, because it is dependent upon that [knowledge]. Otherwise, if there were no application of the mantra to the object which has become an auxiliary of the sacrifice, and if there were no regard for its being a means to the *apūrva* of the ritual action, then [there would be no connection] with the deity.

In order to indicate that subsidiarity (*aṅgatva*) cannot arise from indicative power (*liṅga*) alone—since that would lead to the consequence of fruitlessness due to the impossibility of establishing a specific application (*viniyoga*)—it is stated [in the commentary] "provided there exists a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that makes known the general relationship," drawing upon what will be explained in the section concerning indicative power, order, and name (*liṅgakramasāmākhyāna*).
For this very reason, the traditionalists have said: "When one thing is absolutely impossible without another, the former is subsidiary to the latter, independent of any other [means of proof]."
When one thing arises without another, the former has that [latter] as its purpose; this depends upon a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that makes known a general relationship.
Furthermore, although for this [mantra] there is no context (*prakaraṇa*) that serves as a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for understanding a general connection,

nevertheless, since the designation (*samākhyā*) "invocation of the sacrifice" (*yāgānumantraṇa*) exists as a means of knowledge that indicates such a connection, once a general connection with the ritual is understood through that designation, the specific application to a particular means is effected by the indicative power (*liṅga*). Thus, even in this case, it does not occur without a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).
There arises the contingency of applying [the mantra] in a secondary sense.

Although this name (samākhyā) is weaker than context (prakaraṇa), nevertheless, since it is set aside by the stronger indicative power (liṅga), once it is understood through that indicative power that the purpose is to manifest Pūṣan as the deity—

The sense is that, since there would otherwise follow the contingency of meaninglessness, it is useful as a grasper of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) characterized by being a means to the *apūrva*; thus, it is "strong" because it is supported by a powerful indicative mark (*liṅga*).
As it has been said: "The designation 'invocations of the sacrifice' (*yāgānumantraṇa*) follows the ritual."
Therefore, attainment occurs in a sacrifice dedicated to that deity according to one's capacity.
Thus [it is said].
"Also of excellence."

The meaning is that since there is no other means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to establish a connection between the *manotā* mantra— which illuminates Agni alone— and a sacrifice dedicated solely to the deity Agni, and since its displacement (*utkarṣa*) to such a sacrifice is impossible based on indicative power (*liṅga*) alone, the mantra must be applied right there [in the context] with the word "Agni" used in its secondary sense (*jaghanyārtha*) as a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā) for Agnīṣoma, in order to fulfill the connection with the sacrifice understood through the context (*prakaraṇa*).

However, when the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma itself—aided by the principle that "what is useless for the whole is [useful] for its parts"—is understood as the indicator of the general relationship that "this [manotā-verse] is an auxiliary to the animal sacrifice belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma," then there would be a displacement (*utkarṣa*) of the *manotā* to the *āgneya-savanīya* animal sacrifice based on the indicative power (*liṅga*).

In that case, since the statement "even if the animal belongs to another deity, the *manotā* must be addressed to Agni" lacks the instrumental case or similar markers, it cannot be a direct Vedic injunction (*śruti*); and since a syntactical connection (*vākya*) is overridden by indicative power (*liṅga*), there would arise the contingency of prohibiting displacement. Nevertheless, because of the particle *eva* (only), [the meaning is restricted] to "it must be performed [in this way] alone."

It should be explained that, because of the hearing of the particle *eva* through its connection with the remote [word], or else because the sublation of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is possible due to the superior force of this being a sentence of the Brāhmaṇa according to the method to be stated hereafter, there is a prohibition of transference; thus, even the possibility of transference is non-existent.

Although, by the particle *eva* co-occurring with the word *āgneyī* in this sentence, [there is a restriction] regarding the *āgneya* mantra obtained through the rule of extension (*codaka*) in the case of a *vāyavya* animal sacrifice...

Intending that, since the application of the *āgneya* mantra in its own proper place (*sthāna*) is logically established as a prohibition [of its displacement], it cannot be a prohibition of its displacement (*utkarṣa*), the tenth book of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra* proceeds with the section: "But in the case of the *manotā*, there is no modification because of the scriptural statement" (*manotāyāṃ tu vacanād avikāraḥ*).

Nevertheless, since this sentence can serve the purpose of a contextual result by functioning as a prohibition of displacement, it is more appropriate that it indeed functions as a prohibition of displacement, rather than being assumed to serve the purpose of a non-contextual result.
The tenth section (adhikaraṇa) regarding the *jyotiṣṭoma* should be understood as a hypothetical discussion (*kṛtvācintā*) concerning whether there is an animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni.

For this very reason, it is stated in the *Tantraratna*: “Since, that being the case, it would be impossible to prohibit an elevation (*utkarṣa*) that has not even arisen, the aforementioned statement must be intended to mean that no modification (*anūha*) is to be made.
Therefore, what was said is correct: “as in the case of the *manotā* and so forth.”

Regarding the cutting of grass used for the purpose [of the ritual], the mantra "barhir devasadanaṃ" (the sacrificial grass, the seat of the gods) is [to be recited] according to the prima facie view, but not according to the final conclusion; this has not been explicitly stated because it is obvious.
Thus ends the first section concerning the application by means of indicative power (*liṅga*) to the primary meaning itself.

However, where there exists a statement indicating the intention toward a secondary sense— as, for example, in the case of the fire,
in such passages as "With the verse 'kadācana starīrasi,' one worships the Gārhapatya fire with a verse addressed to Indra"—
there the application is indeed to the Gārhapatya in its secondary sense.

Now, because the derivative suffix (*taddhita*) located in the opening phrase "athaindryā" (with the *aindrī* verse) revives the primary capacity [of Indra], the secondary accusative case itself must, in accordance with that [suffix], be understood through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as denoting the state of being the counter-correlative (the object), meaning "having stood near the *gārhapatya* fire.

Alternatively, even in the subordinate nominal stem (*prātipadika*), there may be a figurative sense (*gauṇī*) based on similarity to being a means of sacrifice, or by connection with the possession of a master (*gṛhapati*).
Or rather, let it be that, due to its conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), the fire itself is the object with respect to the action of standing nearby expressed by the verbal root.
But it does not [refer] to the naming of that which is to be accomplished by a mantra, because that [naming] is not expressed by words.

Nor can it be understood that the root [√i] has "naming" as its implied meaning (lakṣaka), on the grounds that the root's sense of "employing a mantra" is understood from the rule for the middle voice (ātmanepada) in the traditional grammar (smṛti): "The middle voice is used after the prefix *upa* when the employment of a mantra is the instrument."

Since it is understood through the force of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) that the purpose of the recitation is the act of standing nearby, and since it is thus logical for the mantra— by virtue of its relationship as a subordinate element whose function is to express what is to be accomplished— to serve as a qualifier of "standing nearby," there is no evidence for a secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) consisting of "recitation.
Consequently, in the primary sense itself, the Gārhapatya fire is the object (*karman*) of the act of standing nearby.
There is no contradiction in the statement "for you, it is for Indra," because the transitivity of this verbal root has been explained in detail in the Kaustubha itself.
Therefore, if it is asked how the mantra can be applied to a secondary (gauṇa) meaning, the answer is: no.

In the word *aindryā*, because it is conveyed as a single compound by means of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), it is impossible for the mantra—which is presented as the qualified object—to be understood as having Indra as its subsidiary (*aṅga*) when that is not useful for the piling (*cayana*).

Therefore, since it is possible to explain it as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of its capacity to manifest Indra at the time it is being understood, there is no need to resort to metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) or abandon the primary conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) on the strength of the accusative case ending and so forth.
Nor is Agni the object (*karman*) with respect to the act of standing nearby.

In that case, since the act of denotation (*abhidhāna*) is not a subordinate factor (*aṅga*) with respect to the object to be denoted, there would arise a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) caused by the multiplicity of things to be designated; furthermore, because this would contradict the middle-voice (*ātmanepada*) ending, the root itself must necessarily imply a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) characterized by the denotation of its own primary meaning as qualified [by the object].

Consequently, from the very sense of the words, it is understood that the mantra is the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the denotation—which serves as the qualificand—while the Gārhapatya fire, which is to be consecrated by the piling (*cayana*), is understood as the object (*karman*).

Since it is logical to understand that very [fire] as the counter-correlative of proximity, and in accordance with the *brāhmaṇa* passage which indicates the intended meaning (*tātparya*), it is established that the mantra itself is employed for the *gārhapatya* fire through a secondary (metaphorical) application. // 2 / 17 //
Thus ends the second section concerning the application of mantras even to a secondary sense on the basis of direct scriptural statement (śruti).

(B2) Since, in the preceding [section], it was stated that *liṅga* (indicative power) functions as an applicator only with respect to its primary meaning— by refuting its applicatory function regarding a secondary meaning through the postulation of an applicatory *śruti* (direct statement)— this section establishes an exception (*apavāda*) to the absence of applicatory function that had arisen even for *liṅga* when applied to a secondary meaning in the case of the *aindrī* verse by virtue of being assisted by an applicatory *śruti*. Thus, there is an immediate connection (*anantara-saṅgati*) based on this exception.

Since the doubt arises from the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) based on the very conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the preceding section, and since the prima facie argument is clear and thus need not be stated separately, he sets forth only the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) in accordance with the Sūtra—"But because of the scriptural statement" (*vacanāt tu*)—beginning with "But where... (*yatra tu*).

In this regard, the author of the Bhāṣya has cited: “*niveśanaḥ saṅgamano vasūnāṃ viśvārūpābhicaṣṭe śacībhiḥ / deva iva savitā satyadharmendrasya samare vasūnāmityaindyā gārhapatyamupatiṣṭhate*” (He who is the dweller, the gatherer of riches, beholds all forms with his powers; like the god Savitṛ whose laws are true, [he stands] in the assembly of Indra over riches—with this verse addressed to Indra, he worships the Gārhapatya fire).

Since Indra is indicated here as the object of comparison by means of the particle *na* used for comparison, it is understood that Indra is not the primary subject. [The others are: Dhruva, Agni, Soma, Waters, Anila, and Nala.

"Pratyūṣa and Prabhāsa are proclaimed as the eight Vasus. Since Agni, who is denoted by the word *anala*, is remembered as being among the Vasus, and because from this one understands a praise of Agni— namely, that among those mentioned he stood in battle like Indra— and since it is also remembered that Agni alone is the foremost of the Vasus in the statement, "Among the Vasus, I am Pāvaka," [the meaning follows].

Since it is understood that Agni alone is being praised by virtue of his being the "conjunction of treasures" (*vasusaṃgamana*) due to the gathering of other treasures near him, it is improper to cite [the mantra] as being addressed to Indra;

therefore, setting that aside as incorrect, [the author] cites an Indra-mantra found in another Vedic recension (śākhā) as written in the *Bhāṣya* on the section concerning relative strength (*balābala*), namely:
"Just as in the case of Agni... (*yathāgnau kadācana...*).

Furthermore, because the word "gārhapatyam" [in the mantra] naturally functions as a support for the accusative case-ending, it contradicts the final conclusion (siddhānta); therefore, it cannot serve as an example.

As for that which was stated by the author of the *Nyāyasudhā* in the section on relative strength (*balābalādhikaraṇa*)— namely, that since the sublation of indicative power (*liṅga*) by direct statement (*śruti*) will be explained later, one does not need to consider the natural capacity (*svarasasāmarthya*) of the mantra; rather, because the primary status [of Indra] is understood through the direct statement of the *taddhita* suffix denoting a deity, and because even Indra can be the object of praise in the form of a comparison (just as in the expression "the battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa"), the example is appropriate— it has been said.

If one were to establish the *aindrī* status [of the mantra] by adopting a secondary (*gauṇa*) capacity— by abandoning the natural power of that mantra’s own words and instead imagining that it is its own self that serves as its own object of comparison— then, because that [secondary capacity] would merely support the *taddhita* suffix, it would be impossible for the syntactic indication (*liṅga*) supported by the *taddhita* suffix to restrict the direct statement of the case-role (*kāraka-śruti*). Consequently, since the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) would be untenable, one must conclude, upon considering the natural power of the mantra’s own words, that it possesses the capacity only to illuminate Agni.
This is untenable because it contradicts the established conclusion regarding the application [of mantras] in a secondary sense.
Nor is there redundancy with the section on relative strength (*balābala*) regarding the separate example "never at any time" (*na ca kadācana*);

for while here the application to a secondary sense (*gauṇārtha*) has been established by means of the corroborating testimony of scripture (*śruti*), there the possibility of the mantra being a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to Indra by mere indicative power (*liṅga*) alone must be refuted, and thus its resolution is appropriately achieved here.
Therefore, the intention is that this very case is rightly cited as the example.
"The Gārhapatya fire," he said.
The word "in the fire" (*agnau*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) objects with the word "now" (*atha*), in order to demonstrate a contradiction based on the direct hearing of the accusative case in the term "the Gārhapatya fire" (*gārhapatyam*).
"Having stood thus."

By the word *iti*, the completion of the sentence with "one should reveal the Aindra [mantra]" is indicated. He states that the word *gārhapatya* is capable of denoting Indra as well through the etymological derivation "this belongs to the house-lord" (*gṛhapati*), by virtue of its connection with being possessed by a house-lord (*gṛhapatimattva*).
The meaning is: by virtue of being connected with the householder.

Now, one might object: "Since the meaning of the verbal root *tiṣṭhati* (to stand), which is what is expressed [by the suffix], is intransitive, how can fire be construed there as its object? To this, he says: "And just as of this... and so forth.

The meaning is that this has been explained in detail in the *Kaustubha*: since the subsequent sūtra (*akarmakācca*) prescribes the *ātmanepada* for the root *sthā* when it is intransitive, in this present sūtra one may intend the meaning expressed by *sthā* to be transitive by delimiting it with the result consisting of proximity; thus, the connection of fire as the object (*karman*) is established through proximity being related to fire by way of the relation of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā-sambandha*).

Since the second [vocative] case-ending indicates that the mantra serves the purpose of the Gārhapatya fire, its application to the primary referent (Indra) is not possible; for even in the absence of knowledge of compatibility (*yogyatā*), verbal comprehension can occur merely through the absence of a certainty regarding incompatibility, which acts as an obstacle— and thus the scriptural application (*śrauta-viniyoga*) is established— because that very [second case-ending], being a stronger indicator of intended meaning (*tātparya-grāhaka*), exists in the word "Indra" within the mantra.

Alternatively, since there is no incompatibility with the primary meaning of the verbal root—such as its similarity to being a means for the sacrifice—it is not a hindrance to resorting to a secondary (jaghanya) sense.

For it is not possible for the dative suffix (taddhita) to convey that the mantra is subordinate to Indra in the same way that the accusative case-ending conveys that the Gārhapatya fire is subordinate [to the oblation].

This is because the status of being a deity (*devatātva*), which consists in being the primary object to be conveyed by the taddhita suffix, must function as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) relative to the mantra that is to be conveyed.

Because Indra’s status as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) is not quickly perceived— absent the assumption of a reversed relationship between qualifier and qualified due to his being perceived merely as a qualifier— and because the injunction of a mantra dedicated to Indra would result in a violation of the principle of "single impulse" (*ekaprasaratā*),
and because Indra cannot logically be the object of dedication (*uddeśya*) since he has no utility in the sacrificial piling (*cayana*).

Therefore, since it is impossible for the direct hearing of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) to sublate the direct hearing of the accusative case ending, it is more reasonable that the word serves to denote the *gārhapatya* fire; with this intention, he refutes [the opponent's view] by saying "no."
Therefore, it belongs to him.
The meaning is "of the secondary derivative (taddhita)";
[this refers to] the abandonment of conventional usage (rūḍhi).

The meaning is that there is no abandonment [of the conventional sense], because the word *gārhapatya*— by virtue of the rule "in the sense of a name" (*saṃjñāyām*) following from "dhenuṣyā," and by the injunction "the suffix *ñya* is used when connected with *gṛhapati*"— is understood to be conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of the fire.

Having restated what was said—that the Gārhapatya fire is the object (*karman*) with respect to the act of standing nearby, while Indra is the object with respect to the act of addressing—he refutes that with "And not... (*na ca*).
Regarding "suchness" (tathātva): it refers to the state of being thus.

Furthermore, on this view, since the mantra would result in being a merely figurative instrument (*aupacārikakaraṇa*), and because proximity [to the Gārhapatya fire] serves the purpose of consecrating the Gārhapatya, it is impossible for the mantra to serve the purpose of denoting Indra; thus, its status as a figurative instrument by way of that [denotation] is also untenable. Alternatively, if one accepts that the mantra serves to denote Indra in order to conform to the middle-voice ending (*ātmanepada*), then because the Gārhapatya is intended as the goal due to its subsequent utility, it would follow—like the flour (*saktu*)—that it is an unintended object (*aniṣṭakarma*).

Furthermore, since there would arise a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) caused by the multiplicity of things to be enjoined, it is more appropriate to accept the words ending in the third and second case endings exactly as they are heard; then, in accordance with the indicators of the *ātmanepada* (middle voice) suffix, one should accept that the Gārhapatya fire is the object (*karman*) and the mantra is the instrument (*karaṇa*), through the very root meaning itself, characterized by a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) denoting [the action] as qualified by its own primary sense.

The meaning is as follows: although the Gārhapatya fire has no utility as an instrument (*sādhana*) [for the mantra], its existence is established by virtue of being the object of refinement (*saṃskārya*); thus, since it is logical for it to be the referent of the act of naming, one may—by conforming to that requirement—somehow assume that the word "Indra" in the mantra refers to the Gārhapatya fire. Consequently, the application (*viniyoga*) to this secondary sense is established on the strength of the direct Vedic text (*śruti*). The practical purpose (*prayojana*) is not stated here because it is obvious.
Thus ends the second section concerning how a *liṅga* (indicative power) can direct application even to a secondary meaning by virtue of the strength of the *śruti* (direct scriptural statement).
(The Section Concerning Indra)
— (B1) (The Third Section / A.3 Pāda 2 Adhikaraṇa 3) — Likewise.
In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in the Śruti: "Saying 'O preparer of the oblation, come!', he calls out three times while threshing.
In this regard, this mantra is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the act of calling;

for, according to the statement, "The wife herself, as the preparer of the oblation, rises up and, having run toward the gods, threshes," it is understood that [the mantra] is absent [when she is present].
Therefore, by virtue of the instrumental case [in "ataḥ"], it is indeed a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the threshing (*avaghāta*).
Consequently, in this sentence, there is only an injunction for threshing qualified by the threefold repetition, the masculine gender, and the mantra.
And in the sentence regarding the wife (*patnī*), there is an injunction for a separate ritual act (*karmāntara*) precisely because of the [new] quality (*guṇa*).

Regarding these two types of threshing, even though the threshing of rice is connected to the act of refinement by the injunction "one threshes the rice," there is an option between them because it serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*).
Furthermore, in the case of threshing performed by the wife, the mantra "avarakṣodiva" is used.
Therefore, by this sentence, this mantra is enjoined for threshing only in its secondary (*gauṇa*) sense.

The demonstration of its secondary (gauna) nature should be consulted in the Kaustubha. Since the word *āhvayati* signifies "he causes [someone] to call," it would follow—given that it expresses the meaning of the possible action—that it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) intended to manifest the manner of calling. However, this being the prima facie view, [the conclusion is]: since the application (*viniyoga*) is possible in the primary sense of calling itself, there is no evidence for assuming a secondary meaning for either the mantra or the word *āhvayati*.

Because the invocation is also necessarily established— just like the taking up [of the vessel]— through the construction of an injunction for application based on the wording of the mantra, as in "with the *sādhya* [mantra]," etc.; however,
the meaning of the phrase "only the wife" is not that she herself rises without being summoned,
but rather that it is the wife alone and no one else.
Therefore, even this [text] does not indicate the absence of that [primary meaning].

Consequently, since the mantra is already established for the invocation by its own indicative power (*liṅga*), and since the invocation—being for the purpose of assistance—is already established at the very time of threshing, the phrase "while threshing" (*avaghnann*) is merely a restatement (*anuvādaka*). Thus, it is either the mere triple repetition itself, or the simultaneity with the threshing qualified by the triple repetition and the masculine gender, that is enjoined with reference to the invocation; hence, there is no application (*viniyoga*) to a secondary (*gauṇa*) sense of threshing. // 3.18 //
Thus ends the third section concerning the preparer of the oblation (haviṣkṛt).
(B2) "In the case of the New and Full Moon sacrifices."

In the Siddhānta, it is stated that "in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices" in order to demonstrate the means of knowledge that establishes the general relationship [of the mantra] as a subsidiary to the summoning, based on the indicative power (*liṅga*) of the mantra: "O preparer of the oblation, come!
(*haviṣkṛdehi*).

She who prepares the oblation for the sake of the gods is the "wife" (patnī), that is, the preparer of the oblation (haviskṛt); having addressed her, the Adhvaryu says, "Come! The meaning is that the Adhvaryu, having uttered this mantra three times while performing the threshing, calls out to her.
And here, just as in the previous section according to the Śruti, the application of the mantra to a secondary (gauṇa) sense was stated.

In the same manner, since the application (viniyoga) that had been suggested there by the sentence is set aside by means of modification (ūha) and exception (apavāda), and because the connection of the subsequent section as an exception is clear, [the author] does not state it; rather, intending to explain the word "tathā" found in the subsequent sūtra which contains the reason for the previously established conclusion, he states the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa): "Therein... (tatra).

First, he demonstrates the impossibility of enjoining the mantra as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) by way of reminding one of an unenjoined invocation, since no other injunction for invocation is seen that would otherwise be established, and because the particle *eva* in another scriptural passage—“The wife herself, having become the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*), rises and, having run toward the gods, the sages, and the ancestors, threshes [the grain]”—indicates that there is no rule of mandatory invocation (as it implies she rises on her own and is not called).
This is shown in the phrase: “Of that, the wife herself... (*tasya patnyeva*).
By this, the view that—because the injunction for threefold repetition in the mantra serves as an auxiliary, it is merely a restatement of the already established time for threshing—is also refuted;

for since the mantra is not established as an auxiliary to the invocation (*āhvāna*), its occurrence there as a threefold repetition would be untenable, and it would result in the fault of indicating time (*kāla-lakṣaṇā*).

Therefore, by process of elimination, according to the rule *lakṣaṇahetvoḥ kriyāyāḥ*, since the suffix *śatṛ* is prescribed even for the sense of "cause" (which is synonymous with "instigator"), the mantra is indeed an auxiliary to the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) of threshing, just as in the case of the expression *abhicarann yajati*.

Since it is well-established that even when the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is denoted by a primary suffix (*kṛt*), there is a grammatical connection with the factors of action (*kāraka*), it follows all the more easily that a mantra—referred to by the instrumental particle *iti*—can be connected as an instrument (*karaṇa*). With this in mind, he says "Therefore" (*ataḥ*) to avoid the fault of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) that would arise if the threefold repetition and the mantra were both enjoined with reference to the threshing already obtained; he then says "And therefore" (*ataśca*) [to conclude].
Since threshing must necessarily be performed until the husks are removed, even though the injunction for a threefold repetition would otherwise be inapplicable there,
it is nonetheless possible for the masculine gender to connect with the action through the mantra, just as in other cases. Furthermore,

although a threefold repetition might be obtained in some recensions due to the recitation of a mantra containing that repetition, because it is also recorded in other recensions as being recited only once, the injunction is simply for threshing qualified by a threefold repetition as a restrictive rule (niyamavidhi).

For in this case, threshing is not obtained through the sentence concerning the wife; for if it were so, the masculine gender in the word "avaghnat" (threshing) would be untenable as a mere restatement, since the agency of the Adhvaryu priest—established by the name of the ritual (*samākhyā*)—would be sublated by the agency of the wife.
Therefore, the meaning is that there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), because [the action] is enjoined as a qualified whole.

Therefore, he states that in the sentence concerning the *patnī*, there is an injunction for a distinct threshing (*avaghāta*) due to the presence of a quality, saying: "And in the *patnī* sentence... and so forth.

And in this regard, by the sūtra on the excellence of the established conclusion stating, "There would be a contradiction of the injunction in the case of an instruction," [the author] refutes the objection that if the mantra were an auxiliary to the threshing (*avaghāta*), then another mantra such as "Protect [us] from the enemy of heaven" (*ava rakṣo divaḥ sapatnam*) would also apply;
[he does so] by specifying that it is performed by the wife (*patnīkartṛka*).

And thus, intending that the injunction is for threshing qualified by the gender of another [word] while the verbal root and the verbal suffix (ākhyātāṃśa) are restatements (anuvāda), he concludes with the words "Therefore, moreover" (ataśca).

Now, one might object: since threshing is insentient, it cannot logically possess the status of a "haviṣkṛt" (the preparer of the oblation); furthermore, because the meaning of the word "sutrāmāṇam" (well-protecting) cannot be construed with threshing, the mantra lacks the capacity to function in relation to threshing. How, then, can there be an application (viniyoga)? To this, he says: "This [application] is indeed figurative (gauṇa)."
This is the demonstration of its being secondary (gauṇatva).

Even though agency characterized by independence is impossible for an insentient object, since agency can be established through a figurative independence—as in the expression "the pot cooks"—the status of being the *haviṣkṛt* (the preparer of the oblation) is possible. Therefore, by superimposing sentience upon that very [pot], the phrase "O *haviṣkṛt*, come! (*haviṣkṛd ehi*) is justified as manifesting the act of threshing, on the basis of the meaning "become prepared," and by way of indicating the connection between the *haviṣkṛt* and the pot as the cause for the preparation of the oblation.

The meaning is that it is to be seen in the *kaustubha*. He says "and the root *ā-hvayati*" in order to dispel the suspicion that if the mantra were not an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the invocation, its connection with the word "invokes" (*āhvayati*) would be untenable.

The meaning is as follows: by deriving the *ṇic* suffix according to the traditional rule (*smṛti*) "that which one does, or that which one describes," from the sense that "the Adhvaryu priest expresses the act of calling by uttering the word 'ehi' (come) in the mantra 'haviṣkṛdehi'," the usage of the verb *āhvayati* (he calls) becomes logically established. Thus, the connection with *āhvayati* is justified because it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) that reveals the manner of the call at the time when the meaning of the root [to call] is being understood.

Since the word "vacana" (utterance) is compatible even through its connection with the primary act of calling (*āhvāna*), and because a connection with the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) of the primary object—the calling—is more worthy of preference;

since the word "thrice" cannot logically connect with the act of threshing (*avaghāta*)—which would otherwise result in the fallacy of applying it to an unmentioned recitation of mantras; since this would entail the grammatical correctness of the verbal root being subordinate to another purpose and the resulting burden of a complex injunction (*vidhi*); and since, without a specific reason, there would be the fallacy of the finite verb (*ākhyāta*) indicating a meaning such as "he explains"—there is no application of the mantra to the threshing in its secondary sense.
However, intending that it is indeed an invocation, he states the established conclusion: "It is precisely the primary one."

He dispels the doubt that, because the invocation is not prescribed, an injunction for a mantra cannot be possible as a subordinate element of it—by stating "māntravarṇika" (derived from the wording of the mantra).

Just as, even though the consumption of Soma might occur without having first taken up the Soma-vessel, the application of the mantra "I seat thee with the arms of the Aśvins" is established by postulating a restrictive injunction for the taking [of the vessel]—since its manifestation [by that mantra] would otherwise be untenable—so too here, because the invocation would otherwise be unmanifested, one must postulate a restrictive injunction for the invocation; thus, since the invocation is understood to be something to be enjoined, it is logical to enjoin the mantra as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of that invocation. This is the meaning.

By this, the claim of the *Nyāyasudhākāra*—that even though [the invocation] is eternally established, there is an injunction here for the invocation as well, in order to establish that it has the Adhvaryu as its performer, just like the *prathana* and so forth—is refuted.
This is because, when another element to be enjoined exists, it is cumbersome to enjoin an action whose performance is already possible;

furthermore, since the recitation of the mantra is performed by the Adhvaryu, the fact that the invocation also has the Adhvaryu as its performer is established by implication, as it does not require a separate effort.

However, because *prathana* (spreading) is entirely distinct from the function of the mantra, which consists in illumination (*prakāśa*), it takes the form of a separate action; thus, even though the Adhvaryu's agency is fixed by the designation *ādhvaryava* (belonging to the Adhvaryu), the restriction that the Adhvaryu must perform it as its instrument is not established.

On the other hand, since *āhvāna* (invocation) consists in the manifestation of one’s own intention conducive to the arrival of another, and since that [intention] here takes the form of the mantra’s function...

The meaning is that since it is impossible to perform [the action] apart from the one who utters the mantra, the invocation is established as being performed by that same agent—namely, the Adhvaryu—by virtue of the mantra’s being his duty; thus, because of this disparity, an injunction is not necessary even for the sake of establishing that [agency].

By the word "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "just as a wife," he dispels the suspicion that there might be an understanding of the cessation of the restriction regarding the invitation—namely, "just as a wife. This is indicated by the words "just as a wife."
Not otherwise.

By this— namely, because the wife is enjoined as the agent by another sentence, it is understood that the agency of the Adhvaryu priest, which would otherwise be established by the name (*samākhyā*), is set aside; and since the non-abandonment of the mortar and the black antelope skin is enjoined for the Adhvaryu, his agency is indicated through the metaphorical application of the term "agent" (*kartṛtva-upacāra*) even though he acts as the one who causes the wife to hold on (*anvārambhaka*).
"By way of being a companion."

The meaning is as follows: because she assists the Adhvaryu—who is exhausted by the performance of many ritual acts—by granting him intervals, she would [theoretically] attain that status even at times other than her own specific function;

nevertheless, since the invocation of her as *haviṣkṛt* (the preparer of the oblation) is understood to be for the purpose of preparing the oblation, and since that preparation begins with the threshing, she is attained specifically at the time of the threshing, and thus the statement is a mere restatement (*anuvāda*).
Even though, in the phrase "while threshing" (*avaghnann*), there occurs an indication of time (*kālalakṣaṇā*).

Nevertheless, by the rule *lakṣaṇahetvoḥ kriyāyāḥ*, the suffix *śatṛ* is understood here to have the sense of a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), as in the example "the Yavanas eat while lying down" (*śayānā bhuñjate yavanāḥ*). Consequently, since one who has attained the status of being the agent of threshing is understood to be the agent of the invocation, the invocation—performed by the Adhvaryu—is recognized as a temporal sign (*cihna*) for the present act of threshing through the medium of the subsequent grasping (*anvārambha*). Thus, at the time of threshing...
Since it means "invokes," the indication of time is not a fault; for it is sanctioned by grammatical rule as being included within the definition provided by the suffix *śatṛ*.

In reality, however, since it is impossible to be the performer of threshing merely by not relinquishing [the rice], and since resorting to that [non-relinquishment] by way of "taking hold" (anvārambha) would result in the word *avaghāta* being used figuratively (*lakṣaṇā*), this present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) is not used in a figurative sense; rather, it is used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*).
Consequently, the meaning is "he calls for the purpose of threshing," whereby the agency of threshing is co-located with the agency of calling.

The sense is that it is proper to adopt the form of being the prompter (*prayojakatva*); thus, since the invocation for the purpose of threshing is obtained at the very time of the threshing itself, there is no fault whatsoever in the meaning "he invokes while causing the threshing to be performed," even without resorting to indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

As for the attempt by the authors of the *Prakāśa* to establish that the *adhvaryu* is the performer of the threshing (*avaghāta*) on the basis of the injunction regarding the wife’s holding-on (*anvārambha*), that has been disregarded by the Venerable Teacher as improper, since no such injunction for the wife’s holding-on is seen in any *sūtra*.

But it occurs to me as follows: since the statement "striking thrice" is an explanatory restatement (*siddhānuvāda*) that permits the *adhvaryu*’s agency in the act of striking, it is logical that the second striking is performed by the wife who has been summoned while the striking itself is being carried out; thus, the particle *eva* serves merely to exclude assistance, and there is no contradiction in both acting together, which is consistent with the *Kātyāyana-sūtra*.
Even by that much, there is no impairment of the Mīmāṃsaka tenet that the mantra is not to be employed in the secondary act of threshing;

for this very reason, among the followers of Kātyāyana, the performance is observed such that the first threshing is performed by the Adhvaryu priest, while the second occurs after the invocation and is performed by the wife.
And thus, one need not resort to the assumption that the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) has the sense of indicating a characteristic (*lakṣaṇatva*) or some other meaning.

Even though the invocation for assistance during the performance of threshing serves a visible purpose—namely, to provide help in the middle of the process toward the state of being husked—it nevertheless occurs.
"Merely three repetitions."

Furthermore, by the force of the suffix *kṛtvasuc*— which signifies the counting of repetitions of an action— the word "three" is enjoined specifically with respect to the act of summoning itself. In that context, although it might be argued that the mantra should be recited three times according to the principle of the mantra for sprinkling the altar (*vediprokṣaṇa-mantra*), since the summoning does not require any effort beyond the recitation of the mantra— unlike the act of sprinkling— it follows as a matter of course that the repetition of the mantra itself constitutes the tripling.

By this, the position maintained by the author of the *Nyāyasudhā*—who, assuming a connection with the intervening element, asserts that the injunction for the threefold repetition applies to the mantra itself—is refuted;

for since the threefold repetition, although separated by words, obtains its connection with the act of summoning through the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) of the *suc*-suffix itself—just as a case-ending obtains its connection through the direct statement of the case-suffix—it is impossible for it to be connected with the mantra, even though the latter is not separated [from the suffix].

Therefore, since the act of summoning has a visible purpose, and since it would otherwise occur twice, thrice, or even four times as in common worldly practice, the meaning is that the rule of repetition three times is enjoined for the summoning by virtue of obtaining the status of a restrictive injunction (niyamavidhi) regarding the portion of the triple repetition; thus he concludes the final position with the word "iti."
And thus, since an application based on syntactical connection (*vākya*) to a secondary sense is sublated by indicative power (*liṅga*), the application is established in the primary sense alone.

However, in the case of the *aindrī* verse, because its application to a secondary sense is established through the sublation of indicative power by direct statement (*śruti*), this is the proven meaning.

As for the practical purpose: under the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), since there would be an option between the threshing performed by the wife and that performed by the Adhvaryu priest, the *haviṣkṛt* mantra—specifically the portion "drive away the Rakṣas from heaven"—would apply to the threshing performed by the wife, while [the other part] would apply to the threshing performed by the Adhvaryu.
Such is the established rule;
however, according to the Siddhānta, the mantra "ava rakṣo diva" is used for the single act of threshing performed by the wife,
while the *haviṣkṛt* mantra is used for the invocation— this being self-evident, it has not been explicitly stated.
Thus ends the third section concerning the preparer of the oblation (haviṣkṛt).
(B1) (Section 4 / [A.3 Pāda 2 Adhikaraṇa 4]) Likewise, [the result follows] from rising [from meditation].
In the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, [the Adhvaryu] says, while rising, "O Āgnīdhra, distribute the fires," and likewise, "Make the vow," with which he releases his speech.
It is heard in the Śruti: “When about to lead forth the *praṇītā* waters, he restrains his speech; he releases it at the call to the *haviṣkṛt*.
Even there, as before, the application of the mantras is to their primary meaning, and not to the secondary meanings of rising and releasing speech.
For even though the Brāhmaṇa statement is powerful, it can be justified as prescribing the time [for the action], and thus lacks the capacity to indicate a secondary sense.
Nor is there any figurative indication (lakṣaṇā);
for by accepting that the present participle suffix (śatṛ) has the sense of indication through a temporal relationship, the syntactical connection is established by direct statement (śruti) itself.
Therefore, this is indeed an injunction regarding time, meaning that the *viharaṇa* mantra should be recited at the time of rising.

In the phrase *vrataṃ vṛṇuta* ("Choose the vow"), since the particle *iti* refers merely to the form of the mantra itself, it is possible for the temporal relationship alone to appear as the mode of connection (*saṃsarga-vidhayā*); thus, there is no need for indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*). In the sentence concerning the *haviṣkṛt*, however, because the instrumental case can be justified as part of a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) by serving to provide the limit required for the silence (*vāgyama*), and because there is no evidence for a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*), one must accept that the instrumental has the sense of an "indicator of a state" (*itthambhūta-lakṣaṇa*), and that the sentence is intended to enjoin time.

And therefore, since the respective times for the release of speech are understood from the order of recitation of those two sentences at the time of reciting the respective mantras, that too is merely an injunction regarding the time [for that act]. // 4.19 //
Thus ends the fourth section on the grounds for rising from [the assembly].
(B2) "While rising."
The meaning is "rising from the place of the Bahiṣpavamāna.
The word "Soma" is mentioned to indicate the existence of a means of knowledge that establishes the general connection [of the mantra with the ritual]. [The command is] "Vihara" (Disperse).

By means of the particle *iti*, which signifies "beginning with," there is an inclusion of everything from that point up to the end: "Spread the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), prepare the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), and give us the animal victim."
The word "iti" in the phrase "vrataṃ kṛṇuteti" refers to the actual form of the mantra.

Since the term "visarga" used in the Sūtra can include other types of release—just as in the expression "he releases speech"—the mention of the *haviṣkṛt* (the preparer of the oblation) in the eleventh book of the Bhāṣya, in the section concerning the division of seeds, states: "The release of speech [should occur] with the *haviṣkṛt*; likewise it should be so in the case of the division of seeds."
And it has been stated that this is for the purpose of indicating time.

Likewise, having stated, "If it is argued that the invocation [is also included], no; because the injunction regarding time has already been enjoined," and because it was indicated there, the author provides another example here—though not cited in the commentary—which begins with the words "In the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices."
The meaning is that one releases that restrained speech at the time of reciting the mantra "O preparer of the oblation, come!

In this regard, is there an application (*viniyoga*) of these two mantras to the secondary acts of rising and releasing speech—since they are enjoined with reference to these two by the statements "rising" and "releases speech"—or is there an application of the two mantras to their primary meanings, namely the spreading of the fire and the performance of the vow, based on the indicative power (*liṅga*) of the mantras themselves? [This concerns] the rising and the mantra for the vow.

Having stated the doubt that "it is an inclusion for the sake of [specifying] time," and having indicated the thematic connection (*saṅgati*) as one of extension (*atideśikī*) because it will be discussed later, and having not explicitly mentioned the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) since it follows from the prima facie view of the preceding section and is clear, he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) in accordance with the sūtra of extension: "In that case also... (*tatrāpi*).
By the phrase "just as before," the analogical connection (*atideśikī saṅgati*) indicated by the word *tathā* in the Sūtra is shown.

In that regard, since there was a primary action in the preceding case, and since there is no evidence that such an action serves merely for the sake of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva-mātra*), the expression *avaghnann* (while threshing) is justified even without resorting to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), as it can function as a reason (*hetu*) or the like; furthermore, because there is another injunction (*vidheya*) present, the tripartite repetition (*trirabhyāsa*), despite being powerful, [is subordinated].

In the case of the Brāhmaṇa statement, since an alternative interpretation is possible, an application based on indicative mark (*liṅga*) is appropriate; however, in the present case, because there is no other thing to be enjoined, you must admit that the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) in "rising" (*uttiṣṭhan*) has an indicative sense (*lakṣaṇārthatva*). This is because, in your view, it is time alone that is the object of injunction, and thus an indicative sense would result for the injunction itself. Furthermore, by the force of the context, the act of rising is for the purpose of performing the rites prescribed for another location that is about to be undertaken.

Since one who has already accomplished his purpose cannot logically have the recitation of a mantra as his aim, it is impossible for the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) to signify causality in the form of being a cause; therefore, having no other recourse, one must accept that it signifies causality in the form of being a result.
Consequently, it is proper to regard the recitation of the mantra itself as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of rising, by virtue of its figurative capacity (*gauṇasāmarthya*).

Furthermore, since it is possible to kindle or arrange the fires without having risen, rising is the cause for the kindling and arranging of the fires and so forth; thus, because one wishes to express independence [of the action], the primary agency of that [rising] is established, and it is justified to designate it by the word "Agnīdh."

Nor is it untenable to intend [the Agnīdhra] as the agent on account of that [rising], because the rising of the Adhvaryu cannot serve as the means for the kindling of the fire and so forth performed by the Agnīdhra;

for although the status of the Adhvaryu as the agent would be set aside here in the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) by the principle "in injunctions (praiṣas), the authority belongs to another" since *vihara* is an injunction, yet in this case, because the rising— understood as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) through the form of the sentence containing the particle *iti*— is not an injunction, the agency of the Agnīdhra does not otherwise obtain.
Since there is no sublater to the fact that the *adhvaryu* alone is established as the agent by the name (*samākhyā*), [the injunction] remains valid.

For this very reason, in the case of the command "Agnīn vihara" (Bring forward the fires), because the action to be accomplished—such as the bringing forward of the fires—is not yet established, the *loṭ* suffix is accepted as having the sense of "proper time" (*prāptakālatā*). Thus, its meaning is "this is the proper time for the bringing forward of the fires," which makes the passage intelligible. However, in the sentence regarding the vow (*vratavākya*), since there is neither the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) nor the particle "iti," and since the Brāhmaṇa statement—which, though weaker than an indicative mark (*liṅga*) due to being a syntactical whole—is stronger as a direct scriptural statement—it is indeed proper that the release of speech (*vāgvisarga*) is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to that vow.

In that regard also, just as in the *bhakṣānuvāka*— where in the phrase "May Speech, being pleased, be satiated with the Soma," the agency of satiation residing in the eater is metaphorically attributed to Speech, which is the cause of satiation located in the mouth— so too, because of the similarity between the capacity to destroy (the object) residing in the denotation of the verbal root *kṛvi* (meaning "to injure") and the act of eating, there is an understanding of eating through secondary figurative usage (*gauṇī*); thus, the agency of consuming milk, barley-gruel, and so forth— which constitute the arduous practice denoted by the word *vrata*— resides in the person who is the sacrificer.
It is possible to apply [the term "speech"] metaphorically to speech that has entered the mouth for the purpose of eating;

and the plural number may also be applied with the intention of referring to the distinction between the locations such as the palate, since speech consists of sound, and sound is manifested in various places such as the palate and the back of the throat.

Furthermore, although the imperative suffix (*loṭ*) cannot have the meaning of a command because speech itself is not something to be commanded, it is accepted—just as before—that its meaning is the "proper time" (*prāptakālatā*).

He says "But not for the two secondary [meanings]" in order to refute the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) which might be suggested by the specific doubt that the application to the release of speech is indeed possible in a secondary sense, on the grounds that "the time has arrived for you to consume the vow of speech."
Regarding the word "iti": it refers to the particle *iti*.

Since that [word] is indeclinable, its case-ending is elided; therefore, its instrumental capacity is not expressed. Furthermore, if one resorts to figurative indication (lakṣaṇā), it is more appropriate to assume a figurative indication of the locative sense as delimited by a temporal relation.

Thus, it is not proper to resort to a meaning centered on a relationship between parts and whole (aṅga-aṅgibhāva) that is not required; rather, the meaning is simply that "one releases speech at the time of reciting this mantra."

By this, the argument stated in the *Nyāyasudhā*—which accepts the status of the particle *iti* as *śruti* (direct Vedic statement) and thus maintains that, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the mantra is applied to a secondary sense (*gauṇa*) by virtue of *śruti*—is refuted. [The term used there is] "the indicator of a state of being" (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇa*).

The meaning is that since the status of being made known by the recitation of the *haviṣkṛt* mantra is logically possible only in relation to the act of release (*visarga*), it is not appropriate to enjoin the mantra as an independent instrument (*karaṇa*) therein.

Furthermore, this acceptance of the term [in the sūtra] as having the sense of a "characteristic of such a state" (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇa*) is intended merely to demonstrate the validity of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) even in the absence of the word *saha*;

for in reality, since the instrumental case ending is justified precisely through its connection with the word *saha* upon hearing it, one perceives only a concomitance (*sāhitya*) consisting in simultaneity with the recitation of the mantra, and thus there is not even a suspicion of the mantra being an instrument.
The object of meditation (*dhyeya*).

Therefore, just as the time for the rising [of the sun] was determined by the sequence of the recitation of the injunctions concerning the meaning of the subsequent words (*uttarapadārtha*), so too the times for the mantra of the vow (*vrata*) and the mantra of the oblation-preparer (*haviskṛt*) are determined by the sequence of the recitation of the mantras; thus he concludes that in each case it is simply the prescription of a time not previously established, stating "therefore" (*ataśca*).

Although it is more appropriate to regard [the injunction] as a mere restatement (anuvāda)— since the release of speech follows as a matter of course from the impossibility of otherwise completing the recitation of the mantra for the invocation, which requires no separate effort beyond that recitation—

it is nevertheless necessary to regard it as an injunction regarding time in the form of a limit (avadhi). This is required to effect the cessation of speech that might otherwise persist even after that [mantra-recitation], despite the fact that there is no sublation of the vow of silence (vāgyama) in its primary aspect.

Although in the previous case there was a restatement of time (*kālānuvāda*), whereas here there is a prescription (*vidheya*), and thus the application of the principle of extension (*atideśa*) from that previous section as expressed by the word "likewise" (*tathā*) is appropriate;
nevertheless, it should be understood that this is established through the similarity that there is no application (*viniyoga*) in the secondary sense, but rather in the primary sense.
The purpose [of this discussion] is that, according to the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), the mantra for the fires (agnimantra) should be employed before rising;
likewise, the mantras for the vow (vrata) and the preparer of the oblation (haviskṛt) should also be employed before the release of speech (vāgvisarga),
because they function as instruments (karaṇatvāt).
In the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), however, the mantra for the fires at the time of rising,
or the release of speech (*vāgvisarga*) simultaneous with the recitation of the mantras for the vow-offering (*vratahaviṣkṛt*), and so forth, have not been stated because they are self-evident.
Thus ends the fourth section concerning the rising.
— — — — — — (B1) (5th Adhikaraṇa /) (A.3 Pā.2 Adhi.5) Regarding the *sūktavāka*.
In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in scripture: "One casts the prastara-bundle with the Sūktavāka.

In this regard, since the mantra denoted by the term *sūktavāka* has fulfilled its purpose by manifesting the deities who have been worshipped, and since the casting of the prastara-bundle has fulfilled its purpose as the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the prastara that has already been employed, the relationship between them is for the sake of time (*kāla*), just as in the case of the injunction: "Having sacrificed with the Darśapūrṇamāsa, one should sacrifice with Soma."

And here, the third [case-ending], being intended to indicate a particular state (*itthambhūtalakṣaṇa*), is not untenable as it conveys the connection of the *sūktavāka* with the *praharaṇa* (the throwing) by way of a temporal relationship.
Nor does this involve figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*);
for even that [indication] is permissible because it is sanctioned by grammatical rule.

Therefore, since the *sūktavāka* is recited after the *anuyāja* offerings, what is enjoined is the very act of throwing the *prastara* (grass-bundle) while qualified by that specific time, and not the status of the *sūktavāka* as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the throwing. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the reply is: because of its frequent usage and for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), the primary expressive power (*śakti*) of the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) lies in denoting the instrument (*karaṇa*), and not in denoting "characterization by such a state" (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Even though the latter is sanctioned by grammatical rule (*anuśāsanika*), it is justified as being merely figurative (*lākṣaṇika*).

And therefore, since it is understood through direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) that [the *sūktavāka*] is also subordinate to the act of throwing (*praharaṇa*), there is no contradiction in the term "throws" (*praharati*) being indicative of a *homa*—an action having a substrate—by means of postulating a deity based on the wording of the mantra.
For this very reason, the characteristic mark of a sacrifice (*yāga*), namely "the *sūktavāka* itself is the *yājyā*," is also consistent.
Even though its primary status as a *yājyā*—defined by its being the object of the consensus of experts like its status as a *mantra*—is not possible here, [it is still figuratively so].
Since the mantra cannot establish its status as a *yājyā* precisely because it is bound by the particle *eva*,
nevertheless, it possesses the character of a *yāga-liṅga* (an indicative mark of sacrifice) due to its designation as a *yājyā* on the mere basis of being a means for the sacrifice.

Consequently, even though the mantra is an auxiliary to the *praharaṇa* (the throwing) by virtue of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), there is no sublation here of its primary functional capacity.
Because that [application] is possible even in the case of the *praharaṇa* (the throwing away).
Thus ends the fifth section concerning the status of the *sūktavāka* as a subordinate element.
(B2) Regarding the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
This has been stated for the purpose of demonstrating the evidence that establishes the general connection with the mantra.
The mantra beginning with "idaṃ dyāvāpṛthivī madramabhūt" and ending with "namo devebhyaḥ" is of the nature of a *nigada*; its status as a *sūktavāka* will be made clear later.
The meaning of the sentence is that one throws the *prastara*—a handful of *darbha* grass—into the fire by means of that mantra.

In this context, having stated that secondary capacity (*gauṇasāmarthya*) functions as an applicator by being assisted by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), [the author] now demonstrates that primary capacity (*mukhyasāmarthya*) likewise possesses such assistance; furthermore, by refuting the previously mentioned connection for the sake of time (*kālārthasaṃyoga*) in this case, he avoids the lack of topical consistency (*asaṅgati*) with the preceding section of the chapter.
Thus, because the *sūktavāka* is connected as a mere indicator of time, the relationship of the Hotṛ priest with this mantra is for the purpose of indicating time.

Without explicitly stating the doubt—namely, whether "one should throw the grass-bundle (prastara) while the [Sūktavāka] is being recited" at the time of its recitation, or whether it is an auxiliary to the throwing because of its syntactical connection as an instrument of the Sūktavāka—the author states the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) itself, beginning with "In that case... (tatra).
The chosen deity.
The meaning is that Agni and the other deities are specified as the recipients in the rites at the conclusion of the *ājyabhāga* and *anūyāja* offerings. [The word] "upayuktā" means employed.

The meaning of the statement, "He places the *juhū* on the *prastara*, or rather, all the *sruks*," is that [the *prastara*] serves as a disposal (*pratipatti*) for the *prastara* already employed in holding the *sruk*.

For it is precisely the state of having fulfilled its purpose (*kṛtārthatva*), by way of eliminating further expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), that disrupts the relationship between the subordinate (*aṅga*) and the principal (*aṅgin*). Therefore, he states that very reason, as formulated in the Sūtra: "Because it has fulfilled its purpose" (*kṛtārthatvāt*).
And thus, by means of the logic of the fourth [day], he establishes the connection between time and purpose under the guise of an illustration: "by means of the New and Full Moon sacrifices."
Although in this case there is no *ktvā* suffix— as there is in the illustrative example— to indicate a relationship of time, nevertheless,
the very fact that the purpose has been accomplished (*kṛtārthatā*) serves as the reason for establishing the temporal sense according to the previously stated method;
