and the *ktvā* suffix is merely a regulator regarding the specific temporal sequence consisting of priority and posteriority, so there is no fault.

To the question, "How then is the use of the instrumental case in the sense of instrumentality justified?", he says: "And the instrumental case... The meaning is that, according to the grammatical rule "the instrumental is used in the sense of a characteristic mark of a state" (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇe tṛtīyā*), the word *sūktavāka* denotes instrumentality in the form of being a means of communication; and since that [instrumentality] is possible by bringing about its existence at that specific time, the instrumental case is justified.
He rejects the charge of metaphorical usage (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding this sense of being a characteristic mark by saying: "Nor is it thus..."

By this— namely, by the very statement of the definition consisting in being the generator of knowledge— it is refuted that Pārthasārathi and others have asserted the weakness of the *itthambhūtalakṣaṇa* (adverbial) third case relative to the case-inflection denoting a *kāraka*, on the grounds that since the action of knowing (*jñāna-kriyā*) is already included by the mention of the definition itself, a connection with an action through an unexpressed action of knowing is more remote than the instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) defined by the expressed *bhāvanā*. Thus, their position is rejected.

Nor is there any weakness in the status of being a "signifier" (*gamakatva*) due to its non-agency (*akārakatva*), because the cognition of the connection with the meaning of the verbal root depends upon agency as defined by the primary *bhāvanā*.

For even though that which is not an agent—such as a cause (*nimitta*) and so forth—is connected to the *bhāvanā* through the relation of being something to be performed, the same applies to "signifier-ness": its connection to the *bhāvanā* is established through the relation of being the object of the knowledge of the *bhāvanā* produced by itself, in accordance with the parsimony (*lāghava*) of postulating a single causal relationship. This is the intended meaning.

And thus, because the syntactical connection of the mantra here in this context is untenable— just as in the case of the previously mentioned *praiṣa* mantras— the mantra cannot be a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of that [act].

For the meaning of the mantra portion, "This oblation has been enjoyed [by Agni], it has increased, it has made [him] greater and more glorious," namely that "Agni, having increased through the consumption of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), has produced an abundance of splendor within himself, the sacrificer," is not possible in the act of hurling [the firebrand].
Because the description of [the deity] as an existing entity is untenable,
because [the rite] is accomplished [by the mere recitation], and because there is no dependence upon a deity,
he concludes the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) with the words "ataśca" (and therefore), intending that the connection is for the purpose of indicating time.

Regarding the throwing of the *prastara* (grass-bundle), since it is prescribed as a disposal (*pratipatti*) of the *prastara*—which was previously employed for the purpose of holding the ladle (*sruc*) immediately after placing the *prastara* on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*)—its timing remains undetermined because the purpose of holding the ladle has not yet been accomplished.

To indicate this lack of determined time through a negative implication (*vyatireka*), and to establish its timing through a positive determination (*anvaya*), it is stated that it occurs "after the *anūyāja* offerings.
For this very reason, it is said: "qualified by that time."

Although the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) possesses the capacity to signify the instrument even when it denotes the means of comprehension (*gamaka*), nevertheless, the expectancy for a factor of action (*kāraka*) on the part of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) is not the same as its expectancy for a means of comprehension.

Therefore, for the sake of establishing the connection of what is so expected, it is logical that there is no failure to hear the syntactic connection (*anvaya-śravaṇa*), according to the maxim: "There is no overburdening of a statement even when its purpose has already been fulfilled by [the word's] being an instrument."

Furthermore, considering that there is no evidence for postulating a power (*śakti*) even in that case, and that therefore recourse to it is improper without [the presence of] a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇā*), he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words "pracurā... (abundant...).
As for what was stated regarding the unsuitability of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) in the mental cultivation of striking—

that is, even if "he enjoyed" (*ajuṣata*) refers to the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and so forth, it means that although Agni and the others consumed the sacrificial cake and so on, Agni did not thereby become increased by an abundance of brilliance.

As for that which the sacrificer hopes for, such as long life and so forth, it is [fulfilled] by this oblation called the *prastara* (handful of grass), which is directly indicated [by the word "this"], through syntactic unity with the subsequent [text]; or else, because it is impossible to designate the *puroḍāśa* and other offerings already sacrificed by the word "this," it is logical that the direct reference is to the *prastara* itself, and thus the use of the past tense in "he has enjoyed" (*ajuṣata*)— in accordance with the grammatical rule "the past tense may be used for the future when expressing hope"— signifies the act of enjoyment.
Intending to show that [the injunction] is ineffective because it is possible to justify it as having the sense of "do," he says: "And therefore... (ataśca).
Thus, since both types of indicative marks (liṅga) are present, the word "by the Śruti" is used to indicate the superior strength of that which is assisted by direct scriptural statement (Śruti).

Now, an objection is raised: since the act of throwing (praharaṇa) is a form of disposal (pratipatti) and thus does not require a deity, and since it is impossible to reveal that act even by postulating a deity based on the wording of the mantra (māntravarṇika), how can the status of the mantra as an auxiliary (aṅga) be possible?
To this, he says: "The root *praharati*... [and so forth].

Since the mantra functions as an instrument either by manifesting the ritual action or by manifesting that which is related to it, its status as an instrument cannot be accounted for otherwise in its absence; therefore, it is necessary to postulate that the meaning of the mantra possesses the status of an auxiliary (*aṅga*). Consequently, even in the present case, in order to fulfill the status of an auxiliary understood through direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), there is a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—which does not abandon its own primary meaning—referring to the portion consisting of the renunciation of the substance preceded by the dedication to a deity, based on the connection between the substance and the deity derived from the postulation of a deity indicated by the words of the mantra (*māntravarṇika-devatā*).
The meaning is that there is no contradiction because [the action] is oriented toward the result (*phalamukha*).

Since the substance functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the act of relinquishment (*tyāga*), the term "prastaram" (the sacrificial grass bundle) takes the accusative case; this is stated to be of the nature of a "substratum-object" (*āśrayikarma*) in order to resolve the apparent inconsistency of the accusative.

Just as in the *sviṣṭakṛt* sacrifice, the portion consisting of the casting away (*prakṣepa*) serves to consecrate the substance already employed, while the portion consisting of the relinquishment serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*), so it is here as well.

The meaning is that although it has an unseen purpose (adṛṣṭārthatva) by virtue of its sacrificial portion (tyāgāṃśa), its status as a disposal (pratipatti) is established by virtue of its casting-portion (prakṣepāṃśa); thus, [the classification] is justified.

And here is the distinction: in the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, because the portion of the object of reference (*uddeśāṃśa*) included within the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) has as its object the deity Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, who is not otherwise utilized [in the primary rite], even that portion serves only as a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*).
However, by means of the portion of reference contained within its own mantra, it functions as a purificatory act (*saṃskāraka*) by way of reminding one of the intended deity.

In the present case, however, since the deities are indeed those intended [by the sacrificer] through the portion of reference included within the act of renunciation (*tyāga*)—just as by the portion of the mantra—it is exclusively a purificatory act.

Just as the authors of the *Nyāyasudhā* and others have written that the object qualified by the renunciation performed by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is not what is denoted by the root *yaji*, but rather only that which is performed by means of the mantra;
so too, after refuting that position, it will be clarified in the fourth [chapter] that it is precisely that [object] performed by the sacrificer which is denoted by it.

In this regard, since the *sūktavāka* is a *karaṇa-mantra* (an instrument mantra), and because of the rule that "the beginning of the ritual action must coincide with the end of the mantra," it follows that when the *homā* (oblation) consisting of a single *prastara* (grass-bundle) substance is performed immediately after the recitation of the *sūktavāka*,

the requirement for the specific time— namely, its immediate succession— is obtained by implication. Thus, as this is stated in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the venerable Bhaṭṭapāda, the author of the *Nyāyasudhā* [argues] that, like the *yājyā*, the *sūktavāka* is also to be employed at the time of the oblation.

The statement in the text that the praise as *yājyā* is appropriate because of its connection with the quality characterized by the relationship with the substance being offered in the state called *āhuti*,
which serves to describe the simultaneous recitation of the *sūktavāka* and the throwing of the *prastara* bundle— that is indeed incorrect.

Even if it were accepted that the deities associated with each individual sacrifice— such as those of the Āgneya and others— are likewise deities here [in the *iṣṭi-saṃstha*], leading to the consequence of their simultaneous performance through repetition (like the *jyotiṣṭoma*), such simultaneity is impossible because the renunciation of the substance (*dravya-tyāga*) for the sake of each respective deity cannot be accomplished unless the specific words denoting those deities— such as "Agni enjoys this oblation" (*agnir idaṃ haviḥ ajupata*)— are uttered. Thus, there is no possibility of performing them all at once.
For, in that case, if the final constituent word were not recited, the illumination produced by the entire *sūktavāka* would not be accomplished merely by the recitation of its individual parts.

In reality, however, when postulating the injunction of deities such as Agni and others, it is more appropriate to postulate deityhood for Agni and the rest collectively rather than individually; for even though Agni and the others are connected as deities in each individual [verse] such as the Āgneya, it is logical to postulate deityhood for them only in their combined state due to parsimony (*lāghava*). Since the purpose—namely, the manifestation of those respective deities—is accomplished by that much alone, it is not proper to postulate it for each one individually. Thus, without implying another substance called the *prastara* (grass-bundle) employed by another [injunction], [the mantra applies] to only one.

First, regarding the *prastara* (grass-bundle), since the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is established by the performance of a single act of relinquishment immediately after the recitation of the mantra—without repetition—there is no evidence for its repetition; furthermore, simultaneity is impossible according to the logical principle (*nyāya*).

For this very reason, at the very same time as the recitation of the *sūktavāka*, there is a partial offering of the *prastara* through the relinquishment [of it] with the words, "To Agni, this! (*agnaye idam*).

Since the authors of the *Prakāśa* themselves have already exerted great effort to demonstrate that even the performance of cremation has been rejected by the ritualists (*yājñika*), it will not be elaborated upon here for fear of prolixity.
Let us return to the subject at hand: "just like being a mantra."

By this, the following is indicated as refuted: [the opponent's view that] *yājyātva* (the nature of being a *yājyā*) is an indivisible property consisting in the manifestation of a deity who is a subordinate factor (*aṅga*) in the act of offering, characterized by a connection to a substance being abandoned as prescribed by the *Hotṛ-pravacana*, based on the consensus of ritual experts (*yājñika*) and the etymological derivation from its parts; for such a definition is not pervasive across all *yājyās* used in the *Mṛgāreṣṭi* performed by the *Adhvaryu* or in certain *yājyās* belonging to the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*, and there is no evidence to justify assuming a figurative sense (*gauṇatva*) for the term *yājyā* in those instances.
Now, one might object that because the word *yājyā* is employed right here, it is possible for it to be the subject of common usage; to this, he says: "because it is bound by the particle *eva*."

Since the particle *eva* cannot serve to exclude other [optional] *yājyās* due to their non-occurrence [in this context], the meaning understood is that the *sūktavāka* alone is as praiseworthy as a *yājyā*; thus, its being called a *yājyā* is merely figurative.

Furthermore, because the *nigadas* are of the nature of recited formulas (*nigada*), and because elsewhere it is stated that "the *yājyās* are indeed the *nigadas*," which prohibits them from having the status of a *yājyā*, it is impossible for this [sūktavāka] to possess the prescribed status of a *yājyā*.

For this very reason, the primary characteristics of a *yājyā*—such as those expressed in the rule "one performs the sacrifice without pausing" (*anavānam yajati*)—do not apply here. This is the intended meaning.

And thus, if the status of the *sūktavāka* as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the offering (*praharaṇa*) were understood through direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) without regard for its indicative power (*liṅga*)—which points to the purpose of manifesting the deities—and if, conversely, its status as a subordinate element of manifesting the deities were understood through indicative power without regard for its direct Vedic statement regarding the offering, then there would be a contradiction. In that case, since the indicative power would be sublated by the direct statement, the *sūktavāka* (as directed by the *śruti*) would lack the capacity for the offering in any way whatsoever; consequently, it would be impossible for the direct statement itself to function as the applicator (*viniyojaka*). Therefore, in order to accommodate both, [the text] should serve merely to proclaim the desired deities.
If one were to assume that the *sūktavāka* has already fulfilled its purpose and thus accept its connection with the *praharaṇa* (the throwing) as being for the sake of indicating the time,
this would not be the case; rather,

for the sake of conforming to the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), the *sūktavāka*— by means of the indicative power (*liṅga*) through the glorification of the deities who are subordinate to the *praharaṇa*— requires that status as a subordinate element of the *praharaṇa* which is understood from the direct statement.

And because, for the sake of accomplishing the power of the weapon, there is a requirement for the status of being subsidiary to the deity as understood through direct statement (*śruti*) and indicative mark (*liṅga*), and because the conflict between *śruti* and *liṅga* can be resolved since they serve the same purpose, one cannot—on the grounds that it would be impossible to apply it elsewhere—accept that its purpose is fulfilled merely by the recitation of the desired deity and thus conclude that it serves only to indicate the time (*kāla*). With this intention, he concludes the final position (*siddhānta*) with the words: "Therefore... (*ataśca*).
The purpose [of this discussion] is that, according to the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), only the act of striking (praharaṇa) is to be performed;

whereas, according to the established conclusion (siddhānta), the act of relinquishment (tyāga) directed toward the intended deity is also to be performed, and so forth. This has not been stated here because it is clear.
Thus ends the fifth section concerning the status of the *sūktavāka* as a subsidiary element.
— — — — — — — (B1) (6th Topic / ) (a.3 pā.2 adhi.6) Because of the teaching of the whole.

Since it is understood through direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) supported by indicative power (*liṅga*) that the *sūktavāka* is a subordinate element of the *praharaṇa* (the throwing of the wooden sword), its purpose is not merely the recollection of the deities intended for sacrifice by means of indicative power alone.
Furthermore, there is no lack of contradiction here;

for since the term *sūktavāka* is established among students as a conventional designation for the entire anuvāka, if one were to divide and assign it part by part, it would result in the fault of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding the parts, which would lead to a contradiction with the direct scriptural statement.
Nor can the term *sūktavāka* be etymologically derived (*yaugika*) as a collection of words denoting the "well-spoken" (*su-ukta*) intended deity;

for since even the recitation of a few individual words during the study of the *pārāyaṇa* and other rites would result in the fulfillment of the meaning of the term *sūktavāka*, it necessarily follows that the term must be a conventional designation (*rūḍhi*) for the entire section (*anuvāka*).
Let it be granted, then, that the manifestation of the intended deity is merely a secondary result (*ānuṣaṅgika-phala*).

However, since the *praharaṇa* (the act of throwing) is enjoined by direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), it is the motivator for the entire *anuvāka*; thus, it follows that the whole [anuvāka] should be employed at both the New Moon and Full Moon sacrifices. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: even though the *śruti* is more powerful, it cannot override the indicative power (*liṅga*). For if it did, the reference to the deity contained within the *homāntargata* (part of the oblation) would result in a merely indirect benefit (*ārādupakārakatva*). Therefore, in order to obtain a direct benefit (*sannipattyopakārakatva*) through a visible means, the *śruti* itself [must be understood as] having the purpose of manifesting the intended deity based on its indicative power (*laiṅgika*).

Therefore, because the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is more authoritative, it is accepted that the *sūktavāka*, though prompted by the act of throwing (*praharaṇa*), does not cease to function even when the throwing is absent; rather, it is accepted that its role as a prompter is restricted to the portion concerning the distribution of deities, specifically for the purpose of manifesting the intended deities through its indicative power (*liṅga*).
Nor does this result in the word *sūktavāka* being understood as a term indicating its constituent parts (*avayavalakṣaṇārtha*);

for the word *sūktavāka*—derived etymologically from "one who speaks what is well-spoken" (*suṣṭhu uktaṃ vakti*)—is both etymological (*yoga*) and conventional (*rūḍha*) in denoting a specific mantra that reveals the deities of a sacrifice.
Therefore, wherever as many deities as there may be are intended, whether archetypal (*prākṛtī*) or modified (*vaikṛtī*), there the *sūktavāka* consists of exactly that many [mantras].

Therefore, even by following the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) of the nominal stem *sūktavāka*, there is no sublation of the indicative mark (*liṅga*). Nor is it the case that, because the etymological meaning (*yoga*) is set aside in contexts such as Vedic study, one merely postulates a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*);

for in those instances, in accordance with the contemporary Vedic usage, one accepts a fixed metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) within the mantra itself, which is composed of a collection of words denoting the deities of the New and Full Moon sacrifices.

However, in the case of *aśvakarṇa* and similar words, because there is no cognition of a possible relationship [between the parts], one must postulate an additional power (śakti) by subverting the established power of the individual components; this is the distinction.
The purpose [of this discussion] is the application [of mantras] after having analyzed them. // 6 // 21 //
Thus ends the sixth section concerning the distribution of the application of the *sūktavāka*.

(B2) In the preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*), it was established that even when there is application by direct Vedic statement (*śruti*)—as in the case of the *aindrī* mantra—provided there is no conflict with indicative mark (*liṅga*), the application must be to the primary meaning;

here, however, this is challenged on the grounds that for certain words, such an application is impossible because their meanings are not "conjoined" (*asamaveta*) with the ritual act. This constitutes the immediate connection (*anantara-saṅgati*) as an objection.

Furthermore, there is a connection to the chapter (*pāda-saṅgati*) because the application to the primary meaning, which was introduced in the section concerning the general rule (*utsarga-adhikaraṇa*), is now being reaffirmed.

Likewise, when the performance of the *praharaṇa* (the offering of the grass-bundle) takes place on both the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) and the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) days, a doubt arises as to whether the entire *sūktavāka*—which contains words denoting the deities of the new moon—should be recited even on the full moon day, or whether it should be recited by omitting those words denoting the respective deities according to the specific time of the performance.

For this very reason, without stating the subject-sentence of the inquiry—which has already been cited previously—and because it is clear, [the author] states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) itself: "By direct statement" (*śrutyā*).

The meaning is as follows: since the *sūktavāka*—which has no further expectancy because its status as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the sacrifice is established by a powerful means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—cannot have its own *śruti* (direct Vedic statement) inferred through *liṅga* (indicative power) for the purpose of manifesting the intended deities, there is no conflict regarding its function as a manifestor of deities.

Consequently, due to the absence of the specific motivating factor (*prayojaka*) consisting in the manifestation of this or that particular deity, the recitation of the mantra would result in the omission of the words denoting those respective deities according to the fixed time (*kāla-vyavasthā*).

For this very reason, in the case of the mantras for the final *prayāja* and the *sviṣṭakṛt*, their application is established by extracting [the relevant parts] according to their *liṅga*, precisely by the logic of the present Siddhānta.

It should be understood that even though [the subject] is something to be established, it cannot serve as an example because a prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) based on the reason of contradiction with scripture is impossible in that case.
In reality, however, there is indeed a contradiction; thus he says: "And not... (na ca).
"But it is indeed the weapon," [he said].

The word "tu" (but) indicates that when two means of proof (*pramāṇa*) for application exist, it is appropriate to postulate a purpose only for that which is established by the stronger means of proof as the principal (*śeṣin*).

Consequently, although the manifestation of the desired deity is incidental—just like [the mention of] longevity and so forth—the *sūktavāka* is the motivator (*prayojaka*) for the throwing because of its grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the words denoting the desired deity; therefore, the meaning is that as long as that [deity] exists, the recitation of the complete *sūktavāka* remains unimpaired.

Since it is improper to assume a partial recitation— given that the mantra "yad anena haviṣā" directly indicates both the *prastara* offering and the fruits such as longevity— and since, even if the act of offering were the motivator for that portion, the manifestation of the intended deity depends upon the indicative power (*liṅga*) of the mantra, it is based on the assumption that the mantra provides direct assistance (*sannipatyopakāraka*); therefore, the application (*viniyoga*) is made by dividing [the mantra] into its respective parts.

Only the status of being a motivator (*prayojakatva*) is postulated, and not the recitation of the *sūktavāka* even in the absence of the oblation; intending this, he says "for this very reason" (*ata eva*).

For this very reason, in the *apūrva* *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) where there is no act of throwing (*praharaṇa*), the *sūktavāka* is not recited for the purpose of manifesting the deities intended for the auxiliary parts such as the *ājyabhāga* offerings—this is the sense.

By this, [the following objection is addressed]: "In the *Nyāyasudhā*, it was stated that 'in reality, because the throwing (*praharaṇa*) is taught as being subsidiary to the ritual act, and because the primacy of manifesting the *prastara* (grass-bundle) currently being performed is understood, there is no syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) even from the perspective of the meaning. If that were so, since the [sūktavāka] would have the manifestation of the *prastara* as its purport, it would follow that it is prompted by the act of throwing; and since that [act] has the manifestation of the deity as its purport—just like the *kapāla* of the sacrificial cake—it would be prompted solely by that [deity]."

Having raised the objection that [the mantra] would be useless because it is not desired in the Siddhānta due to its application to something else (*sato viniyogena*), the authors of the *Prakāśa* have refuted this by stating: "Since it is the primary factor through its role as the agent of the act of silently placing the grass-bundle (*prastara-joṣaṇa*), its purport lies solely in manifesting the intended deity who is present in the entire ritual performance.
Because it is enjoined for the act of throwing (*praharaṇa*) precisely without obstructing that [manifestation], it possesses the capacity to bring about the deity. This [position] is rejected:

Just as in the case of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), the performance of the husk-scattering (*tuṣopavāpa*) necessitates the procurement of the potsherds at a later time, so too here, to avoid that same contingency, it must necessarily follow that the *sūktavāka*—

which is prompted by the manifestation of the intended deities— is prompted by the act of throwing (*praharaṇa*). This is because, by its very nature as manifesting the substance connected with the throwing,
it inevitably results in being prompted by that throwing.

Otherwise, if one were to perform the recitation according to one's capacity, it would follow that even in the absence of the *prastara-homa*, the *sūktavāka* must be recited after the *anūyāja* offerings in order to manifest the deities intended for the sacrifice; therefore, just as the *bhedana-homa*— though not employed in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* itself— is nevertheless performed whenever there is a breaking [of the vessel] because it is prompted by that specific contingency, so too is the manifestation of the intended deities produced by certain words contained within the *sūktavāka* prompted by the act of throwing (*praharaṇa*).

Since the designation by the term *sūktavāka* is established by taking its status as an instigator (*prayojaka*), and since it is accepted that even the act of throwing (*praharaṇa*) has as its purpose only the manifestation of the intended deity, there is a mutual restriction (*anyonyaniyama*) between them.

However, in the case of the *puroḍāśakapāla* (the cake-pan), because it is impossible for it to be instigated by the taking up of the cake at the time of scattering the husks, the word *puroḍāśakapāla* is understood as a reference to something already established; thus, its status as being instigated is established even without the scattering of husks.
This constitutes an inconsistency.

Therefore, when the status of being a motivator (*prayojakatva*) for a particular part is established by another source, one does not postulate the status of being a motivator for that same part for either of the two [the other factors], due to the principle of parsimony (*gaurava*).

Consequently, there is no contradiction whatsoever in the fact that, regarding the aspect of distributive application (*vibhajya-viniyoga*), the manifestation of the desired deity is the motivator, while regarding the aspect of performance (*anuṣṭhāna*), the act of offering (*praharaṇa*) is the motivator.

This being the case, even the *Vārttika* statement— "Therefore, because it depends on the manifestation of the desired deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), the *praharaṇa* [offering] is not the motivator (*aprayojaka*)"— must be explained as intending that there is no motivatory force only with respect to the portion concerning the distributive application (*vibhajya-viniyoga*), since the reason provided therein is "because it depends on the manifestation of the desired deity. Indeed, one cannot deny the fact that the *sūktavāka* is prompted by the manifestation of the desired deity, as this is clearly understood from the word *sūktavāka* itself.
The intention is that it is authorized by scripture itself, according to the manner previously stated.

And here, having raised the objection that— even if the entire *sūktavāka* is enjoined with reference to both offerings occurring in the two usages by accepting the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) of the word *sūktavāka* on the strength of the natural sense of the sūtra, "Because there is no division of the context, the word 'entire' applies to both"—

that "the performance is established part by part for each individual offering," [the author] addresses the resolution of this contradiction with the Śruti in the passage beginning with "in the word *yājyā*..."

Because it would result in a figurative application (*lakṣaṇā*), and because it is impossible for the aggregate as a whole to be the means of accomplishing the fruit, the individual members themselves—whose unity is intended with respect to being the objects to be attained toward the fruit—are the means. However, since they are connected to the portion of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) as things to be enjoined (*uddeśya*), their unity is not intended there; thus, just as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, the throwing (*praharaṇa*) is connected to the procedure individually. Consequently, the *sūktavāka*, which is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to that [throwing], is also connected individually.

The author of the Bhāṣya refutes [the opponent's view] by stating that since each [deity] is attained through its own respective sequence (*anvaya*), and because the three [deities] share a single time, their performance would necessarily occur as a single integrated whole (*tantra*) due to the dependence on the same ritual act (*praharaṇa*); thus, a performance in parts is not established.

Furthermore, because the words denoting the deities lack mutual syntactic connection (*parasparānvaya*), they cannot convey a single unified meaning; therefore, there is not even a single *sūktavāka*, but rather many distinct *sūktavākas*, each consisting of a separate word for a deity, excluding those words common to the entire set (*tantrapada*).

And therefore, since the *sūktavāka* as divided [into parts] is an auxiliary to the *praharaṇa* (the throwing) by virtue of the third-case ending, there being no contradiction between the nominal stem and the third-case suffix, the singular number is justified as referring to the *sūktavāka* in its general sense. At that time, because the status of being a *sūktavāka* consists precisely in its containing words expressive of the deities required for that occasion, there is no risk of deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) in the performance of the *praharaṇa* when it is carried out with only that much [of the text]. Consequently, in accordance with the indicative function (*liṅga*) consisting in the manifestation of the intended deity, the words belonging to the single performance of the *praharaṇa* [are to be used].
The author of the Vārttika refuted the argument that even with a single recitation, the recitation of three *sūktavāka*s is possible, thereby resolving the contradiction.

Although individual words do not denote a single unified meaning, nevertheless, through syntactic unity in the phrase "whatever he desires by means of this oblation," they possess a single purpose and thus a single meaning.
In that case, because the manifestation of the respective deities is the sole motivator, it possesses primacy by implication (*arthataḥ*).

Nevertheless, according to the method previously stated, since the *praharaṇa* (the act of hurling) also possesses the status of a primary element (*aṅgin*), there exists primacy both verbally (*śabdataḥ*) and by implication; thus, the fact that they share a single purpose is established.

And if one were to accept that the manifestations of those various deities alone possess verbal primacy and thereby maintain that they constitute multiple sentences (*nānāvākya*), [then the following would apply].

Consequently, just as in the case of the mantra "yā te agne" and so forth, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to recite the *tantra* words separately through their repetition (*anuṣaṅga*) on all sides.

Furthermore, by the force of the singular number in "sūktavākena," there would result the application of only a single *sūktavāka* according to the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), since its application is unrestricted. This is because it is logical that the purpose of the mantra is to manifest the intended deities, thereby attaining the status of being an auxiliary that directly assists (*sannipatyopakāraka*) in that very portion [of the rite]. Moreover, there is no evidence for the recitation of three *sūktavākas*, and it is impossible for [the mantra] to have as many deities as there are principal offerings.

Therefore, just as in the case of the Vaiśvānara passage, because there is a single syntactical unity due to the identity of the opening and the conclusion, it cannot be established as a plurality of sentences; since the entire collection constitutes a *sūktavāka*, if there were a contradiction with the direct statement (*śruti*) regarding the nominal stem, it would be difficult to avoid its application part by part.
And thus: "Just as the word 'water' (*toya*) is accepted to apply both to the individual [drops] and to the collection..."
"Because it has the nature of a substance that is in contact [with others], as is the case with the term *sūktavāka*."
Having thus reflected upon the purport of the Vārttika, he resolves the contradiction with the Śruti as follows: "Of the word *sūktavāka*..."
It has been said.

The meaning is "the deity intended for the *ājyabhāga* offerings and so forth. By this, although the status of being a *sūktavāka* is possible in the mantra because it contains the word *sūktavāka*— due to its designation as "you are the *sūktavāka*" (*sūktavāg asi*) which serves to address Agni, just as in the case of "he offers the *ardhendrāṇi* [oblations]"— here, one takes the meaning revealed by the words contained within the mantra.
It is indicated that it is not proper to abandon a possible internal compound (*antaraṅga*) in favor of resorting to a non-internal compound formed by separate words (*pada-ghaṭita-yoga*);

therefore, in accordance with the purpose of manifesting the chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), when one utters only the word that manifests the chosen deity and does not utter the word denoting an undesired deity, [the desired result follows].

The meaning is as follows: since the status of being a *sūktavāka* is established through its logical impossibility [otherwise], and since that status is not lost, there is no contradiction with the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) of the word *sūktavāka*.

On the contrary, if one were to utter words concerning undesired deities that are not required, the statement "he enjoyed" (*ajuṣata*), which describes a specific form already mentioned, would become false; thus, it would result in the status of being a *duruktavākya* (a poorly spoken sentence).
Therefore... [the phrase] "by that."

Just as, for example, in the case of the mantra beginning with "This sacrificer desires that [person]," which is filled by the names of Devadatta and others mentioned in the sacred tradition (āmnāta) through the transfer of the function of the pronoun (*sarvanāma-ati-deśa*), its entirety is determined by reciting it together with the appropriate [names], so too here, by determining the entirety of the *sūktavāka* through recitation accompanied by reasoning, the meaning is that only that much of the *sūktavāka* is to be recited.
As it has been stated in the Vārttika: "Therefore, the *sūktavāka* is established as being to be understood in three ways."
Regarding the time of private recitation (*svādhyāya*) and the time of ritual action— both in the archetypal (*prakṛti*) and the modified (*vikṛti*) rites—
it is held that during private recitation, [the mantra] has all the archetypal deities as its object.
In the archetypal rite, however, for both collective groups [of mantras], the deities are extracted from their midst.
"And the word 'sūrya' (sun) and so forth is determined within the modification."
Because of the sublation by yoga.

The meaning of the objection is as follows: since there is no status as a desired object at the time of recitation and so forth, and since it lacks the nature of a mantra that reveals a deity intended as a fruit-bearing recipient, the application [of the term *sūktavāka*] is obstructed.
If, to avoid this, one were to accept its capacity based merely on formal suitability (*svarūpayogyatā*), then even words revealing undesired deities could be employed based on mere suitability;

consequently, since it is well-known that the entire *sūktavāka* is used at the time of recitation and so forth, it is necessary to assume a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*). This is the sense of the doubt raised.
"In the case of the *aśvakarṇa* tree and others."
The meaning is that it refers to words such as "aśvakarṇa" and so forth.

Therefore, since there is no contradiction with the Śruti, and considering that even the primary capacity (mukhya-sāmarthya) is fit to be a factor of application by virtue of its being that upon which [the Śruti] depends, he states the purpose: "The purpose," etc.

The meaning is that when the *praharaṇa* (the ritual act of throwing) is performed as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the primary rite (*pradhāna*) occurring at a particular time, the *sūktavāka*—which contains words denoting the deities connected to that primary rite at that specific time—must be recited after extracting those words denoting deities connected to primary rites belonging to different times.

By stating the purpose of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the purpose of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is indicated by implication: namely, that the entire [formula] serves a purpose for either the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) or the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) sacrifice.

As for the other purpose stated by the *Prakāśakāras*— that in the *pūrvapakṣa*, because the *sūktavāka* is prompted by the act of throwing (*praharaṇa*), it is not employed in cases of the loss, defect, or theft of the *prastara*; whereas in the *siddhānta*, because it is prompted by the manifestation of the deities to whom sacrifice is offered (*iṣṭadevatāprakāśana*), it is employed— that [purpose] is irrelevant, since the performance of the oblation with clarified butter (*ājya*) in the event of the loss of the *prastara* and so forth is equal in both the *pūrvapakṣa* and the *siddhānta*.

In the *Kaustubha*, it is stated that [the recitation of the *sūktavāka*] is improper because the performance [of the *prastara-homa*] is established by the existence of the *prayojaka-homa*; furthermore, even in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the performance of that [recitation] is not observed in the absence of the *prastara-homa*, since it would merely follow the requirement to manifest the intended deities during the *avabhṛtha*.

Here too, this is indicated by the very pretext of refuting the status of the manifestation of the intended deities as being the *prayojaka* for the recitation of the *sūktavāka*, even in the absence of the *homa*.
Thus ends the sixth section concerning the distribution and application of the *sūktavāka*.
— — — — — — — (B1) (7th Topic /) (A.3 Pāda 2 Adhikaraṇa 7) Indicative Mark (liṅga).

In the section on optional sacrifices (*kāmyeṣṭi-kāṇḍa*), optional sacrifices dedicated to deities such as Indra and Agni are recorded; in that very same order, in the section on mantras (*mantra-kāṇḍa*), the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* mantras bearing the respective indicative marks (*liṅga*) are recorded under the heading "the section of optional *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* mantras.
By virtue of those indicative marks, they are subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) to any ritual action dedicated to deities such as Indra and Agni.
However, it is not a subsidiary element of all optional sacrifices (kāmyeṣṭi) merely in accordance with the weaker evidence of the name (samākhyā).
Nor is there an impossibility of application by means of indicative power (liṅga) alone in the absence of a means of knowledge that establishes a general connection;

for even in the absence of such a means of knowledge, the application of a mantra to the manifestation of deities such as Indra and Agni is established by its indicative power aided by the mantra’s own requirement for a purpose.

Nor should it be argued that, because [the mention of] the essential nature of Indra and Agni would be purposeless, sequence and other factors are required for the purpose of indicating their status as means to the *apūrva*;
for the indication is appropriate since deities such as Indra and Agni are never dissociated from the sacrifice, just like the *juhū* ladle.

Or, even if there were such dissociation, since worldly fire and so forth would be excluded by virtue of being useless, the status of being for the sake of the *apūrva* is established by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*).

Therefore, since the *liṅga* (indicative power) alone sublates both *krama* (order) and *samākhyā* (name), it follows that [the mantra] serves all purposes. To this we reply: since the capacity (*yogyatā*) consisting of *liṅga* cannot function as an applicator in the absence of an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), and since there is no such expectancy for a purpose within the mantras—because all mantras have their expectancy satisfied by being applied in the *Vācastoma* sacrifice—it is not possible to establish that [the mantra] serves all purposes based on *liṅga* alone.

Therefore, when the connection with various sacrifices is understood through the sentence, context, and other means that establish a general relationship by giving rise to the respective requirements (*ākāṅkṣā*), it is only the specific means (*dvāra*) that is understood from the indicative power (*liṅga*).
Nor is there a sublation of context and the like by the sentence concerning the *vācastoma*;

for those [means] which pertain to specific mantras cannot be sublated by that sentence—which is not present at the time when the requirement for the purpose of the mantra arises during the recitation of the mantra collection.

Nor does it follow that, even when something has been enjoined by a stronger means of proof, it could subsequently be enjoined by a weaker one—such that the *pūṣānumantraṇa* mantra, though elevated [to a primary role], would have to be applied in a secondary sense (*gauṇa*) by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*).

This is because both means of proof share the same object, and at the time the mantra’s purpose is required, the stronger means of proof is already present, making its sublation (by the weaker) logically impossible.

Therefore, since sublation is precluded in the present case, the mantras must relate exclusively to the optional sacrifices (*kāmyeṣṭi*), in accordance with their position in the sequence (*krama*) and their name (*samākhyā*).
Nor is there anything else that gives rise to expectancy;
for there is no evidence that the invariable connection with the sacrifice and so forth can give rise to expectancy.
In fact, even such invariability does not exist here.

For in the case of the *juhū* (sacrificial ladle) and other such items, their causality does not exist elsewhere in reality; thus, it is appropriate that they have an inseparable connection with the sacrifice (*kratu*).

However, in the case of words such as "Agni" which denote a deity, since they possess causality toward the communication of their own meaning just as they do toward the sacrifice—by virtue of being specific sequences of phonemes—they do not have an inseparable connection with the sacrifice. This is the point of distinction.

And therefore, because of this deviation (*vyabhicāra*), or even in cases where there is no deviation, because it is impossible for [the word] to give rise to an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), there is no application (*viniyoga*) elsewhere. For this very reason, wherever natural expectancy does not cease— as in the case of the knowledge of the meaning or the knowledge of the Self produced by the Upaniṣads— there, since there is no purpose in giving rise to expectancy, the application occurs through the indicative power (*liṅga*) alone, even without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes a general relationship.

In the present case, however, there is a difference: since the natural expectancy has already been satisfied, there is a dependence on a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that establishes a general connection which then arouses the expectancy.
Nor is the *samākhyā* (name) redundant because it would be established by strong *krama* alone;

for instance, where two *āgneya* mantras are recited in the sequence of a ritual dedicated to Agni—just as in the case of the number seventeen (*sāptadaśya*)—the application to the *sāmidhenī* verses would initially follow from *krama*, as there is no reason to bypass the first mantra and because it does not contradict the sequence. However, [the name prevails].
By virtue of its designation (*samākhyā*), [the mantra] is assigned to the function of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā*;
however, in the case of the *sāmidhenīs*, there is the introduction of other [mantras].
Nor is the presentation of the sequence thus rendered useless.

In a case where, after the recitation of the *yājyā* verses for a preceding sacrifice dedicated to another deity, *ṛc*-verses addressed to Agni are recited prior to the *yājyā* verses of the subsequent sacrifice, it is impossible to employ those verses— despite their possessing the appropriate indicative marks (*liṅga*)— in the function of a *yājyā*. Therefore, even though the conventional designation (*samākhyā*) is set aside, they are assigned to the function of the *sāmidhenī* verses of the subsequent sacrifice solely on the basis of their position (*krama*), because they are recited in the very place where those *sāmidhenīs* belong.
Therefore, it is established that the application [of the mantra] is specifically to the optional sacrifices (kāmyeṣṭi). // 7 // 22 // //
Thus ends the seventh section concerning the relative strength of indicative mark, order, and name.
(B2) These are the sacrifices performed for the fulfillment of specific desires.

The meaning is that these [rites] are prescribed by such scriptural statements as: "One whose kinsmen (*sajātāḥ*) have departed should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni," and "One desiring luster should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara.
The word *vīyuḥ* means that the kinsmen (*jñātayaḥ*), being of one mind, should become estranged or divided.
They possess those very characteristics.
The meaning is that those [mantras] which have the same characteristic as those found in the *iṣṭis*— namely, the words denoting deities such as Indra and Agni—
are the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* mantras.
The meaning is that [the verses] beginning with "indrāgnī rocanā divaḥ" and so forth [are intended].
The terms "order" (*krama*) and "name" (*samākhyā*) are employed here to establish the fixed arrangement that will be explained later.

In this regard, since the application by indicative mark (*liṅga*) is being investigated, there is a connection both to the [preceding] section (*pāda*) and the [preceding] chapter (*adhyāya*). For, while it was stated previously that direct assertion (*śruti*) depends upon indicative mark, the present discussion—by demonstrating that indicative mark itself depends on other means of proof—establishes both a contextual connection (*prāsaṅgika*) and an immediate sequence of topics (*anantara-saṅgati*).

Likewise, without stating the doubt— namely, whether these [mantras] are subsidiary only to the permanent and optional rites dedicated to the deities Indra and Agni on the basis of their indicative mark (*liṅga*), or whether they are subsidiary only to the previously mentioned optional sacrifices (*kāmyeṣṭi*) on the basis of both order (*krama*) and name (*samākhyā*)— he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the word "likewise" (*tathā*).

Since the collection of mantras taught by the injunction for private recitation (*svādhyāya-vidhi*) possesses a requirement for a purpose, it is established— by means of the indicative power (*liṅga*) in the form of semantic fitness, assisted by that requirement— that the mantra serves the purpose of manifesting Indra and Agni; because this indicative power does not depend on any means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to establish a general connection,
a fixed determination [of application] is achieved through order (*krama*) and name (*samākhyā*).
There is no restrictive rule that the *liṅga* (indicative power) can only function as an applicator once a general connection with a sacrifice has been understood through a specific means;

for, just like *śruti*, the application is possible through *liṅga* alone when aided by expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), even if a prior connection with a sacrifice has not been understood—this is the meaning.

Since the status of being a deity (*devatātva*) is defined solely in relation to a sacrifice and is non-worldly (*alaukika*) because it consists of being enjoined, he establishes its invariable connection with a sacrifice [with the words]: "Indra, Agni, etc. (*indrāgnyādīti*).

Although divinity is non-worldly (*alaukika*), it is not manifested in that form within the mantra; furthermore, since Indra, Agni, and others—who are merely substrates—are presented in the mantras, explanatory passages (*arthavādas*), and so forth as residing in the heavenly world and the like without performing sacrifices, they are understood to be worldly (*laukika*).
With this in mind, [the author] says: "Or, even if there is deviation (*vyabhicāritva*)."

By the phrase "also because there is a lack of evidence for Indra and others residing in heaven and so forth," it is indicated that since the *mantras* and *arthavādas* have other purposes, they do not serve as proof for such a residence.
This follows by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*).

The meaning is that, since the status of a deity is understood from words such as "Indra" through a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) precisely by virtue of its non-deviation from the sacrifice, there arises an understanding of its being a means to the *apūrva* (the transcendental result) through the presentation of the sacrifice itself by way of a reminder.

Having thus indicated that the argument previously advanced by the ancients— that the *liṅga* (indicative power) depends on a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that establishes a general connection in order to bring about the presentation of something as a means to an unprecedented result (*apūrvasādhana*)— is futile, [the author] states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), demonstrating his own view that it depends on such a means because mantras arouse expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*): "In the absence of expectancy."

The meaning is that even for a person who is capable of carrying [a load], if there is an absence of expectancy (*nairākāṅkṣya*), no application to the act of carrying is observed; thus, mere capability is insufficient to effect an application when expectancy is lacking.
The term "Vācastoma" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the Brahmayajña and other such rites.
[The phrase] "by means of sentence, context, and so forth" refers to syntactical connection (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), and the rest.

In this regard, the distinction is as follows: for the mantras beginning with *vaṣaṭkāra*, the sentence "This indeed is the seventeenfold" [serves as the context]; for the mantras of cutting, it is the *prakaraṇa* (context); in the present case, both *krama* (order) and *samākhyā* (name) apply; and in the case of the *pūṣānumantraṇa* and similar rites, there is merely *samākhyā*.
This very point constitutes the fact that *liṅga* (indicative power) is dependent upon other means of proof (*pramāṇa*) that establish a general connection.
The meaning is that, because the scripture itself is what gives rise to that [cognition], it does not depend on anything else;
this refers to the specific mantra.

The inclusion of the word "particular" (*viśeṣa*) is for the purpose of indicating that [the particular] possesses the power to subvert [the general] by way of the principle of the relationship between the general and the particular;
[this is expressed by the phrase] "by the weak one."
The phrase "by raising an expectation" is to be understood as the ellipsis;
[the reference is] "to the two means of valid cognition."

The meaning is as follows: at the time when the mantra requires its purpose, the sentence that enjoins the *vācastoma* is not present; therefore, there is simply a sublation [of the mantra by the injunction], but it does not mean that the two weaker [means of knowledge] are sublated by it.

In this case, since two means of knowledge are simultaneously present, the stronger merely sublates the weaker; thus, there is no possibility of the stronger giving rise to the expectation for the weaker—this is the distinction.
And not elsewhere.
The meaning is: those rites other than the optional sacrifices (kāmyeṣṭi) that follow in sequence.
Because there is a lack of valid means of cognition (pramāṇa).

Regarding the recitation in a specific context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth, even if an expectation arises—namely, "How can I [the mantra recited in this context] assist this [ritual]"—there is no evidence for its capacity to generate expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). This is because, although that [expectation] might invalidate the lack of necessity due to its being of the nature of a pervasion (*vyāpti*) with an invariably connected ritual, it does not actually produce expectancy. For instance, when an inference regarding fire has already occurred for one who is free from expectancy concerning fire, expectancy regarding that same object does not arise merely through the presence of pervasion.
The meaning is that, for this reason, it is impossible for that [the sacrifice] to produce an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*).

This is because its nature—consisting in an invariable connection with the ritual—is otherwise difficult to establish; and even though a property delimited by the factor that delimits the status of being a means (as determined solely by the *apūrva*) must necessarily be defined here as having the form of an invariable connection with the *apūrva*, such a thing is impossible in this context. Thus he says: "But in reality... (*vastutastu*).
"Also with respect to the communication of its own meaning."
If that [word] were not a cause with respect to that [object], then, due to the absence of the capacity to convey meaning, the designation of "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*) would be untenable.
Even if the word *juhū* (ladle) is a cause in that regard, there is a disparity because it is necessarily a cause only for an object qualified by a specific form with respect to the sacrifice.

Therefore, since there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for postulating that the meaning here is a means to the *apūrva*, the word cannot be non-deviant from the *apūrva* even through that [meaning]. This is the sense.
"Natural."
The meaning is that for that which is inherently expectant [of completion], there is no dependence on a means of valid cognition to arouse that expectancy.
"Upaniṣad," it is said.

And here—[there is] one knowledge of the eternal Self as a transmigrating agent and enjoyer, which is free from connection with the body and its modifications consisting of merit and demerit (dharma-adharma) denoted by the word *mātrā*, and which arises from the Upaniṣadic passage: “Verily, this Self is indestructible, O beloved, its nature is not subject to annihilation; however, it has contact with the *mātrās*.
Likewise [there is the knowledge arising from]: “He is free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true, whose resolves are true.”

The second [type of knowledge] is the knowledge of the Self characterized by qualities such as being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*), which consists of an inquiry (*jijñāsā*)— defined as the ascertainment of the Vedāntic texts— as enjoined by the scriptural statement, "He is to be sought, He is to be desired to be known" (*so 'nveṣṭavyaḥ sa vijijñāsitavyaḥ*); this inquiry takes the form of reflecting upon the nature of the Self as ascertained therein, and its accomplishment depends solely upon mere resolve (*saṃkalpa*), without requiring effort for the attainment of desired fruits or freedom from defects such as sins incurred through the violation of Upaniṣadic injunctions.

Likewise, although self-knowledge is threefold— consisting of that which is enjoined by injunctions such as "one should meditate upon the Self" and so forth, which concerns the attributeless (nirguṇa) Self and culminates in immediate, direct realization (aparokṣa-sākṣātkāra)— nevertheless, since the second and third types of self-knowledge, being of the nature of meditation (upāsanā), lack any visible purpose either in the ritual action or in the person, and since their status as auxiliary elements of a sacrifice (kratvaṅgatva) is untenable due to the absence of scriptural evidence (śruti) and the like for their dependence on an unseen result (adṛṣṭa), [the text says]: "He attains all worlds and he attains all desires."

In the section on Grammar (*Vyākaraṇādhikaraṇa*), the Teacher [Bhāṣyakāra] established that the fruit of the second knowledge of the Self is that which is presented by the supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*) beginning with "He who knows the Self overcomes grief," and likewise, the fruit of the third knowledge of the Self is that which is presented by the supplementary passage beginning with "Verily, he who conducts himself thus until the end of his life reaches the world of Brahman and does not return again," both of which constitute the human goal (*puruṣārtha*).
In this context, self-knowledge must be understood as the primary thing to be grasped at the very outset.
Its status as an auxiliary to the ritual sacrifice follows from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) alone.
Even though a fruit offered by a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) might be possible here as well, [the former remains the primary basis].

Nevertheless, because it is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) according to the principle of the "leaf-made ladle" (*parṇamayīnyāya*), the meaning is that it possesses only the status of an auxiliary (*aṅga*).
This is what is meant by "application" (*viniyoga*).

Furthermore, while the knowledge of the ritual meaning (*arthajñāna*) possesses direct efficacy toward the rituals because it does not depend on an intermediate factor that might deviate, and thus its application to the ritual is possible through the mere indicative mark (*liṅga*) alone; the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*), by contrast, lacks direct efficacy toward the rituals because it does not have the ritual as its object. Since the nature of the knowable Self is common to both worldly and Vedic contexts, it lacks the necessary non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) from the sacrifice. Therefore, how could [the Self] be applied [to the ritual] through that alone?
It should not be said that [the knowledge of the Self] is a constituent part (*aṅga*) of ritual action (*kratvaṅgatva*);

for the engagement in worldly actions is established even without the knowledge of a self distinct from the body and so forth. Therefore, to exclude that [worldly activity], there is no requirement for an invariably concomitant means (*avyabhicaritadvāra*).
Since only those actions which are the means to achieve results in the next world are required, such [knowledge] is established by its mere capacity (*sāmarthya*) alone—this is the meaning.
This will be established in detail in the fourth section concerning the Viśvajit sacrifice.

And here, just as the knowledge of the Self (ātmajñāna) is a subsidiary part of ritual action (*karmāṅga*) by virtue of its utility for the performance of the rites to be carried out, so too it is not a subsidiary part of prohibited actions;
for if that were the case, the commission of the murder of a Brahmin by one who lacks knowledge of the Self would not result in the production of sin (*pratyavāya*).
Rather, it is precisely its status as an auxiliary to cessation (nivṛtti), which is the fruit thereof.
As it is stated in the Vārttika: "For the knowledge of the Self is understood to serve both the purpose of the ritual and the purpose of the person, due to its connection with each separately;
because without that [knowledge], engagement in or withdrawal from rituals whose fruits pertain to the next world would be impossible."
Thus it is said.

However, this much is the distinction: since cessation in the form of the observance of prohibitions does not produce an *apūrva* (unseen merit), the knowledge of the Self characterized by its eternality and so forth has utility in that context only as being useful for its own sake (*svarūpa-upayogitayā*), because the *apūrva* generated by the restrictive rules (*niyama*) of the Upaniṣads is of no use there;
thus, the restrictive rules of the Upaniṣads are not required.
However, it should be understood that this [requirement] also applies to enjoined actions (*vihitakarman*).

Alternatively, just as the rule for studying the prohibitions (*niṣedhādhyayananiyama*), though not directly applicable to the prohibited acts themselves, is nevertheless applicable to the expiations (*prāyaścitta*) by way of determining the occasion (*nimitta*), so too the rule for the aforementioned knowledge of the Self (*uktātmajñānaniyama*), though not applicable to the prohibited acts, is to be seen as applicable to the expiations by accomplishing a cessation (*nivṛtti*) caused by remorse (*anutāpa*), which serves as the basis for the qualification (*adhikāra*) for expiation.
And since the indicative mark (*liṅga*) alone cannot be a means of application anywhere without a means of knowledge that establishes a general connection,

[the application of the two mantras] occurs by setting aside the context (*prakaraṇa*), even from the two sentences read in the section on the meditation on the *udgītha* in the *Chāndogya*: "Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*), that alone becomes more powerful," and "One should meditate on the *udgītha* as 'Om'."

This was stated with the intention of refuting the objection formulated by Pārthasārathi— that although the author of the *Nyāyasudhā* maintains that being an auxiliary to a sacrifice (*kratvaṅgatva*) does not follow from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) alone, it is nonetheless untenable because it is impossible for this [mantra] to be an auxiliary to all sacrifices due to the sublation of its context (*prakaraṇa*) by these two sentences.

Since the authors of the *Prakāśa* themselves have exerted great effort in both presenting the view of the *Nyāyasudhā* author and in presenting the refutation thereof, it is not elaborated upon here.

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), however, if one were to assume an injunction for that which is already eternally attained—as in the case of agriculture and the like—there would be no basis for its being an object of injunction due to the absence of authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, even if there were a cognition of mere production, it would be impossible for it to be a subordinate element (*aṅga*). Therefore, it is to be understood that the venerable teacher [Bhaṭṭa] has stated in the *Kaustubha* that these two sentences alone, beginning with "Whatever [one does]," must be accepted as conveying the status of being a subordinate element.
Therefore, by assuming that the form *karoti* is in the *leṭ* (subjunctive) mood, it should be understood that the view stated in the *Nyāyasudhā* is somehow correct.
"The designation would be meaningless."
The meaning is that the designation "Section on the Yājyā and Anuvākyā Verses" would be rendered purposeless, and its inclusion in the Sūtra would likewise be useless;
[this is illustrated] by the case of the seventeen-fold nature (sāptadaśya).

In that ritual action which has Agni as its deity and takes the form of the *pāthikṛtī* sacrifice, the *sāptadaśya* (the quality of being seventeen) that is an auxiliary of the *sāmidhenī* verses is obtained through the extension (*atideśa*) of mantras; thus, there is no requirement for a *yājyā* verse in the primary sacrifice itself,
because of the scriptural injunction (*vācanika*) prescribing *sāptadaśya*,
and because there is a requirement for two *ṛc* verses addressed to Agni among the *sāmidhenīs*.

In that context, since there is no reason to bypass the first [mantra] of the two Āgneya mantras prescribed in their respective specific sequences, and since they would otherwise have to be inserted among the *sāmidhenīs* without violating the order, it follows that their insertion must occur in the function of the *yājyā*; therefore, the necessity of that [insertion] is established by the very name (*samākhyā*) itself— this is the meaning.
Therefore, in such a case, it is the principle of supplying what is required (*apekṣitavidhāna*) alone that is sublated by the name (*samākhyā*),
and not the sequence (*krama*) which undergoes any restriction.
Regarding the *sāmidhenī* verses, he states the introduction of two others: "In the *sāmidhenīs*," etc.

In that case, since the desired result is established by the designation (samākhyā) itself—namely, "the section of Yājyā-Anuvākyās for optional sacrifices" (kāmyayājyānuvākyākāṇḍa)—one might suspect the introduction of the order (krama) to be redundant; anticipating this, he refutes it with the words: "And it is not so."
"In which [place]" means:

Having recited the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses dedicated to those respective deities in the sequence of the *Agnivāruṇī-īṣṭi*, because of the recitation of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses dedicated to those same deities as they are handed down in the sequence of the *Somāraudrī-īṣṭi*, the *Ṛgvedic* verses addressed to Agni (*āgneyyaḥ*) and the *Pṛthupājavatī* verses are also transmitted therein.

Since their application there is precluded by other mantras whose application is determined by *liṅga* (indicative power), it is untenable for them to be applied to the function of the *yājyā* of the subsequent sacrifice merely on the basis of *samākhyā* (name/designation). Thus, when there arises the possibility of their application elsewhere through *samākhyā* aided by *liṅga*, that [possibility] is set aside by *krama* (sequence).
The meaning is that the sequential mention [of the verses] is for the purpose of securing their placement as the *sāmidhenī* verses of the *uttareṣṭi*.
Now, one might object that the sequence is common even to the first sacrifice; therefore, he says: "That [sequence] belongs to the *sāmidhenī* verses."

The meaning is that because the position of the *sāmidhenī* verses of the preceding sacrifice is interrupted by the recitation of its own *yājyā* and other formulas, they are recited precisely in the position of the *sāmidhenī* verses of the subsequent sacrifice.
He concludes the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) with the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*).

The purpose [of this discussion] has not been stated because it is clear from the presentation of the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) and final (*uttarapakṣa*) positions; likewise, it has not been stated due to the purpose of the prima facie and final positions of the tenth book’s section on the *manotā* mantra, namely that "there is no modification because of the specific scriptural statement" (*manotāyāṃ tu vacanād avikāraḥ*).

Thus ends the seventh section concerning the dependence on the means of knowledge that establish the connection through general indicative marks (*liṅga*), order (*krama*), and name (*samākhyāna*). (The Section on Indicative Marks, Order, and Names).
— — — — — — — (B1) (8th Adhikaraṇa /) (a.3 pā.2 adhi.8) Regarding the governing rule (adhikāra).

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, regarding the injunction "one worships the Āgnīdhra with an *āgneyī* [verse]," there arises a deliberation: is every Ṛg-verse in general, regardless of its context, a subsidiary (*aṅga*) for the worship of the Āgnīdhra, or are only those verses from the present context that have already been employed in the Stotra and other rites? In this inquiry, since the term *āgneyī* applies without distinction to all such verses, it is untenable for the context (*prakaraṇa*) to restrict its scope; therefore, by means of a subsequent restrictive injunction (*viśeṣaṇa-vidhi*) following the qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭa-vidhi*), it pertains to every Ṛg-verse addressed to Agni as its deity.
The injunction is for the purpose of serving as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) for the *upasthāna* (worship) of the Āgnīdhra fire-altar;

however, the verse addressed to Agni (*āgneyī*) is not the intended object (*uddeśya*) here, such that— out of fear of its becoming purposeless— it would be restricted by the context (*prakaraṇa*), as is the case with the *vrīhi* grain.
Because it is understood as something to be adopted by means of the third [case-ending].

And where there is a suspicion of futility regarding the essential nature of the *upasthāna* (attendance), even if it enters into the context (*prakaraṇa*), the word *āgneyī* does not result in referring to the subject at hand (*prakṛta*).
Nor can the word *āgneyī*—whether by virtue of being etymological (*yaugika*) or being a derivative suffix (*taddhita*)—be taken as referring to what is proximate;
for there is no evidence that etymological words denote proximity, since they signify merely the individual entity qualified by the meanings of its constituent parts.

Furthermore, even if the derivative suffix were to denote proximity, the verses in question, though belonging to the same context (*prakaraṇa*), do not possess proximity because they are situated in different locations.
Or, even if it were the case that only those [priests] mentioned in the immediate context are grasped by the secondary derivative (taddhita),

nevertheless, in cases where the secondary derivative is not heard— such as in the case of the consumption of the *brahmaudana* or in the injunction "one should feed four Brahmins"— there is no means of proof for grasping the priests mentioned in the primary context (*prakṛta*).

Nor should it be argued that there is a restriction to the *prakṛta* (original) mantras because their status as means to the *apūrva* (transcendental result) is already established, and thus there is simplicity (*lāghava*) in establishing a connection with the *agnīdhropasthāna* (the attendance upon the Agnīdhra priest) merely as a subordinate means (*dvāra*), whereas for the *aprakṛta* (non-original) mantras, there would be the fault of complexity (*gaurava*) in establishing both [the connection to the *apūrva* and the connection to the *upasthāna*]. For even if the *prakṛta* mantras were accepted, if the mere form of the *upasthāna* were the subordinate means, then there would be no occurrence of *ūha* (modification), etc., in that which takes over its function; therefore, the definition of being a means to the *apūrva* is necessarily required.
For even in the case of the subject matter at hand, there is no cognition of a novel meaning (*apūrvārthatva*) through the assumption of a separate sentence based on the context (*prakaraṇa*);
because if that were the case, while the rice-grains (*vrīhi*) would attain the status of being the means (*dvāra*) by their own nature, that status would not apply to the barley-grains (*yava*).
Therefore, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), the object of reference (*uddeśyatā*) is precisely as the stotra that serves as a means to the *apūrva*.
And because, by that much alone, one does not obtain the status of being a means for the *apūrva* (transcendental result) of the attendance (*upasthāna*),
there is indeed a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of "being a means for the *apūrva*" even when the rule is understood as referring to the subject matter at hand (*prakṛta*).

Furthermore, even if the status of being a means for the *apūrva* of the *stotra* is assumed, the subject matters at hand do not thereby acquire the status of being a means for the *jyotiṣṭoma-āpūrva* produced by the attendance.

Therefore, it follows that all [mantras] are to be taken, or rather only those not mentioned in the context (aprakṛta), because they require a purpose to be fulfilled; such being the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), [the siddhāntin replies]: if the non-contextual ones were taken, it would be impossible otherwise for them to serve the purpose of attending upon [the deities] as means to the transcendental result (apūrva).

Since it would follow that the status of having an unseen result (*apūrvārthatva*) must also be postulated— as it is for the *vrīhi* grains and so forth— and since the status of having an unseen result is already established for the primary elements when there is an injunction teaching their connection to another function, the restriction to the primary elements is adopted by one who relies on parsimony (*lāghava*). Furthermore, even though the primary *Āgneyī* verses might not be connected to the unseen result of the Jyotiṣṭoma through the medium of the stotra— following the logic of the restriction of speech (*vāṅniyamanyāya*)— such a connection is possible through the medium of another function.

Even though the Āgneyī verses are employed at the beginning of the stotra, their connection with that specific apūrva is understood precisely because they are recited separately within the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
This very principle is the one that determines the status of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) in the consumption of the *brahmaudana*.
However, this does not imply that the same restrictive rule would apply to the statement, "He gives gold to the descendant of Atri."
Because being an Ātreya is not invariably established among the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*),

for this very reason, in cases such as "one should praise while placing the fire nearby," since the connection with the *apūrva* (transcendental result) of the hymn to be inferred is not established in the *āhavanīya* fire and so forth, there is no rule for that; rather, it will be stated that, in the absence of a specific scriptural injunction, because it is impossible to exist outside its proper locus, it must be the worldly [fire] itself.
Therefore, it is established that, in accordance with the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*), only that which is under discussion (*prakṛta*) is to be understood. // 8 // 23 //
Thus ends the eighth section concerning the rules established in the Agneyī [chapter].
(B2) [The sacrifice] called Jyotiṣṭoma.
The term "Jyotiṣṭoma" is mentioned to indicate the means of knowledge that establishes the general relationship;
[the term] "Āgneyī" [is used for the specific instance].
The meaning of the statement "he worships the Āgnīdhra shed with a verse addressed to Agni" is as follows;
and this also serves as an illustration for the two sentences, "the Sadas with one addressed to Indra" and "the Havirdhāna with one addressed to Viṣṇu.
Although in these cases the application [of the verses] is determined by direct Vedic revelation (śruti);

Nevertheless, since the previous section (adhikaraṇa) considered application (*viniyoga*) by means of indicative mark (*liṅga*), which depends on a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that establishes a general connection, it follows by implication (*prasaṅga*) that verbal testimony (*śruti*)— which has arisen [in this context]— is also declared to be an applicator because it likewise depends on that [general connection]. Thus, having acknowledged the incidental connection to the chapter (*pāda-saṅgati*), and without explicitly mentioning the immediate connection for its obviousness, [the author] addresses the category of those who grasp only what is not the subject at hand (*aprakṛta-mātra-grahaṇa-koṭi*).
In order to refute what has been stated by some through delusion, he shows the doubt that must necessarily be addressed with the word "kim" (what?).

For the position that one may take only what is not already prescribed would be possible only if it were impossible to take what is prescribed— either because those items have lost their freshness (*yātayāmatva*) or because they have already been employed elsewhere;
however, neither of these two conditions exists here,
since the statement "the *kuśa* grasses, the ladles, and so forth" records that there is no fault [in using them].
Furthermore, because there is the possibility of a double application (viniyukta-viniyoga), as in the case of the sacrificial cake's potsherds (*puroḍāśa-kapāla*),
the position that accepts only what is relevant to the context (*prakṛta*) is shown to be untenable by the statement regarding its applicability to both the relevant and the irrelevant.
"Those very ones."
