Although, because the *āgneyī* verses are to be taken up as a whole, there is no possibility of multiple verses being used due to the intention to express the singular number inherent in them; nevertheless, the plural "those" (*tāḥ*) is to be understood either by taking into account the plurality of *āgneyī* verses present in the context, or by intending other Ṛks such as the *aindrī* and *vaiṣṇavī*.
Thus, the meaning is: "only those which are recited in the context and specifically employed in other hymns, such as 'O Agni, come for the feast' (*agna āyāhi vītaye*) and so forth."
He states the reasoning for the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) with the words: "of the word *āgneyī*."

Regarding the third [alternative], although there is no contradiction in taking the subject matter as it stands, the phrase "of the word *āgneyī*" is stated to indicate the occurrence of a sublation in the form of a restriction of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), which otherwise would apply without distinction. Furthermore, by stating that [the *āgneyī*] is to be enjoined by a subordinate injunction (*viśeṣaṇavidhi*)—which arises from the impossibility of explaining the qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) otherwise—it is indicated that the *āgneyī* possesses the status of being something to be adopted (*upādeyatva*). This serves both to dispel the doubt that the *āgneyī* might be intended merely for the purpose of a future action, and to indicate the injunction of the attendance (*upasthāna*) as already established.
Or else, it is because [the word] ends in a *taddhita* suffix.

The meaning is that because the word *āgneyī* ends in a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), and because such a derivative functions as a pronoun denoting what is proximate, it does not refer to something not under discussion.

Regarding this point, the author of the *Nyāyasudhā* and others argue that since being "dedicated to Agni" (*agnidevatyatva*) and being a "verse" (*ṛktva*), along with proximity and so forth, serve as qualifiers for a specific mantra, and since the required function of the archetype (*prakṛta*) is accomplished by a single qualifier, there is no need for further qualifiers; thus, because "being dedicated to Agni" and "being a verse" are equally mentioned in the scripture (*śruti*).

Although both [the masculine and feminine forms] serve as indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*), it has been resolved that the term "all" (*sarva*) is included because, since they are understood through pronouns situated within the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*), their cognition is delayed, and thus they are not intended to be expressed.

This is so even though, in the section on Qualities (*guṇādhikaraṇa*), it was established that a specific individual (*vyakti*) indicated by proximity is also denoted by the secondary derivative (*taddhita*).

Considering it improper—according to the method shown in the Kaustubha—that proximity (*sannihitatva*) could be treated as a mere secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) because the delay in cognition due to being inferable from "femininity" (*strītva*) is equal [in both cases], he offers a rebuttal even while accepting that point, stating: "Of the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*)."
The refutation of the solution stated by the aforementioned author of the *Nyāyasudhā*—even in the case of its denoting that [the individual soul]—is indicated by the word "also" (*api*).
"Yathā" means "just as."

The meaning is that, because there is no mention of a pronoun (sarvanāman) here, and because the rice remains from the oblation intended as a disposal (pratipatti) for the consecratory rite of the *brāhmaudanika* fire lacks the purpose of being a consecration for the priests (*ṛtvij*), and because no performance of eating again is observed upon its loss, it is impossible for them [the priests] to be the objects of reference; thus, there is no evidence for taking the subject matter of the current context.

Now, one might object: even if there is no other restrictive factor for taking the *prakṛta* (the subject at hand), since taking the *aprakṛta* (what is not the subject) would result in meaninglessness—because its nature as a ritual act of worship (*upasthāna*) for the Āgnīdhra priest would have no purpose unless it were assumed to serve a transcendental result (*apūrva*)—it is necessary to assume that it serves an *apūrva*. Since it is simpler to assume that the established *apūrva*-serving function belongs to the *prakṛta* itself by merely connecting it to another means in the form of the Āgnīdhra-worship, and since the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) of the injunction—which depends on that [assumption]—justifies restricting the stem-meaning (*prātipadika-śruti*) accordingly, the inclusion of the *prakṛta* is thus justified. With this intention...
He raises an objection with the words "And not... (na ca).

Given that it is impossible to understand the enjoined [act] as having an unprecedented (*apūrva*) purpose through the context (*prakaraṇa*) by postulating another independent sentence, one might ask: "By what means, then, is that understanding attained? In response to this expectation, the answer is that it occurs where there is an application (*viniyoga*) for the sake of something; there, by accepting the word denoting the object of reference (*uddeśya*) as indicating the status of being a means to the *apūrva*, the same principle applies even to that which is not the subject at hand (*aprakṛta*). With this intention, he says: "Therefore, on account of parsimony (*lāghava*)."

Thus, having first established the apprehension of both relevant and irrelevant [objects], he now establishes—by means of reasoning—the position of those who claim that only the irrelevant are apprehended, as the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), with the words: "Or rather, only the irrelevant...
and so forth.

In the case of the *puroḍāśa* cake-pan, because of the force of a scriptural injunction (*vacana*) whose application is not otherwise established, one has resorted—out of necessity—to the application of that which is already applied and lacks further expectancy; however, in the present case, since there is no application in that form and the principle of "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*) is exhausted, it is not proper to resort to the application of what is already applied and lacks expectancy. Therefore, due to the mutual expectancy between the two, it is more logical to accept verses from the *Daśataya* collection even if they are not part of the primary context (*aprakṛta*).

In reality, however, since that [mantra] also lacks a requirement for a function due to its application in the *Vācastoma* and other rites, it must be established that this direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) effects the inclusion of only those mantras not already connected to the context— prior even to the assumption of an application based on indicative power (*liṅga*), which occurs only after a general connection with the sacrifice has been understood through a means of knowledge indicating a general relationship, such as order (*krama*) or name (*samākhyā*), which give rise to the requirement.

Although such [a verse] is indeed an Āgneyī even when it serves as a constituent part of a stotra, the intention is that it is not to be taken [as the primary subject], because it has no further expectancy (nirākāṅkṣatva) with respect to the stotra itself.
He states the established conclusion: "Not being the primary subject," etc.

Although, because a mantra is enjoined as a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the *upasthāna* (ritual attendance), there arises the contingency of its being purposeless in its own form— thereby necessitating an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) toward its being a means to the *apūrva* (transcendental result)— nevertheless, whenever an auxiliary is enjoined with reference to an auxiliary that has become a means to the *apūrva*, its injunction for the sake of the *apūrva* is necessarily implied by the force of the context (*artha*), since otherwise the injunction would be inexplicable; this very principle was accepted out of necessity in the case of the injunction regarding threshing (*avaghāta*).

In the present case, however, if there were an inclusion of what is not relevant (*aprakṛta*), there would result the fault of excessive complexity (*gaurava*) because both—the connection with the *apūrva* and the connection with its means—would have to be effected by the directly heard injunction through both word and sense. On the other hand, since the connection with the *apūrva* is already established when the relevant (*prakṛta*) is included, simplicity (*lāghava*) is achieved by effecting merely the connection with that which serves as a means to the *apūrva*. Therefore, it is the inclusion of the relevant alone that is adopted by one who relies on this principle of simplicity.

The meaning is that, because it is authorized by the injunction, even though the nominal stem (prātipadika) is restricted in accordance with the primary injunction (vidhiśruti), there is no sublation [of the sense]; thus, the grasping of only what is under discussion (prakṛta) is established.

[Objection: But how can there be a connection with the *apūrva* (transcendental result) of the Jyotiṣṭoma for this [upasad], which is under discussion as being a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the *upasthāna* (waiting upon)? Since its connection with that [Jyotiṣṭoma] occurs through the medium of the *stotra* (hymns), it is necessary to postulate an injunction for its connection with that *apūrva*. To this, he says: "And it is possible... (*saṃbhavati ca*).

Even if that [direct connection] is impossible here by way of the door of praise (*stotra*), since a connection with the *apūrva* of the Jyotiṣṭoma is possible through another effect in the form of attendance (*upasthāna*), there is no unfitness for connection with that *apūrva*.

Therefore, the sense is this: although the connection with the *apūrva* is rendered free of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣa*) by the specific connection with another effect—which is presented by its own postulator—nevertheless, it is not untenable for that [connection with the *apūrva*] to depend upon it precisely because of that very expectancy at that time.

An objection might be raised: "Even in the Siddhānta, since it is necessary to postulate that the connection with the *apūrva* produced by the act of worship (*upasthāna*) serves as the means (*dvāra*), the resulting complexity (*gaurava*) is no different from the Pūrvapakṣa; for even if one has already established the connection of the relevant *Āgneyī* mantra with the *stotra-āpūrva*, one must still postulate its connection with the *upasthāna-āpūrva*.

To this, the reply is: when a connection with a specific *apūrva* (the "object of objection") has been established elsewhere for the sake of another function, the subsequent establishment of a connection with a different function elsewhere—by relying solely upon that prior determination—is precisely what constitutes the logic of this particular section (*adhikaraṇa*).

To the question, "How is the establishment of the restriction regarding the subject matter accomplished through the application [of the rule] in the sentence concerning the *āgneyī* verses? he says: "Of the *āgneyī* verses..."

Even though it is necessary to postulate a connection with the *apūrva* (unseen potency) produced by the *upasthāna*, one need not postulate a connection with the Jyotiṣṭoma through that medium when the context (*prakaraṇa*) is taken into account; for the connection [with the Jyotiṣṭoma] is established by the mere recitation even without the *stotra*.

Therefore, just as there is a postulation of being mediated solely by the *apūrva* of the *stotra*, here too there is only the postulation of being mediated solely by the *apūrva* produced by the *upasthāna*.

The meaning is that, since it would follow that even that [relation] would be a conceptual construction if one were to apprehend something not previously established through conceptualization, there would be the fault of prolixity (gaurava); therefore, it must be demonstrated that the connection with the apūrva, which is to be inferred, is already established.

Even in the statement regarding the consumption of the *brahmodana* (the Brahmin’s rice), since the consumption— which is part of the injunction for the Brahmins who constitute an auxiliary to that *brahmodana*— serves a visible purpose as a form of disposal (*pratipatti*), and since the connection with the *apūrva* (transcendental result) of that [consumption] is for a visible purpose through the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the means to the *apūrva* of the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) and so forth, and since such a connection is already established as a constant requirement because the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are inherently auxiliary to the performance, the author says the following, intending to show that the reference to the subject matter at hand (*prakṛta*) is justified.
And this very [point].
Because it is necessarily not attained.

The meaning is that, because there is an absence of necessary concomitance (niyamataḥ prāpti) in that case, the scriptural injunction necessarily implies a connection with an unseen potency (apūrva); therefore, even when the [required] entity is present in the context, there is no such rule of necessity.

Regarding the term "āyatana": it means a sphere or base. Specifically, the six internal bases (ādhyātmikāyatana) are the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; and the six external bases (bāhyāyatana) are visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects. These twelve are called the "bases" because they serve as the locations for the arising of consciousness. Furthermore, the eighteen elements (dhātu) are also included within these, as they are subsumed under the categories of the internal and external bases. Thus, the term "āyatana" refers to the totality of these twelve spheres.

The meaning is that externalization is inappropriate, because an expiation is prescribed for the case where the fire of one who has established the sacred fires goes out, according to the scriptural statement: "He is deprived of sense-power and vigor; he whose fire goes out should collect it again, for this is one [fire]. This indicates that such an expiation would apply to the loss of the sacrificer's sense-power and vigor resulting from the fire going out—that is, from its being outside its proper receptacle—and thus externalization is logically inconsistent.
He concludes the established tenet with the words: "Therefore."
The purpose has not been stated because it is self-evident.

The ritualists (*yājñika*), however, perform the touching (*abhimarśana*) with the verse addressed to Agni, "O Agni, lead us by a good path" (*agne yaṃ nayasi supathā*), based on the sequence of the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni; they do not perform the worship (*upasthāna*).
In this regard, the authority for the statement "one should touch the Āgnīdhra fire-altar with a verse addressed to Agni" should be seen as the *Taittirīya* Śruti itself.
Thus ends the eighth section concerning the rules pertaining to the original form of the Agneyi.

By means of indicative mark and name. (A.3 Pā.2 Adhikaraṇa 9)
In some cases, a mantra is heard that is designated by the name *bhakṣānuvāka* (the recitation on consumption), beginning with the words "O, enter me for the sake of eating" (*bhakṣe hi mā viśa*).
Among those [parts], that portion which explains only the act of consuming is employed in that very context;

however, as for the portions that explain the seizing (*grahaṇa*), the inspection (*avekṣaṇa*), and the proper digestion (*samyagjarana*), are they to be employed in the seizing and so forth, or rather...?

In the deliberation that [the mantra] pertains only to the act of consumption because it forms a single syntactical unit with the mantra for consuming— since acts such as taking hold (*grahaṇa*) are not explicitly enjoined, they lack both the status of being subsidiary to the *apūrva* (transcendental result) and the capacity to produce it— the taking hold is only incidentally established as producing the consumption; nevertheless, since the taking hold performed by means of both arms, as stated in the phrase "having grasped with both arms," is in no way established [by other means], [the mantra applies] to the inspection (*avekṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, since [the acts of] grasping and so forth do not produce eating, they are not established [as subsidiaries]; and because the act of proper digestion, or the activity conducive thereto, occurs subsequent to eating, these acts lack the capacity to produce eating and thus cannot even serve as motivators for the *apūrva*.

Since it would otherwise result in meaninglessness if they were intended for the purpose of grasping and so forth, they must serve the purpose of eating alone, by virtue of forming a single syntactical unit with the mantra of eating.

Thus, when it is argued that the designation (*samākhyā*) is also thereby rendered appropriate— [we reply]: even in the absence of direct injunctions (*pratyakṣavidhi*) for the acts of taking up (*grahaṇa*) and so forth,

once the connection with the act of consuming (*bhakṣa*) is understood through the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) aided by the designation, and the injunctions for taking up and so forth are inferred from the indicative power (*liṅga*) of the respective mantras via their wording, then since the attainment [of those acts] is established, the application of the mantras is appropriately justified as being for that very purpose.

It is not tenable to assume that two verbal words, which are individually independent, form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) in some way and thereby postulate a figurative sense (*gauṇī*) of "eating," nor is it reasonable to assume that they reveal the acts of "taking" and so forth as qualifiers of "eating" through their primary power (*śakti*).
Furthermore, even if this were the case, since the act of complete digestion cannot be accomplished by human effort (*kṛtisādhya*), an injunction (*vidhi*) would be impossible.

Because it is precisely a specific posture conducive to proper digestion that is to be performed as the enjoined duty, and because of the scriptural injunction of expiation for vomiting or purging, consumption must extend until proper digestion is achieved; thus, its utility lies in its being a form of disposal (pratipatti). 24/9.
