And this has been written according to the sequence recorded in the Bhāṣya.
However, in the Taittirīya recension, after the mantra *avakhyeṣam*, one reads from *mandrābhibhūtiḥ* up to *bhakṣayāmi*, and then *hinva me* is recited.
It is stated that [the mantra] is thus designated for the sake of its utility in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
In that context, in order to dispel the suspicion that everything might be an example, he distinguishes the scope [of the definition] with the word "therein" (tatra).

Since it is clear that the portion beginning with *mandrābhibhūtiḥ* and ending with *juṣāṇa* serves to manifest the consumption [of the Soma] preceded by the manifestation of its fruit through satisfaction— and since it will be established in the subsequent section (*uttarādhikaraṇa*) that the portion ending with *tṛpyatu* manifests the act of consumption—

it follows without dispute, by virtue of both indicative mark (*liṅga*) and name (*samākhyā*), that the portion beginning with *vasumat* [is used] after having pressed [the Soma] and offered it into the Āhavanīya fire, while returning westward.
The meaning is that [the passage] "having gone to the assembly, he consumes the portions" establishes the status of consumption as a subordinate element (*aṅga*).

Furthermore, regarding the words *prātaḥsavana* (morning pressing) and so forth occurring therein, as well as the words *indrapīta* (drunk by Indra) and so forth, their application according to the respective pressing (*savana*) is as clear as that [of the consumption], by virtue of the principle established in the section concerning the division of the *Sūktavāka*. Therefore, they do not serve as examples [for the present discussion].
"Of the portions."

The meaning is that there is an allocation (*viniyoga*) of the respective portions as follows: the portion beginning with "bhakṣehi" and ending with "sadhyaṣam" is for the taking [of the draught]; the portion beginning with "nṛcakṣasam" and ending with "avakhyeṣam" is for the gazing; and the portion beginning with "hinva me" and ending with "atigāḥ" is for the thorough swallowing.

In that regard, according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), since the application (*viniyoga*) is made in accordance with the indicative mark (*liṅga*), there is a connection between the section (*pāda*) and the chapter (*adhyāya*) through the determination of the delimiting factor of the objective (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) suitable for that [application]. Similarly, in the preceding topic (*adhikaraṇa*), having stated that the present [text] refers to the archetype (*prakṛta*) because a connection to a door (*dvāra*) unrelated to the sacrifice is untenable, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) arises as follows: if the archetype is grasped, then since there is no connection to the transcendental result (*apūrva*) in the case of grasping what is not prescribed in any way, there can be no status as a "door. Thus, the prima facie view is raised.

Without explicitly stating the connection of immediate sequence (*anantara-saṅgati*) because it is obvious—since it takes the form of a counter-example—and first indicating the extreme clarity of the connections between the quarters (*pāda*) and chapters (*adhyāya*) by introducing the position of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), he shows the doubt with the words: "What [is it]? (*kimiti*).

If the purpose [of the mantras] were merely the act of grasping and so forth, then even if there were a mere indicative mark (liṅga), it would follow that the restriction of the mantra would be rendered useless if its purpose were simply the essential nature of grasping and so forth. Since those acts are not themselves enjoined, they lack the status of being subsidiaries to the transcendental result (apūrva) or the capacity to produce it;
consequently, because it is impossible to avoid their uselessness by characterizing them as means to that apūrva, the application of the mantra as a subsidiary to those acts is not tenable.

Furthermore, intending that [the recitation] is indeed a subordinate element (aṅga) to the prescribed eating, he states the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa): "of the taking up [of the vessel], etc. (grahaṇādeḥ).
"Only by virtue of not being a producer of enjoyment."

The meaning is that since eating is impossible without grasping, even though there is a possibility of its [grasping] being included under the alternative [of eating], inspection is entirely unestablished [as a rule], because in the world it is not determined to invariably produce that [grasping];
this is indicated by the phrase "by occurring subsequent to eating."

Nor should it be argued that, just as the mantra beginning with "aganma" (we have gone) possesses subsidiarity to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices by way of manifesting a fruit arising from the consumption that occurs subsequent to the [initial] consumption, so too does it possess subsidiarity to the act of consumption itself;

for the reason is that consumption, consisting of the contact of the mouthfuls with the palate, takes the form of a disposal (*pratipatti*) of what is being consumed and thus lacks the fruit of complete digestion—this is the intended meaning.
Because it forms a single syntactical unit with the mantra for consuming [the sacrificial food].

Even though there is a difference in the verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*), because there is unity between the opening and the conclusion (*upakrama-upasaṃhāra-ekya*), and because the presence of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*)—which is the cause for forming a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*)—is observed in the Vaiśvānara passage, here too, since the opening with "Eat, O... (*bhakṣehi*) refers to the act of eating itself, and the conclusion ending with "...I eat" (*bhakṣayāmi*) likewise refers to that same act, the unity of the opening and conclusion is perceived; therefore, by the mark (*liṅga*) consisting of expectancy, which is the cause for forming a single syntactical unit, [the entire passage constitutes one sentence].
The meaning is that the word *bhakṣa* (to eat) has the sense of eating as characterized by taking up, inspecting, properly digesting, or else by the act of consuming itself.

Thus, when a worldly application is impossible, there is no contradiction in an application based on *samākhyā* (name), even though it is weak, being supported by the previously mentioned *liṅga* (indicative power) in the form of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*). He says "for this very reason" (*ata eva*), even though this [name] is worldly.

Nevertheless, because it is beginningless, it is appropriate as a regulator for the understanding of the connection with the *bhakṣa* (consumption), and thus it is logically established that it conveys the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*). Otherwise, one would have to resort to a figurative application (*gauṇīvṛtti*) based on the presence of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the substrates of the collection of both *bhakṣa* and non-*bhakṣa* [mantras]. Therefore, although in the Āpastamba Sūtra—"having waited while the [cup] is being taken up with 'bhakṣehi' etc. and "having received it with 'aśvinostvā bāhubhyāṃ sadhyāsam'"—this portion, "bhakṣehi," is used for the act of waiting; ...it is understood that its primary application is to the act of consumption itself. This is because the word *bhakṣa* primarily denotes the act of eating, and since the mantra is recited at the time of consumption, it is logical that it serves as an auxiliary to that very act. Consequently, the mantra "bhakṣehi" is employed in the context of the consumption of the Soma. Thus, the conclusion is that the mantra "bhakṣehi" is indeed an auxiliary to the act of consuming the Soma. This is the view of Bhaṭṭa Someśvara. Alternatively, this may be explained as follows: the mantra "bhakṣehi" is applied to the act of waiting because it is recited during that interval. However, since the word *bhakṣa* is etymologically derived from the root *bhakṣ* (to eat) and primarily signifies the act of consumption, it is more reasonable to apply it to the act of consuming itself. Furthermore, since the mantra is recited at the time of consumption, it is logical that it functions as an auxiliary to that act. Therefore, the mantra "bhakṣehi" is employed in the context of the consumption of the Soma. This is the view of Bhaṭṭa Someśvara. Or yet again, it may be explained as follows: the mantra "bhakṣehi" is applied to the act of waiting because it is recited during that interval. Nevertheless, since the word *bhakṣa* is derived from the root *bhakṣ* and primarily denotes the act of consumption, it is more reasonable to apply it to the act of consuming itself. Moreover, since the mantra is recited at the time of consumption, it is logical that it serves as an auxiliary to that act. Therefore, the mantra "bhakṣehi" is employed in the context of the consumption of the Soma. This is the view of Bhaṭṭa Someśvara. In short, the mantra "bhakṣehi" is indeed an auxiliary to the act of consuming the Soma. This is the view of Bhaṭṭa Someśvara. [End of section] [Note: The provided source text contains repetitive fragments. The translation above reflects the core argument regarding the application of the mantra "bhakṣehi" to the act of consumption rather than waiting.]

Nevertheless, considering that it is improper because the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for [the consumption] is not perceived at every moment, and intending that the entire section (*anuvāka*) constitutes a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) of the consumption (*bhakṣa*), he concludes the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words: "Thus, this being the position...
(*iti prāpte*).

Even though, in this case, a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) might be established through the identity of the opening and the conclusion (*upakramopasaṃhāraikya*), nevertheless, the status of the portion of the mantra that illuminates the *grahaṇa* (taking) and so forth as being subsidiary to the act of consumption (*bhakṣaṇa*) is established by direct statement (*vākya*) alone; thus, its sublation by the stronger indicative power (*liṅga*) is justified. In reality, however, because the opening is common [to both], and on the contrary, it is more reasonable to restrict it to the subject of *grahaṇa* and so forth in accordance with the primary capacity [of the words], there is no single syntactical unity even when there is a difference in the verbal roots (*ākhyāta*).

Nor is the phrase "for long life" (dīrghāyutvāya), which expresses the fruit of the consumption, a non-sequential indicator of the intent toward the purpose of consumption when it is taken [as part of the injunction for drinking];
for its connection is established as a praise by expressing the fruit of the consumption that results from the fruit of the taking.

Therefore, since the syntactic unity would be broken by the indicative mark (liṅga) [if it were taken otherwise], and intending that it is indeed an auxiliary to the taking and so forth, he establishes the final position (siddhānta) while first proving the injunction for the taking and so forth in order to avoid meaninglessness.
"Because of grasping and so forth."

The meaning is that because the *kalpaka-mantra* is an auxiliary part (*aṅga*) of the consumption (*bhakṣa*), it follows that the acts such as the taking up (*grahaṇa*) prescribed by the injunctions formulated therein are also established as being auxiliary parts of the consumption.
[This is] precisely because they serve that purpose.

Although it is not possible for these [roots] to have the sense of grasping, looking, digesting, or manifesting— since *sadha* has the meaning of harming, *cakṣiṇ* has the meaning of speaking, and *hinoti* has the meaning of going— nevertheless,

just as the root *nirvap* (to pour out) signifies the continuity of seed and thread, the root *sadha* indicates "grasping" through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), because it is invariably associated with the act of harming performed by means of the two arms, and because it is fit to have the two arms as its instrument. Furthermore,

even though the form *khyeṣam* would be unestablished due to the absence of the augment *iṭ* in the substitute *khyāñ* prescribed by the rule *cakṣiṅaḥ khyāñ*, [the intended meaning is still conveyed].

Because the addition of *khyeñ* is prescribed as an extension based on what is observed in the Vedic language (*chandasi*), or because the suffix *sic* is applied according to the rule "the suffix *sic* is frequently used in the *leṭ* tense," the word *avakhyeṣam*—

which denotes the manifestation known as the clarity of the object of speech— is used here merely to signify the manifestation known as fame, which consists in being universally known; this is seen both in worldly usage such as *khyātaḥ* (famous) and in the Veda, such as in *nṛcakṣāḥ* (one who is looked upon by men).

Because it is employed by one intent upon that [practice], and due to its syntactic unity with the word *sucakṣas* ("having good vision"), it is not contradictory to explain it as teaching illumination in the form of observation known as visual cognition.
Furthermore, since the root *hinoti* is also used in the sense of "pleasing," by the word *hinva*, [the meaning is]: "O Soma of green color (*haritavarṇa*), please my limbs;
[please] my *gaṇas*—that is, the groups of senses—or, according to the writing of the Vedabhāṣyakāra, my sons and so forth, making them free from thirst for the drinking of Soma."

"Be auspicious to me; O Seven Seers, do not depart from my mouth"—this is understood to mean: "Do not go by way of the wind through the mouth, having bypassed the navel," since that [departure] is impossible without proper digestion, and because the purpose is to indicate proper digestion, which results in the nourishment of the body. [The seers are addressed as such] because they are the seven vital breaths (*prāṇa*) moving within the apertures of the head, consisting of the pairs known as the two eyes, the two nostrils, and the two ears, with the mouth as the seventh. Be auspicious to me! Do not depart! This is the sense. And this [mantra] serves to establish proper digestion, which has the result of pleasing the limbs.
The meaning is that the application [of the mantra] is solely for the purpose of that [act] which is possible [to be manifested by it].

Even though one might attempt to argue that the mantra is not an auxiliary to the act of drawing [the cup], by accepting the unity of the mantra—on the grounds that, just as the mantra "To Agni, what is pleasing" reveals the deity and the pouring out, this mantra also reveals the drinking characterized by the acts of drawing and so forth; [nevertheless, the following applies]:

Nevertheless, in the absence of the capacity for the sentences to attain the status of a single syntactical unity—characterized by the identity of their opening and conclusion and so forth—the contradiction of the primary denotative meaning residing in each respective verb as it is naturally perceived constitutes the very absence of evidence for accepting a division of mantras; this has been indicated in some way by the word "kathaṃcit" (in some way).
[The phrase] "vomiting and purging" [is used].

Regarding the injunction, "One who has vomited Soma should offer a caru-oblation of Śyāmāka grain to Soma-Indra," since a penance is prescribed for vomiting as a means to remedy the physical impairment caused by the absence of proper digestion— and because a penance is also recorded in some cases for purging— it is understood that the act of eating is intended as a restorative rite (*pratipatti*).
Since such a rite is untenable without proper digestion, the meaning is that a specific posture conducive to that digestion is enjoined as being useful for the consumption [of the oblation].

By this, the argument that—“like satiety, [the act of eating] does not require the mantra because it is not to be performed as a separate subsidiary act” —is refuted; for, since it must be performed with a distinct effort like the drawing of the cup (*grahaṇa*) and so forth, its dependence on the mantra is logically established.
And thus, the meaning is that the designation (*samākhyā*) “Bhakṣānuvāka” applies neither directly nor indirectly [to the act of eating].
The purpose [of this discussion] is as follows: according to the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), there is no fixed rule regarding the drawing of the cup (grahaṇa) and so forth;
rather, it is established that the consumption (bhakṣaṇa) occurs at the end of the recitation, following the sequence of the mantra-text.
According to the final conclusion (siddhānta), however, the drawing of the cup and so forth must be performed with necessity at the end of each respective mantra mentioned previously.

Since the sequence of mantra recitation written in the Bhāṣya is set aside by the sequence of meaning, it was not explicitly stated that the mantra "hinva me" follows immediately after "mandrābhibhūtiḥ."

Thus ends the ninth section concerning the subordinate status of the *bhakṣa-mantra* with respect to the act of taking [the soma], [also known as] the section on indicative power and name (*liṅgasamākhyānādhikaraṇa*).
(B1) (Section 10 / [A.3 Pā.2 Adhi.10]) Because of the mention of a quality.

In that very same section (*anuvāka*), the mantra beginning with *mandrābhibhūtiḥ* and ending with *tṛpyatu* should be employed for the purpose of satiation, just as it is employed for the act of taking [the Soma] and so forth; such being the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*)—it is replied: because satiation is not something to be performed like the acts of taking and so forth, it cannot be manifested by the mantra. Nor can it be argued that the mantra implies a multiplicity of acts of eating—which consist of activities conducive to satiation—similar to the act of "properly digesting" (*samyag-jaraṇa*). For such an assumption is untenable, as it would contradict the scriptural statement, "He eats a small amount."
Therefore, since satisfaction is not produced by the act of eating, it cannot be established as something to be manifested merely by its being produced—unlike heaven.

Consequently, since the application by means of an indicative mark (*liṅga*) is impossible, even though the two verbal forms are inherently independent of one another, one must assume the ellipsis of the particle *iti* and construct a single syntactical unit with the mantra for eating, such that "I eat so that [the gods] may be satisfied. Thus, one must accept that its function is solely to manifest the act of eating as qualified by its own specific purpose.
And its own purpose, according to the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), is satisfaction alone;
however, regarding the aspect of manifesting that [satisfaction], it serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*).
Alternatively, by means of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it is a praise of the act of eating.
In no way is there an application [of a mantra] based on its indicative mark. // 10.25 //
Thus ends the tenth section, concerning the designation of qualities.

(B2) As before, since the connection between the section and the chapter, as well as the immediate connection which serves as an exception, are clear, they are not stated; rather, demonstrating that the subject matter pertains to a specific portion of the preceding section, he states the prima facie view:
"In that very same [case]... etc.
Generally, the meaning is clear up to the end of the section.

The purpose [of this discussion] is as follows: according to the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), after performing the consumption [of the soma] with the formula beginning with "Of the Vasumadgaṇa... and ending with "...I consume," one would recite the mantra beginning with "Mandrābhibhūtiḥ... and ending with "...tṛpyatu" afterwards, thereby overriding the order of the text (pāṭhakrama).
However, according to the established conclusion (siddhānta), it is clear that one should act exactly according to the textual sequence.
Thus ends the tenth section concerning the non-subordinate status of the taking of the *mandrābhibhūti* cup, which is the section on the designation of qualities (*guṇābhidhāna*).
— — — — — — — (B1) (11th Adhikaraṇa /) (A.3 Pā.2 Adhi.11) Because of the mention of a specific gender.

Regarding the doubt as to whether the *bhakṣa-mantra* (the mantra for consuming) is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) only to the repeated consumption dedicated to Indra, while consumption in repetitions other than that is mantra-less; or whether it applies to those others through modification (*ūha*), or perhaps without modification (*anūha*):

although the context (*prakaraṇa*) establishes that the *bhakṣa-mantra* pertains to all offerings, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the phrase "drunk by Indra" (*indrapītasya*) restricts its status as an auxiliary solely to the offering dedicated to Indra. Nor should it be argued that there is no conflict with the indicative mark because one may accept a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "in which libation (*savana*) [of Soma] was drunk by Indra," thereby treating it as a qualifier of the specific *savana* connected to the Soma. This is not so.

Because, in comparison with a *vyadhikaraṇa* (non-co-referential) *bahuvrīhi* compound— which would require the imposition of a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) upon two words and would thus fail to conform to the definition [of a compound]—

the *tatpuruṣa* compound alone is more parsimonious, as it requires the imposition of a secondary signification denoting a relation only on the first member, in the sense that "it was drunk by, or appropriated by, Indra" (*indreṇa pītaḥ svīkṛtaḥ*).

Furthermore, even in the absence of actual acceptance (*pratigraha*), there exists for the deity an act of appropriation (*svīkāra*) in the form of a specific relationship, by virtue of scriptural injunctions such as "one should not take the property of a god.
Nor can the status of this as a *bahuvrīhi* compound be determined solely by accent, as in the case of the word *sthūlapṛṣatī*;
for here, unlike that instance, the accent itself is overridden because the compound does not conform to the grammatical definition [of a *bahuvrīhi*].
Furthermore, that there is no contradiction regarding the accent even under the *tatpuruṣa* interpretation has been established in the *Kaustubha*.

Consequently, since it is understood from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that the mantra is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) only to the offering dedicated to Indra, for those offerings not dedicated to Indra—because the sacrifice is a single act and thus lacks the relationship of original and modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*), making "modification" [*ūha*] impossible—the mantra is applied without modification, just as one says "of rice-grains" (*vrīhīṇāṃ medhaiḥ*). Thus, for the non-Indra offerings, [the mantra is used] without the [modified] mantra.

The first position is that [the offering] is a consumption (*bhakṣaṇa*). The second position, however, is not contradictory because, even though the ritual action (*karman*) is one, the offerings (*pradāna*) are distinct; thus, there exists a relationship of original form and modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*).

Furthermore, since the mantras for measuring the cups (*māna-grahaṇa-mantra*), such as "For Indra accompanied by the Vasus," have by their indicative power (*liṅga*) as their scope only Indra, [the modification] follows in accordance with them.

Furthermore, since it is understood that the measuring and the taking [of the Soma], which are manifested by that [mantra], as well as the Soma to be refined by it, its refinements such as the pressing, and the other auxiliary parts mixed with them, all pertain exclusively to the Indra-rite, it is logical that there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the ritual properties (*adharma*) to the others. Moreover, a restriction of the primary rite (*pradhāna*) on account of the auxiliaries (*aṅga*) is indeed possible.

Because the sacrifices, in accordance with the requirement for the *agnyādi* (the fire-altars and so forth), pertain to those who have established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), the *bhakṣa-mantra*—which reveals the deities of the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*) and has entered into the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) by way of its function—indeed undergoes modification (*ūha*) according to the respective deity. This being the case, there follows an intermediate deliberation. // 11 // 26 //

Thus ends the eleventh section, concerning the specification of particular marks (*liṅgaviśeṣanirdeśādhikaraṇa*). (The Section on "Drunk by Indra" [*Indrapītādhikaraṇa*]) (B2) And herein, regarding the non-Indra offerings (*anaindrapradāna*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) to be demonstrated is that the application of mantras is based upon the authority of their indicative mark (*liṅga*).

Since [the opponent] does not accept either of the two prima facie views, and since the connection with the section and the chapter, as well as the incidental connection with the immediately preceding topic, are clear and thus need not be stated, [the author], showing that very mantra as the subject matter, states the doubt: "The *bhakṣa*-mantra..."
Regarding those [cases], it is by means of inference (*ūha*).

By this, the statement in the *Nyāyasudhā*— that the position of *ūha* (modification) lacks connection with the definition of a "quarter" (*pāda*) and thus does not constitute an independent alternative,
but is merely an implied consequence of the non-mantric nature of those verses not addressed to Indra which results from the first alternative—

is refuted; for, as explained by the aforementioned method, the introduction of *ūha* as a counter-argument to the position intended by the Siddhāntin establishes a logical connection, and there is no purpose in implying the result of a non-conclusive prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Therefore, the meaning is that this [reason] also possesses the status of being an independent category.
"Non-contradiction with the gender marker."
The meaning is that there is no contradiction, because even for Soma dedicated to another deity, its manifestation as being connected to the aforementioned *savana* (pressing) is possible;
thus, [the term] "of two words" (*padadvaya*) is used.

In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) resides in the first member alone as the related object. In a *bahuvrīhi*, however, there is an indication of the meaning of another word in both members; thus, it entails indication in both members.

Even if one accepts that in a *bahuvrīhi* the indication of the qualified meaning resides in only one member while the other serves merely to capture the intended sense, there remains the burden of complexity regarding the delimitors of the indicated object (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka-gaurava*).

There is the fault that even though the other indicator of intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*) participates in the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), it would nonetheless [be considered] a nominal stem (*pratipadika*) by implication.

Although there is a primary denotative power (*śakti*) for the "other referent" (*anyapadārtha*) in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, nevertheless, because the cognition of that "other referent" depends upon the presentation of the meanings of the constituent parts, there is complexity (*gaurava*) in that regard.
The meaning is that, in every respect, the *tatpuruṣa* compound is indeed lighter.
He also states the fault of not conforming to the definition: "not conforming... etc.

Since Kātyāyana’s traditional rule states that a *bahuvrīhi* compound is intended for words in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), it is untenable for it to apply to words in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*). Although one might resort to a locative-ending *bahuvrīhi* in cases such as *kaṇṭhekālaḥ* by the force of the metarule *saptamīviśeṣaṇe bahuvrīhau*, there is no authority for such a resort here; thus, [the definition] lacks consistency with the general characteristic.

In the case of a *tatpuruṣa* compound, however, its status as being prescribed by the grammatical rule "the agent and the instrument [are compounded] with a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix, in many instances" (*kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*) is established.

Furthermore, since the purpose of manifesting the mantra—as an essential requirement for establishing its status as an auxiliary to the act of consumption (bhakṣaṇa)—is fulfilled by manifesting either the consumption itself or its related object, the Soma, this is possible under the *tatpuruṣa* interpretation; it is not proper, however, to resort to a *bahuvrīhi* compound which would prioritize the manifestation of the *savanas* (pressings), which are subordinate and not required [by the mantra]. This is the meaning. Now, one might raise the objection: "Since the word [the mantra] is the deity, how can the sense of 'appropriated' (*svīkṛta*) be logically established? He dispels this doubt even in the case of the *bahuvrīhi* by means of the necessary mode of interpretation: "And it exists," and so forth.
Is it not the case that this is not a *tatpuruṣa* compound?
For if it were so, the rule *samāsasya* would require the final syllable to be udātta,
whereas this word *pīta* is actually udātta on its initial syllable.
However, the word denoting Indra is inherently acute-accented on its first syllable;

this being the case, by the rule *bahuvrīhau prakṛtyā pūrvapadam*, which prescribes that in a *bahuvrīhi* compound the preceding member retains its original accent, the entire word becomes acute-accented on its first syllable.

Therefore, thinking that once the *bahuvrīhi* nature is determined by the accent—as it is in the case of *sthūlapṛṣatī*—it is possible for the term to refer to the *savana* (pressing), he raises the following objection: "And not... (*na ca*).

Since even a *bahuvrīhi* compound can possess coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), it does not fall under the definition [of a *tatpuruṣa*]. When one of the two—either the compound accent or the literal meaning—must be assumed to be unavoidable, it is proper to resolve the matter by assuming that the accent alone is non-Vedic (*chāndasa*) and thus subject to sublation, because accent is a property of the constituent member (*aṅga-dharma*);
it is not proper, however, to abandon the primary sense of the word itself. This is the meaning.
And as it is said:

The meaning is that, because the rule *tṛtīyā karmaṇi* prescribes that when a word ending in the suffix *-kta* follows as a subordinate member (*upapada*), the preceding member ending in the third case retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*), and because the rule *kte ca* likewise prescribes that same accent, there is no conflict regarding the accent even under the analysis as a *tatpuruṣa* compound; this has been demonstrated in the *Kaustubha*.
He concludes the initial prima facie argument with the words "Therefore, etc. (ataśca).
It is like the expression "the essence of rice" (vrīhīṇāṃ medhaḥ).
The meaning is that, as in the case of using barley when the text says "the essence of rice," its application here is inappropriate;
thus [it refers to] those [oblations] which are not dedicated to Indra.

By means of a general statement, there is an indication that, just as the remnants of the *camasa* offerings are without mantras, so too the remnants of the *graha* offerings are without mantras; thus, the remnants of the oblations dedicated to deities such as Mitra and Varuṇa are mantra-less.

Furthermore, although terms such as "drunk by the ancestors" (*pitṛpīta*) apply to those specific deity-offerings, even when other terms are applied distributively, the consumption of the *aindra* (Indra-related) offerings during all three *savana*s is performed with mantras through the use of the term "drunk by Indra" (*indrapīta*).
The meaning is that it is not so for other gifts.
In that regard, he says "For Indra, thee" in order to establish that the offerings to Indra constitute the archetype (prakṛti).

The meaning is as follows: from the indicative power (*liṅga*) of the measuring mantra, which begins with the words "I measure thee for Indra accompanied by the Vasus," and of the drawing mantra, "I draw thee for Indra accompanied by the Vasus," it is understood that these are subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) to the offering to Indra; therefore, even the Soma-scripture (*somavākya*), though it applies generally, refers only to that specific [offering].
"Also by way of the limbs."
The meaning is that by means of the mantra-form and its limbs, there is a contraction of the primary [practice], such as the grasping of the measure (māna) and so forth;
[this is done] "according to the deity."
The meaning is that their consumption [of the Soma] is accompanied by mantras through the recitation of the modified mantra beginning with "mitrāvaruṇapītasya.

Since it is impossible to conduct a subsequent discussion concerning that [topic] once the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) regarding modification (ūha) has been refuted, and since the position of modification remains unrefuted and thus finds its opportunity, he begins the inquiry by inserting an intermediate section— consisting of five topical discussions (adhikaraṇas) of specific analysis— concerning that subject, saying "evam" (thus).
Thus ends the eleventh section, concerning the specification of particular gender.
— — — — — — — (B1) (12th Adhikaraṇa /) (A.3 Pā.2 Adhi.12) Regarding the [Soma] that has been drawn out again.

When all the cups dedicated to Indra at the beginning of the *savana* have been offered—including those of the *hotṛ*-assisted priests such as the Maitrāvaruṇa and others—but before they have been consumed, more Soma is added to them and offered to other deities, such as Mitra and Varuṇa; it is then consumed. In this regard, there arises a deliberation as to whether Indra, who was the deity of the previous offering, should also be mentioned (*upalakṣaṇīya*) or not. [The conclusion is: At the time of the addition of the Soma, there is no reference to another deity.
Since that which has already been drawn out is connected with it, the connection of the former portion with its previous deity would not be lost;

however, at the time of offering, because the mixed substance itself is connected with another deity, there is the perception of the removal of the connection with the previous deity, and thus [the previous deity] is not to be mentioned as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [we reply]: even though there is no formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) regarding the deity at the time of drawing out the portion, by the very force of the situation (*sāmarthya*), the drawing out is understood to be for the sake of the ritual act that is about to be performed.

Even though the remnant of the previous [offering] is mixed [with the current one], since there is no evidence that it serves this specific purpose, the deity of the previous [offering], whose connection has not been removed, must also be mentioned as a secondary reference (upalakṣaṇīya). // 12 // 27 //
Thus ends the twelfth section concerning the re-offering.

(B2) Here, having raised an objection to the status of the *bhakṣa-mantra* as an auxiliary to the offering to Indra— as asserted in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the preceding section— and having provided its resolution, the author states the subject matter— namely, "in the *savanamukhīya* [offerings]"— without explicitly mentioning the connections between the sections (*pāda*) and chapters (*adhyāya*), as they are obvious.

At the beginning of the three *savana*s—the morning (*prātaḥsavana*), midday (*mādhyandina-savana*), and third (*tṛtīya-savana*)—there are specific portions of *soma* juice contained in the *camasa* vessels, known as the *savanamukhīya*s, so called because they occur at the commencement (*mukha*) of each *savana* in relation to the distribution of the *camasa*s. Their consumption occurs in the morning and midday *savana*s after the drawing of the *śukra* and *manthin* cups; however, in the third *savana*, their consumption occurs after the drawing of the *āditya* cup.
When these are being performed, [the officiants] are the Hotṛ, Brahman, Udgātṛ, Yajamāna, Maitrāvaruṇa, Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, and Potṛ.
They are designated as the cups of the Neṣṭṛ, the Agnīdh, and the Acchāvāka.
Among the four officiating priests beginning with the *hotṛ*, the designation is "those who act from the middle" (*madhyataḥ-kārin*).
For the remaining six, beginning with the *maitrāvaruṇa*, the designation is "the *hotṛ*-assistants" (*hotṛka*).
In that context, at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), there is no oblation with the *acchāvāka* cup along with the nine cups.
However, at a later time, having set that aside, one first offers once to Indra from the new cups;

thereafter, from the cups of the *hotṛ*-assisting priests—which already contain the remnants of what was offered and consumed during the previous *vaṣaṭ*-call—one draws up another portion of Soma from the *droṇakalaśa* vessel and offers it to other deities such as Mitra and Varuṇa, after which it is consumed; such is the sequence of the ritual performance.

Regarding the cups (*camasa*) of those who perform the rite in the middle, since there is no possibility of modification (*ūha*) due to their being dedicated to Indra, and specifically because there is no subsequent refilling (*punarabhyunnayana*), for this very reason the cup of the *acchāvāka*—even though it is not dedicated to Indra and thus could be a subject of modification—is not a subject of discussion during the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), as there is no subsequent refilling.

As for the two subsequent pressings, although there is subsequent refilling, because all offerings in the midday pressing (*mādhyandina-savana*) have Indra as their deity, they do not fall within the scope of modification according to the method to be explained hereafter; therefore, that [cup] is not a subject of discussion.

In the third *savana*, however, because it is possible for there to be a distinction of deities through the act of pouring out [the Soma] for the sake of the deities Indra and Viṣṇu, it certainly remains a subject for deliberation.

For this very reason, even at the morning *savana*, although there is a second pouring out into the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*’s cup, since both offerings share a common deity—just like the *sānnāyya*—the recitation of the word "drunk by Indra" (*indrapīta*), uttered once as a *tantra*, successfully reveals the Soma characterized by both deities; thus, there is indeed modification (*ūha*).
Because it is possible [to perform them], they do not fall within the scope of deliberation (*cintā*).

Regarding the four cups belonging respectively to the Maitrāvaruṇa, Potṛ, Neṣṭṛ, and Agnīdhra— in which the deities are, in order, Mitra and Varuṇa, the Maruts, Tvaṣṭṛ and his wife, and Agni— when these cups contain mixed remnants, there is both the drawing up (*unnayana*) and the modification (*ūha*).
The meaning is that investigation arises from the possibility [of its occurrence].
He shows the nature of *vicāra* (investigation) with the word "therein" (*tatra*).
"Indra too," so it is said.

Although there is the presence of indicative marks (*upalakṣaṇa*) through the modification (*padoha*) of the words denoting the four previously mentioned deities, he refutes the prima facie view— which is contrary to the established conclusion— by demonstrating that even in the case of a mixture, it is possible to mentally extract [the portion] for the Vāyu-cup, the Indra-Vāyu cup, and the Soma cup, merely by means of the distinction made at the time of drawing [the portions], despite the presence of the original word "Indra" in the phrase "of that which has been drunk by Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, and so forth. This is stated in the passage beginning with "at the time of pouring out" (*unnayanakāle*).

The opponent’s thesis is that at the time of the *unnayana* (the second drawing of the Soma), there is no connection with another deity; for although such a connection might be possible at the time of the initial *grahaṇa* (drawing) due to the existence of a relationship with a deity, no injunction for such a relationship is observed during the *unnayana*.
Furthermore, since there is no evidence for connecting the mere *unnīta* (drawn-out) portion with a different deity, the removal of the previous deity is logically established.
Thus, at the time of the *unnayana*, there is no connection with another deity.
The meaning of the root text is "by which connection with another deity. He establishes that very point [with the verse]: "But at the time of offering... and so forth.

Since the connection with a deity—deducible from the wording of the *yājyā* mantra—at the time of the offering pertains to a combined [deity], it is impossible to extract [the individual deities]; therefore, because the connection with the previous deity is removed by the connection with another deity, it need not be indicated as a qualifier.

Nor should it be argued that, "if there were no injunction of a deity at the time of the *unnayana*, the deity would be obtained merely as a subordinate element (*yāga-śeṣa*) through the wording of the *yājyā* mantra, which would result in the loss of its 'unmanifest' (*avyakta*) character. This is because, even if such an unmanifest character is impossible, there is no contradiction in accepting that this [offering] is indeed a sacrifice distinct from an *iṣṭi* whose deity is not prescribed in its originative injunction (*utpatti-vākya*).

Nor is it tenable that the former deity should be indicated as a secondary characteristic (upalakṣaṇa), because even when the remnant is offered with reference to a subsequent deity, the connection with the former deity still exists;

for even before the sacrifice is completed, ritualists (yājñika) treat the oblation— from the initial pouring out (nirvāpa) until its final disposal (pratipatti)— as being connected to another deity, since a connection between the substance and the deity, which is destroyed by the final disposal, must necessarily be postulated.

The meaning is that because the means of knowledge apprehending the substratum (dharmin) reveals a contradiction with the connection to any other deity, it is impossible for [the substance] to coexist with that [other deity] while being characterized by its absolute absence; therefore, when the remaining portion is connected to the subsequent deity, there is necessarily a cognition of the removal of the connection to the previous deity, and thus it need not be indicated as a secondary qualifier (upalakṣaṇīya).

At the time of relinquishment, although there is no perception of distinction due to the state of being mixed, even when the act of lifting occurs—whether in the archetype (*prakṛti*) or the ectype (*vikṛti*)—there is an absence of connection with a deity. Since in the archetype the lifting serves a visible purpose and is understood to be a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) for the sacrificial substance, in the ectype as well, by way of restating the archetypal lifting, there is merely an injunction to bring it to the *droṇakalaśa* vessel; thus, it is not an injunction for a separate lifting, but rather functions like the archetypal action.

Alternatively, since the *abhyunnīta* (the portion drawn out) is understood to be fit for sacrifice—just like the fruit-cup (*phalacamasa*) or the heart and other parts—and since the previous remnant serves as the vessel containing the sacrificial substance, it is understood to be merely a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the *abhyunnīta*, similar to the milk prescribed in the injunction "he mixes the cup for Maitrāvaruṇa with milk. Therefore, there is no evidence for its being intended for a subsequent sacrifice; thus, [it remains] the eating of the remnant of the oblation belonging to the previous sacrifice.

Intending that the previous deity must indeed be indicated because the connection with that deity has not been removed due to the requirement of performing the ritual according to the tantra, he states the final conclusion: "at the time of the drawing up [of the Soma]."
In this context, the meaning of the term *unnayana* (drawing out) is that by which the filling of empty vessels with Soma is performed;

whereas the meaning of the term *abhyunnayana* (re-filling) is that by which the filling with another portion of Soma is performed while those very vessels still contain the remnants of the previous Soma.

Although there is no need for this non-permanent investigation—since the modification (*ūha*) lacks permanence and its connection is restricted solely to the offering to Indra—with respect to a permanent purpose.

Therefore, it has been stated by the learned: "In the case of an objection (*ākṣepa*), an exception (*apavāda*), the attainment of a rule (*prāpti*), or the definition of an action (*lakṣaṇakarma*), as well as in the case of that which operates after having performed something else (*yatkṛtvāpravartate*), a purpose (*prayojana*) need not be stated.

Nevertheless, [this is necessary] for the investigation consisting in determining whether or not there is the status of being an auxiliary to the subsequent sacrifice (*uttarayāgāṅgatva*), which serves as the cause for the present inquiry and is a continuation of the preceding section (*pūrvaśeṣavṛtti*).

Regarding the permanent [offering], since it serves as the fruit in another example, the purpose— which must necessarily be stated as consisting in the consideration or non-consideration of the connection with the deity at the time of the subsequent sacrifice immediately after it has been drawn up— has not been explicitly mentioned because it is obvious.
Thus ends the twelfth section, concerning the re-offering.
(Section concerning the indication of the previously offered deity)
— (B1) (Thirteenth Section / [A.3 Pāda 2 Adhikaraṇa 13]) But in the case of the *pātnīvata* [offering].
The remnants of the dual-deity offerings, beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu, having reached the vessel of Aditi, then proceed to the vessel of Āgrayaṇa.
And the portion for Pātnīvata is drawn from the Āgrayaṇa; when that is being consumed, the dual-deity offerings must also be indicated [as part of the same consumption].

As previously [argued], since the *āgrayaṇa* itself is connected with the deity Patnīvat, [the cup] should belong to it. However, this being the case, [we reply]: because of the scriptural statement of the ablative case, "He draws the *pātnīvata* from the *āgrayaṇa*," the status of being *pātnīvata* belongs to that which has departed from the *āgrayaṇa*, and not to the *āgrayaṇa* itself. Furthermore, just like the *āgrayaṇa*, even that which is not the *āgrayaṇa* [becomes *pātnīvata*] because of its mixture; therefore, it is that which has departed. Thus, even for a cup belonging to two deities (*dvidevatya*), the connection with the previous deity is lost through the connection with another deity.
And because they are not observed in their original nature due to their past course, they are not to be characterized. // 13 // 28 //
Thus ends the thirteenth section concerning the non-indication of deities in the Pātnīvata offering.

(B2) Herein is the sequence of performance: first, at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), having drawn the Soma by stream into the cups for the Aindravāyava, Maitrāvaruṇa, Śukra, and Manthin draughts, one then takes [Soma] from the Āgrayaṇa vessel by means of two streams— namely, from a great stream and from the stream of the residue remaining in the Antaryāma cup— and places it on the mound (*khara*).
All those cups and the *sthālī* (vessel) are set down.

Then, after some time, following the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant, comes the drawing of the *āśvina* cup. When the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) has commenced and it is the time for the offerings, the remnants of the offerings to Indra-Vāyu, Mitra-Varuṇa, and the Aśvins are poured into the *āditya-sthālī*, even though it is still empty.
Based on the injunction, "He pours the residue into the Āditya vessel," it is placed there after being covered with the wooden cup known as the *savanīya-āditya*.

Then, at the time of drawing the cups in the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*), that which is in the Āditya vessel and that which is in the Āgrayaṇa vessel are drawn together in a stream into the Āgrayaṇa vessel.
Thereafter, having taken the residue of the double-deity offering (*dvidevatya*) from the Āditya vessel using the Āditya wooden cup, that residue is offered to the Ādityas.

Because of the injunction, "The fourth stream [is drawn] from the residue remaining in the Āgrayaṇa vessel after the pouring out for the Āditya cup," there is no residue left for consumption due to the prescription of that fourth stream.

Then, because of the injunction, "He draws the Pātnīvata [cup] from the Āgrayaṇa using the Upāṃśu vessel," one sets aside the portion in the Āgrayaṇa vessel and takes what remains; that residue is then offered to Agni Patnīvat.
Since there is no other application for this residue at that time, its consumption is accompanied by mantras.
With reference to this sequence of performance, he indicates the subject matter with the words: "of those [offerings] belonging to two deities."
By the phrase "of those beginning with the Aindravāyava," just as the deities Maitrāvaruṇa and Aśvin are included, so too is the deity Vāyu who precedes Indra and Vāyu included;
for the sacrifice is performed with that very same dedication.
In that regard, in the previous section, among the *camasa* cups at the commencement of the *savana*, the offerings dedicated to Indra serve as the archetype (*prakṛti*) for the others.

Having established that those offerings not dedicated to Indra (*anaindra*) constitute a modification (*vikṛti*), it was proven that in the deliberation on *ūha* (modification of mantras), the employment of words denoting the original deity must also be performed. Now, by the same principle, since there exists a relationship of archetype and ectype (*prakṛti-vikṛtibhāva*) between the offerings to Indra and those not to Indra among the cups (*graha*), the employment of words for other deities would also follow—just as in the case of the *patnīvat* cup where one says "drunk by Agni"—in the *ūha* of the mantra "drunk by Agni. To provide an exception (*apavāda*) to this, which constitutes the immediate connection (*saṅgati*), [the Sūtra] addresses the non-Agrayaṇa cups based on the inherent capacity of the thing itself, namely their being distinct from the Agrayaṇa.

Since the connection between the *pāda* and the *adhyāya*—arising from the incidental discussion regarding whether the form (*rūpa*) of the preceding [portion] is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the *pātnīvata* sacrifice—is clear, [the author], without stating it, presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "In that... (*tasmin*).
The phrase "the portion belonging to two deities" is also an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) for Vāyu;
by the word "also" (api), the existence of a modification (ūha)—namely, the formula "drunk by Agni together with the wives"—is indicated.
Thus, they are to be indicated.

The meaning is that [the deities] should be indicated by means of modification (*ūha*), just as in the formulas "of that drunk by Vāyu, Indra, Vāyu, Mitra, Varuṇa, and the Aśvins with their wives" and "of that drunk by Indra, Mitra, and Varuṇa.

Here, however, there is a distinction: since the remnant remaining in the Āditya vessel also exists in the Āgrayaṇa jar according to the previously stated method, the Āditya must also be indicated; this, though not mentioned by the ancients or the moderns, has been stated by Somanātha.
And here, regarding the Āgrayaṇa jar which was set down after being filled with two streams during the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), the Soma therein—[is] "those... [and so forth].

Because [the Vaiśvadeva cup] is grasped with the mantra, "O gods, you eleven who abide in heaven," and because it is understood to be connected with the sacrifice through the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra, "May those gods enjoy this sacrifice," it is thus connected as a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) to the Vaiśvadeva cup which has such deities by virtue of its connection to the totality of the gods.

Since there is no subsequent application of the remnant of that oblation elsewhere, consumption alone follows as the result; therefore, [the rule] serves to remove the connection with those specific deities.
Because [the Vaiśvadeva] is clearly specified, there is no possibility of its being included as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) in the consumption of the *pātnīvata* cup.

Furthermore, just as in the case of the *vaiśvadeva* draught all deities—both those of the subsidiaries and the principal—are indeed deities, so it has been elaborated by the authors of the Sūtras and the Bhāṣya in the twelfth book. Or rather, it is possible that the *viśvadeva* deities—who possess the power to distinguish milk from water—perceive the Soma, which was taken with a mantra containing the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of all deities, as belonging to themselves alone as their own portion, even though other remnants exist.
[This is] for the purpose of accepting [the offering].
Therefore, in the act of settling [the vessel], there is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of settling for the sake of the Viśvedevas found in the mantra: "This is thy womb; for all the gods, thee.
Nevertheless, [there is also]: "O Viśvedevas, hear this my invocation, you who are in the intermediate space and you who are highest in heaven."

The indicative mark (*liṅga*) of a mantra whose deity is identical to that of the drawing [of the cup] is also appropriate in the *yājyā* mantra: "O you who have Agni as your tongue, or you who are worthy of sacrifice, sit upon this sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and rejoice!
Furthermore, there is the specific assumption of an unknown deity in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*): "This Āgrayaṇa is indeed unrecognised.
Even though nothing from the Āgrayaṇa vessel is actually offered to the Viśve Devas;
Nevertheless, because that cup is occupied with the purpose of setting aside the remnants intended for the deities remaining from what was taken for the Pātnīvata offering,

and because the performance of the Hāriyojana draught follows after taking [the Soma] from the Droṇakalaśa vessel, there is no fault whatsoever in offering it from another vessel, even though the specific vessel has not been presented, on account of the scriptural injunction.

Therefore, although there is the possibility that Savitṛ and the others are to be mentioned as secondary indicators (upalakṣaṇa) when consuming the remnants of the Vaiśvadeva offering, the author of the Nyāyasudhā maintains that the deity Viśvedevas need not be mentioned because, in the case of the Pātnīvata offering, there is no remnant belonging to them, and thus their connection as deities has been removed. Having all this in mind, [the opponent asks]: why is there no mention of the Viśvedevas who constitute the deities of the Āgrayaṇa?

In the *Nyāyasudhā*, it is stated that the commentary [of Śrīkaṇṭha] explains the word "tataḥ" (therefore) for the purpose of indicating the resolution— namely, that the doubt raised by the phrase "it is being considered" (*cintyate*) is removed because its removal is beyond doubt.

This being the case, the authors of the *Prakāśa*, having restated this, argue that in no Vedic recension (*śākhā*) is an offering made from the *āgrayaṇa* vessel to the Viśvedevas; since that [offering] has already been drunk by the Viśvedevas, a suspicion might arise regarding the indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) in the formula for the *pātnīvata* offering—namely, the modification (*ūha*) of the term "drunk by the Viśvedevas" (*viśvadevapīta*). Therefore, they say: "Thus, what the talkative one has said was done without considering the actual performance."
The objection that both the doubt and its resolution are inconsistent has been refuted;

for, according to that [opponent's] view, since the Āgrayaṇa lacks a connection with all deities as its form, the contradiction with the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra— "O gods, enjoy this sacrifice"— would be difficult to avoid in other ritual applications where a connection with all deities is absent.

Furthermore, because it would entail a contradiction in performance, [the author] has indicated through the venerable teachers (*pūjyapāda*)— under the guise of indifference based on the reasons of the removal of the connection with the Viśvedevas as deities and the clarity [of the text]— that [this view] arises solely from the influence of the qualities of being one who speaks much by incessantly contemplating what is hateful.

Since the *pātnīvata* is not previously established and thus cannot be construed as the object of the action, when there is an expectancy for an object for the verb *gṛhṇāti*, it is the well-known *āgrayaṇa* itself [that is understood].

When there is an association with "objecthood" (*karmatva*) through the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) functioning as a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the meaning becomes: "One should make that which has the Āgrayaṇa as its object [of the act of] taking (*grahaṇa*) possess the Pātnīvata deity. Consequently, just as the connection with the subsequent deity applies only to what remains in the Āgrayaṇa vessel when it is partially drawn out (*abhyunnīta*), so too is the connection with the Pātnīvata deity perceived to apply only to that which remains in the Āgrayaṇa; thus, even if it were mixed, the remnant of the two-deity offering (*dvidevatya-śeṣa*) that does not reside in the Āgrayaṇa is excluded.
Intending to provide the logical justification that there is no removal of the connection with the previous deity due to the absence of a connection with a deity as a "wife" (patnīvat), he says:
"as before."

Although the action is not explicitly heard [in the text], nevertheless, because it is impossible for that which is heard as the *apādāna* (ablative source) to be construed as such [in its literal sense], and because there is no evidence for metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and because only that which has departed from the Āgrayaṇa vessel is present,
and because that which is referred to by the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) "pātnīvata" is construed as the object (*karman*), and because of this state of having departed—
Since everything arises immediately upon being mixed, there is the cognition of a connection with the subsequent deity;

and since, according to the reasoning already established, that [connection] is untenable without the removal of the connection with the previous deity, such removal is necessary. With this in mind, intending that it is not a mere secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*), he states the final conclusion: "The *pātnīvata* [cup]."
Now, in order to dispel the doubt that "even when the connection has been removed, let it still serve as a designation by way of its former state," he says: "And by way of its former state."

The meaning is as follows: because the suffix *-kta* in the word *indrapīta* (drunk by Indra) expresses, through its denotation of an existing state (*bhūtārtha*), the fact that the action has passed away while being simultaneous with the result in the form of an existing relationship; and because such a [past] action cannot serve as a defining characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*) here—since in the archetype (*prakṛti*) it is characterized precisely by the existence of that relationship, whereas here, if one were to characterize it by a deity with whom there is no existing relationship, it would follow that it performs a non-archetypal function (*aprākṛtakārya*)—therefore, such [a past action] cannot possibly serve as a defining characteristic.
Thus ends the thirteenth section concerning the non-indication of dual deities in the Pātnīvata offering.
— — — — — — — (B1) (14th Section /) (a.3 pā.2 adhi.14) Tvaṣṭṛ.

Regarding the Pātnīvata cup, since the mantra "O Agni, accompanied by the wives (patnīvān), together with the god Tvaṣṭṛ, drink the Soma" indicates that Tvaṣṭṛ also possesses the status of a deity, it follows [from the prima facie view] that he too should be invoked alongside Agni. To this, we reply: it is correct that the word *patnīvān*—being etymological (*yaugika*) and thus requiring a substantive—is understood as the substantive through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) when applied to Agni; however, in the case of Tvaṣṭṛ, the instrumental case-ending indicates merely his association [with Agni].
Furthermore, this [quality] is not invariably concomitant with the act of drinking,

because there are instances of deviation, such as in the statement, "The she-ass carries the load together with her ten sons," and because even when drinking occurs, divinity is not established by authoritative means of knowledge.
Therefore, because of the independent secondary derivative (taddhita) "pātnīvata," Agni Pātnīvata alone is the deity; thus, he alone is to be indicated, not Tvaṣṭṛ. 14.28.
Thus ends the fourteenth section concerning the fact that Tvaṣṭṛ is not a deity for the Pātnīvata offering.
(B2) He indicates the object [of the rule]: "only the pātnīvata [offering]."

Furthermore, by this discussion regarding Tvaṣṭṛ’s status as a deity and his role as a constituent element (*aṅga*) in the Pātnīvata sacrifice, the connection to the chapter and the section is established; likewise, since the substance was previously examined in that context, the examination of the deity follows by way of immediate relevance (*prasaṅga*), thus indicating the sequential topical connection (*anantara-saṅgati*). Moreover, by examining whether Tvaṣṭṛ is a mere secondary reference (*upalakṣaṇa*), the connection to the section on modification (*ūha*) is also indicated.
The mantra passage "agnā" is also cited as a reason for the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) under discussion, even though it is not an actual example.

In the word *agne*, by the rule "The *e* and *o* vowels are *pragṛhya* when used in address from a distance; the first half [of the vowel] becomes a protracted (*pluta*) *ā*, and the second half becomes *i* or *u*," the first half becomes a protracted *ā* and the second half becomes a half-mora *i*. Therefore, following *āgnā*, a third mark is sometimes written to indicate that the subsequent vowel is a three-mora protracted sound (*trimātra-pluta*).
Thus, the reading *evam agne āri* found in some manuscripts is an erroneous reading (*apapāṭha*).

Although the *Kaustubha* records the mantra according to the reading of the Āpastambas, *pātnīvataḥ sajūr devaiḥ*, nevertheless, there is no fault here even if one writes *pātnīvatsajūḥ* in accordance with the reading of the Vājasaneyins, since the meaning remains the same.
"From the mantra," it says.
Although the status of being a deity for the "possessor of a wife" (*patnīvat*) alone is expressed by the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*),

nevertheless, because the word *patnīvat*— being etymological (*yaugika*)— is always in need of a substantive, it necessarily requires a substantive to be supplied from the wording of the mantra. Furthermore,

since the word *sajūs* (together) indicates the companionship of Tvaṣṭṛ as well as Agni, and since the act of drinking is not possible without both having the status of deities, [Tvaṣṭṛ must also be a deity].

Since that which is understood as a deity is construed as the substantive (viśeṣya), it too must be indicated by the indicator (upalakṣaṇīya). In this regard, there are two possible ways: because they are expressed by separate words, and because a collective substantive status (*vyāsajyaviśeṣyatā*) for both Agni and Tvaṣṭṛ is impossible, they are each [to be understood] individually through conjunction (*samuccaya*).

Because [Agni] is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), just as the renunciation (*tyāga*) is made with the formula, "This is for Agni Patnīvat and Tvaṣṭṛ, not mine," so too in the mantra for consumption (*bhakṣamantra*), there must be a modification (*ūha*) such as "drunk by Agni-Patnīvat and Tvaṣṭṛ. Alternatively, since the mantra mentions Agni as qualified by his association with Tvaṣṭṛ, one should assume that he is likewise the qualificand in the injunction; therefore, the renunciation is made accordingly, and thus [the consumption] should be characterized as "drunk by Agni together with Patnīvat and Tvaṣṭṛ. This is the meaning.

Intending that the deityhood belongs to the word *agni* itself—since, through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *patnīvat*, it is perceived that *agni* alone provides the substantive (*viśeṣya*)—the author states the final conclusion (siddhānta):
"It is logical."
After the word "in the fire" (agnau), the phrase "the status of being a deity" (devatātva) is to be supplied as an ellipsis.

In that context, by another scriptural statement, "He performs the subsequent sacrifice with 'O Agni, enjoy the Soma' (*somasyāgne vīhi')", the substance Soma is established through the rule of the mantra (*māntravarṇika*).

When [the ritual] has been assigned, and there arises a desire for further details regarding its dharma, since this [rite]— though a subsidiary of the Jyotiṣṭoma according to the context— is similar to the Vaimṛdha in having Soma as its substance, the extension (atideśa) of its specific injunctions applies; thus, when the consumption of Soma and its mantra have become applicable,

Regarding the immediate connection: since the deity indicated by the words of the mantra (*māntravarṇika-devatā*) is beyond doubt, the author of the *Nyāyasudhā* maintains that the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) arises here as a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) to the principle established in the preceding section concerning the non-indication of the nature of deityhood. Thus, there is a connection by way of a counter-example.

As for the point that— by way of overturning the previous logic (*pūrvanyāyātyaya*)— the application of a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇasaṅgati*) occurs only where the absence of the previous probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) is stated as the established conclusion (*siddhānta*); whereas in cases where, by overturning the previous logic, there is merely a prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣamātra*) and the very same previous probandum is the established conclusion, [the application is] "extended" (*ātideśikī*)— having established this distinction with great effort after first refuting that view, [it is concluded that] because it is the very same previous probandum that has been established as the conclusion...
The authors of the *Prakāśa* state that the connection is one of extended application (*ātideśikī*).

However, since they have already indicated a connection by way of a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa-saṅgati*)—merely by raising an objection (*pūrvapakṣa*) in the sections concerning "being named after it" (*tat-prakhya*) and "designation by it" (*tad-vyapadeśa*), even though the object to be established (*sādhya*) is identical—it follows that such a [new] arrangement contradicts what was stated previously. Because the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* sacrifice is determined to be a disposal (*pratipatti*) due to its character as a disposal, and because it is praised as having the nature of a *sviṣṭakṛt* sacrifice for the purpose of disposing of the substance—based on the statement: “When he performs the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* with ‘O Agni, eat the Soma,’ by that they consume the Soma-offerings that have been concluded; that itself is the *sviṣṭakṛt* of the Soma”—its status as a ritual of disposal is beyond dispute.

Otherwise, if it were a primary act (*arthakarman*), there would follow the necessity of performing it according to the *tantra* (the main ritual procedure), which is impossible here.

The meaning is that, by virtue of the logical application of extended injunction (*atideśa*), even though the two acts of consuming the Soma— which constitute parts of the *vaṣaṭkāra* and *anuvaṣaṭkāra* sacrifices— are performed simultaneously (*tantra*), the indicative mention (*upalakṣaṇa*) of both deities must nevertheless be made in that very context.
