To this, he says: "by way of direct injunction."

The meaning is as follows: just as in the case of the *yava* (barley) application, where—due to the lack of efficacy of the mantra "the essence of rice" (*vrīhīṇāṃ medha*) and because there is no modification (*ūha*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*)—its omission is prescribed, so too here its omission alone would follow.

For this very reason, when the consumption is obtained through direct instruction (*upadeśa*), even though the mantra is applied according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the section on "drunk by Indra" (*indrapīta-*)—since there is no difference in their connection to the *savana*—there is no possibility of designating that specific deity.
He concludes the established conclusion with the words "and therefore" (*ataśca*).

The meaning is that although there exists the status of being a drinker of the substance that has become an integral part of one's own sacrifice, because there is no extension (*atideśa*) to that [status] in this case, there is no substitution for the function of the original deity (*prākṛtadevatā*); thus, just as when the drinking is performed by the *adhvaryu*, even though it was drunk previously by the *hotṛ*,
one should not characterize it as "drunk by the *hotṛ*," in the same way, the deity of the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* is not to be characterized.

It should be understood that in the Sūtra, by the word *vaṣaṭkāra*, the deity of the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* sacrifice is indicated through *lakṣita-lakṣaṇā* (indirect indication based on a primary indication), due to its connection with the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* which is itself connected to the *vaṣaṭkāra*. Regarding this, although the author of the *Nyāyasudhā* established that the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* sacrifice is a *pratipatti-karman* (concluding rite of disposal), and although the *Prakāśakāra*s refuted that and asserted it is an *artha-karman* (primary rite for a purpose), the *Kaustubha* rejected that as well and accepted it as a *pratipatti-karman*; thus, here too, it is treated as such by the phrase "of that which is of the nature of a *pratipatti*."
It has been shown.
Thus ends the sixteenth section concerning the secondary *vaṣaṭ* call (*anuvaṣaṭkāra*).
(Section on the Non-Indication of Deities by the *Anuvaṣaṭkāra*:
Section 17) (B1) (17th Section / A.3 Pāda 2 Adhikaraṇa 17) Metre (*chandas*).
Having thus reflected, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) now refutes that [argument] once more:
there is no modification (ūha), because the ritual action is one and the same;
furthermore, there is no evidence for the various repetitions (abhyāsas) being subject to different injunctions (asamānavidhāna), just as in the case of the fruit-cup (phalacamas).
It is not proper to restrict the objects intended [by the mantra] merely on account of the mantra used for measuring and taking;

however, in the case of fire (agni) and knowledge (vidyā), since they are prompted by their own respective injunctions and lack prompting by the ritual injunction, it is proper that the eligibility for the ritual be restricted, as one depends upon fire and knowledge employed by another.
Therefore, let the mantras for measuring and taking pertain at will to the offering of Soma dedicated solely to Indra, but the measuring and so forth themselves should not be restricted.
In reality, however, since the term *vasumata* denotes other deities as well, those [offerings] also have the universal purpose (*sarvārthatva*) alone.
Therefore, because the consumption mantra (*bhakṣamantra*) pertains specifically to the offering made to Indra, the consumption of non-Indra offerings is to be done without a mantra. // 17 // 31 //
Thus ends the seventeenth section concerning the mantra-less consumption of [the Soma] belonging to those other than Indra.

(B2) Thus, having relied upon the second prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the section concerning "drunk by Indra" (*indrapīta*) and having demonstrated five hypothetical deliberations (*kṛtvācintā*), [the author] now states:

"Thus," etc., whereby the proponent of the first *pūrvapakṣa* of the section concerning "drunk by Indra" opposes [the current position] by way of negating the day [of performance] established by the second *pūrvapakṣa*, in order to achieve his own purpose through the two *kṛtvācintā*s that are about to be presented.
He states the very manner of the refutation: "Not so."

Since the rite called *yāga* possesses a fruit and is primary, it is capable of receiving the *soma* and other materials as its constituent parts (*aṅga*). However, because the individual offerings (*pradāna*) are of the nature of repetitions (*abhyāsa*) and are subordinate (*guṇa*), they cannot receive constituent parts according to the maxim "subordinates exist for the sake of another" (*guṇānāṃ ca parārthatvāt*). Consequently, since [the offering] cannot be a modified form (*vikṛti*), and because the *yāga* remains one and the same despite each repetition—such that repetition is inherently impossible within itself—it is not [performed] with the mantra through modification (*ūha*).
The consumption [of the remnants] belongs to those offerings not dedicated to Indra;

for these other offerings are not connected with another sacrifice, such that— because they would constitute separate rites— they could stand in a relationship of archetype and ectype (*prakṛti-vikṛti-bhāva*) based on a distinction between them.

The meaning is that since it is possible for the sacrifice enjoined by the direct Vedic text, "One should sacrifice with Soma," to be the very basis [for the ritual procedure], there is no authority for postulating other sacrifices; and even though the ritual properties (dharmas) belong to the single Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the restriction of the mantras is justified on the basis of their indicative power (liṅga). Therefore, only the consumption of the remnant of the Soma from the offering to Indra is to be performed with the mantra.
Granted that even though the repetitions (abhyāsa) are subordinate (guṇa), they possess fruitfulness through a traditional succession;

nevertheless, it is not the case that they acquire their specific properties (dharma) according to a fixed rule (vyavasthā), as is the case with the repetitions of the Soma and the fruit-cup (phalacamasa). Thus he says: "Even of the repetitions... (abhyāsānām api).

In the case of the *phalacamasa*, there is no contradiction regarding the connection between the permanent and the non-permanent; thus, even if there were no commonality of injunction (*asāmānavidhya*), there is no evidence whatsoever for assuming it here.

Nor is there an explicit scriptural injunction stating that it is for the purpose of the repeated offering to Indra—such as "he mixes [the cup] for Maitrāvaruṇa with milk"—and therefore, there is no lack of commonality of injunction. This is the meaning.

Now, one might object: since here too the measuring and the taking (grahaṇa) have as their sole object the offering to Indra (aindrapradāna), and because—following that—the Soma which is to be refined by them, the refinements such as pressing (abhiṣava), and even the Dīkṣaṇīyā and other rites associated with them, are understood to have as their sole object the offering to Indra, it is possible that there is no equality of injunction (sāmānavidhya). To this [the author replies]:
He said: "No."
It is logical.

In the present case, however, since the measuring and the taking-up mantras, as well as their intended objects, are not prompted by anything else, it is necessary to assume that they are prompted by the injunction of the sacrifice (*kratu-vidhi*).

Furthermore, since all repetitions (*abhyāsa*)—due to the lack of distinction in the context (*prakaraṇa*)—are capable of establishing both the application (*viniyoga*) and the performance-injunction (*prayoga-vidhi*), there is no justification for such a restriction. This is the meaning. For this very reason, although the measuring and taking-up mantras—just as the *vrīhi* mantra has *vrīhi* as its object—might, on the basis of indicative power (*liṅga*), have as their object only the offering to Indra (*aindra-pradāna*), [they must nevertheless apply to all].

He says "therefore" (ataḥ), meaning that since pride and the other [defilements] pertain to all objects— just as the establishment of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) pertains to all [the deities]— there is no flaw even if the grasping of the cup for those [defilements] is performed without a mantra.
Even though the two mantra-recitations are performed while still in the state of the creeper (*latā*), their performance is indeed by way of a single ritual procedure (*tantra*);
or rather, because they are performed solely for the sake of the offering to Indra, they incidentally (*prasaṅgataḥ*) benefit the others as well.
Thus, since there is no separate performance, there is no distinction whatsoever in the performance based on whether it is "with mantra" (*samantraka*) or "without mantra" (*amantraka*).

Nevertheless, the meaning is that even when all the Soma has been destroyed after the offering to Indra, since the Soma is being measured and taken for the sake of subsequent offerings, the state of being without mantras is established. For this very reason— even though it is understood that the Siddhānta of the *Indrapīta* section, which consists in the application of mantras to non-*Aindra* [Soma cups], is possible through the *bahuvrīhi* compound itself, and thus the Siddhānta also accepts this commonality of rule (*sāmānavidhya*) without rejecting it— [the conclusion remains as stated].
In response to the objection—"What is the purpose of mentioning that [which is] irrelevant to the final conclusion (siddhānta) under the guise of a *kṛtvācintā*?"—it is said:

even though there is no distinction in the *bhakṣa-mantra*, if there were a relationship of archetype and ectype (*prakṛti-vikṛti-bhāva*), there would be an application by modification (*ūha*) in non-Indra [deities] for these two measuring-and-grasping mantras: "For Indra, thee, accompanied by the Vasus" and [the other].

However, Bhaṭṭa Someśvara has written in some places that, because it is impossible for them to have the same ritual application (*sāmānavidhya*) and because they lack the capacity [to function] there as they stand, there is simply no performance [of the mantra]; yet, this must be understood as referring only to the modified application (*ūha*) of the mantra— which is obtained through extension (*atideśa*)— when one performs the measuring of the Soma intended for a second offering necessitated by the total destruction of the previous Soma.

This being the case, although this response was not recorded in the *Nyāyasudhā*, it has been cited here under the impression that it was; however, it was refuted by the authors of the *Prakāśa* as follows: "Since in offerings not dedicated to Indra (*anaindra-pradāna*), only the separate measures of the *māna* and *grahaṇa* are performed, how could there be any occasion for the modification (*ūha*) of these two mantras even if they stood in the relationship of archetype and ectype (*prakṛti-vikṛti-bhāva*)? How much less, then, could there be non-employment on the grounds of having a common injunction (*sāmānavidhya*)?"

In that regard, under the guise of establishing the specific performance previously mentioned concerning the Kaustubha gem, the venerable Pūjyapāda himself indicated that [the opponent's view] is incorrect;
for, in reality...

Since the quality of possessing wealth (*vasumattva*) is not heard in the injunctive sentence (*vidhivākya*), it would follow that the manifestation of Indra’s possession of wealth would be purposeless;

therefore, according to the method stated in the *Vārtika*, the word *vasumat*—which denotes the deity—is capable of expressing deities other than Indra who are connected to the offerings not belonging to Indra.

Thus, the meaning is that because the vessel is filled elsewhere also with the formula "to Indra accompanied by other deities" (*itaradevatāyuktāyendrāya*), the drawing of the Soma is performed with the mantra.

However, since the *bhakṣa-mantra* lacks a designation of a deity connected to any offering other than that dedicated to Indra, and because the offerings are distinct such that the consumption of their respective remnants must also be performed separately, it is appropriate to apply the mantra— functioning as an instrument— to the consumption of the remnant of the Indra-offering alone,

as its application is established by the context (*prakaraṇa*). Thus, by virtue of its indicative power (*liṅga*), the mantra is employed specifically for the consumption of the remnant of the Indra-offering.
However, in the case of consuming the remnants not belonging to Indra, there is no possibility of application whatsoever; intending this disparity, he concludes with the words "therefore" (ataḥ).

As for that which the authors of the *Prakāśa* have stated— that the purpose of the equal application (*sāmānavidhya*) is the attainment of desires based on qualities regarding the *yājyā* verses, such as "if one should desire that [the sacrificer] become worse off, he should pronounce the *vaṣaṭ* with a lower tone for his *yājyā*," which applies even to non-Indra-related [offerings], but not when they are modifications (*vikṛti*);
that is not correct.

Even though the repetitions (*abhyāsa*) are modifications (*vikṛti*), since the rite (*karman*) is one and the same, that very rite— which is the object to be accomplished by the modified repetitions— is connected with the fruit by virtue of being the *Jyotiṣṭoma*.

Consequently, because the substratum consisting of the *yājyā* verses, which serves as the means for the *apūrva* of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, remains present even in those repetitions, the attainment of the results of the optional qualities (*guṇakāma*) is logically established.
For there is no basis for [the latter] being the substratum there by virtue of being the *yājyā* connected to the offering to Indra, as there is no evidence for this;
nor is there any status as a subsidiary to the offerings not dedicated to Indra, nor any other distinct result.

Since this would result in the sacrifice to be accomplished by that [rite] being a distinct ritual act from the Jyotiṣṭoma— thereby making it impossible for it to possess the nature of a Jyotiṣṭoma— the venerable teacher has set aside this proposed purpose as untenable.
Thus ends the seventeenth section concerning the mantra-less consumption of [soma] belonging to those other than Indra.
— — — — — — — (B1) (Section 18 / [A.3 Pāda 2 Adhikaraṇa 18]) Regarding the offering to Indra and Agni.
This being the case, there arises further reflection:
even in the case of the repeated offering to Indra-Agni, the consumption must be accompanied by the mantra "of what was drunk by Indra" (indrapītasya) alone;

for although the act of relinquishment (*tyāga*) functions as a collective whole (*vyāsajyavṛtti*), the act of drinking—or rather, the acceptance (*svīkāra*) indicated by the word "drunk"—functions with respect to each [deity] individually.

Since it can be designated by one [priest] just like [the portion] belonging to one's own mother, and since the act of relinquishment (*tyāga*) pertains to the aggregate of both the offered and the unoffered portions—thereby lacking the status of being restricted solely to the portion of the offered part that is currently being consumed—there is no indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of "having been relinquished" by the word "drunk" (*pīta*). Consequently, because it does not fall within the scope of the section concerning the fourfold division (*caturdhākaraṇa*), its consumption should also be accompanied by the mantra. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: True, the word "drunk" does indeed indicate "appropriation" (*svīkāra*); [but this appropriation is not yet final].
Because drinking is prohibited in the ninth [chapter],
and because "renunciation" cannot be indicated according to the method you have stated,

whereas "acceptance"— which is postulated as being based on terms such as "the deity's property" and so forth— must necessarily be postulated as referring only to what remains after the oblation has been offered, the indication (lakṣaṇā) is appropriate.

Nevertheless, because it is more parsimonious to postulate that [the property] resides only in the collective whole (*vyāsajyavṛtti*), and because there is no evidence for its residing in each individual part—thus making it possible for it to be the object of the "fourfold division" (*caturdhākaraṇa*)—there is no mantra-accompanied consumption of it.
This concludes the eighteenth section concerning the mantra-less nature of the consumption of the *aindrāgna* [cup].

(B2) Since this section involves an inquiry into whether the *bhakṣa-mantra* is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the consumption of the remnants of the oblation offered to the deities Indra and Agni, or not, the connection to the [preceding] chapter and section is established.

Furthermore, because the initial prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) proponent established in the previous section that the consumption of the remnants of oblations from offerings other than those to Indra is mantra-less, and because that point is here challenged and subsequently resolved, the immediate connection based on such a challenge (*ākṣepikī-saṅgati*) is not explicitly stated as it is clear; thus, the matter remains settled.

Thus, having established the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) for today, he shows the investigation as being by way of a hypothetical discussion (kṛtvācintā), [beginning with] the word "evam" (thus).
He states the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa): "In the case of the offering to Indra and Agni as well..."
"Of renunciation," it says.

Although, according to the principle of the section on "dividing into four parts" (*caturdhākaraṇādhikaraṇa*), Indra and Agni possess a collective mode of existence (*vyāsajyavṛttitva*), and thus the word *indrapīta* cannot designate Indra— the deity included within the pair Indra-Agni— on the basis of the etymological derivation "offered to Indra"; nevertheless,

since there is no evidence for the word *pīta* to signify "offered" through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and because a genitive compound (*caturthī-samāsa*) is improper as it is not sanctioned by grammatical rule.

Even if there were some way to provide an instruction, since the aggregate of both the offered (*huta*) and the unoffered (*ahuta*) was previously relinquished, its destruction by the act of offering would mean that what remains unoffered is not fit for consumption; consequently, it could not be designated by the term *indrapīta* (drunk by Indra). Therefore, "drinking" (*pāna*) must either consist of the tasting of the flavor residing in the deity, or—since that [tasting] will be refuted in the ninth book—it must consist of the casting of the offering into the mouth of the Āhavanīya fire, or else it must refer to the offering itself.

Furthermore, since it is impossible to designate [the fire] by the term "that" (tatpada) while it is being consumed by the fire— otherwise, the designation "that" would be untenable— and since this would necessitate a figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) of the whole in order to include its constituent parts,

one must either accept that the referent of the word "pīta" (yellow) is necessarily the substrate of the color yellow and so forth, or else state that the meaning of the word "pīta" is, through figurative indication, the nature of the relation itself.
And thus, a genitive compound (*tṛtīyā-samāsa*) is also obtained as sanctioned by the grammatical rules (*anuśāsana*).

In this way, since the acceptance (*svīkāra*)—conceived as common to both the part and the whole—is logically established through a distinct conceptualization for each respective deity, it follows that even though the offering is made collectively (*vyāsajya*), the designation of that portion as "belonging to Indra" is justified because half of it has been accepted by Indra. This is the meaning.
It is like the example of one's own mother.

The meaning is that, just as in the case of the mother of Ḍittha and Ḍabittha, because the relationship consisting of the status of offspring and progenitor—which is subsumed within the referent of the word "mother"—exists in each one individually, the designation "mother of Ḍittha" can be applied by means of even one of them; so too is it appropriate here.

Since the status of the deity itself is already expressed by the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix in the act of "dividing into four," there is no inclusion of a deity that functions as a collective whole (*vyāsajyavṛtti*).
It is with this intention—namely, that there is thus no tautology—that he states the distinction: "Therefore, [the rule applies] to 'fourfold'."
"By way of brevity."

In a case where a deity exists as a collective whole (*vyāsajyavṛtti*), since it is possible to postulate the acceptance of a single entity existing as that collective, there is no need to postulate plurality therein;
the meaning is that this is due to the principle of parsimony (*gaurava*).

As for the presentation of the established conclusion (siddhānta) in the Vārttika and other works by means of the figurative sense (lakṣaṇā) of "having been abandoned," it was stated in the Kaustubha that this is for the purpose of demonstrating rhetorical boldness (prauḍhi); that [explanation] should be consulted in that very same work.

Even if the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the absence of mantras remains established, the purpose of examining that position is as follows: even in the case of consuming [the soma] dedicated to Indra and Agni (*aindrāgna*),

when the mantra— applicable by virtue of being a qualification of the *savana*— is employed, at the time of reflecting upon its meaning according to the prima facie view, because it involves the acceptance of distinct [deities], there must also be a reflection on the meaning of the term "drunk by Indra" (*indrapīta*) based on Indra’s being included within the [dual deity] Indra-Agni.

In the final conclusion (siddhānta), however, because that [cup] is a single entity and lacks the status of being an object "drunk by Indra," there is no mental synthesis (anusandhāna); since this is self-evident, it has not been explicitly stated.
Thus ends the eighteenth section concerning the absence of a mantra for the consumption of the offering to Indra and Agni.
(B1) (19th Topic /) (A.3 Pāda 2 Adhikaraṇa 19) And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after the word *chandas*.
In that very mantra, the words "of the Gāyatrī metre" and so forth are heard.
In this prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), this [phrase] is indeed a qualification of Soma.
Consequently, it applies only where there is an offering to Indra, such as in the Bṛhaspatisava and others, because of the scriptural statement: "This day becomes of the Gāyatrī metre."
In that very case, there is its excellence,
but not its inclusion within the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice;
because there is no offering consisting solely of verses in the Gāyatrī metre.
Nor is there an absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that makes known the connection with the general [category];

for since the status of having Indra as the deity, the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), and so forth do not exist elsewhere—such as in the ordinary world—the Bṛhaspatisava is established through the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*).

This being the position reached, [the author replies]: even in the Bṛhaspatisava, because another *ṛc* verse is recited at the commencement of the pressing (*savanamukhīya*), and because of the statement "this is a Gāyatra [hymn]," etc. [it follows that the rule does not apply].

Since the explanation is established even by way of abundance (bhūman), and because there is an absence of exclusive *gāyatrī* meter in either the archetype (*prakṛti*) or the ectype (*vikṛti*), a compound is justified through its constant requirement [of other meters]; thus, the application is to the archetype alone.
In reality, however, since the *gāyatrī* is a means individually, there is not even a suspicion of breaking the compound when other *ṛc*-verses are present. // 19 // 33 //
Thus ends the nineteenth section concerning the application of specific mantras to various meters.

(B2) Taking as its starting point the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that this mantra applies only to the consumption of the remnants of the offering to Indra, this discussion— which is treated as a hypothetical inquiry (*kṛtācintā*) concerning what is to be performed—

Without explicitly stating the connection to the chapter (*adhyāya*) and the section (*pāda*), as well as the immediate contextual connection (*anantara-saṅgati*)—since these are clear—the author states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding that very mantra, preceded by a demonstration that it pertains only to a specific portion [of the Veda], with the words: "In that very [mantra]... (*tatraiva*).

If the word *gāyatrachandasaḥ* were a qualifier of the *savana* (pressing) as in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), then the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)— which holds that the offering to Indra consisting solely of verses in the *gāyatrī* meter is for a specific purpose— would not be established. Therefore, although, like the term *indrapīta*, it cannot be a *tatpuruṣa* compound referring to Soma (as in "drunk by Indra"),

Nevertheless, since the status of the term *indrapītasya*—introduced immediately prior—as referring to Soma has been established through its being a *tatpuruṣa* compound, then by virtue of its co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with it, the terms *gāyatracchandasaḥ* and so forth must also refer to that [Soma] alone, and not to the morning libation (*prātaḥsavana*) and other elements presented by the preceding words. He demonstrates that very attainment of the characteristic [of the goal] with the words: "And in the state of being yellow."

This is because the portion of Soma that was destroyed by the oblation cannot be designated by the direct statement using the word *te* (those), as it is for the purpose of addressing [the remaining] Soma.

By the word *pītapada* (the "drunk portion"), there arises the contingency of a further indication (*lakṣaṇā*) within the *tatpuruṣa* compound for the sake of denoting the part consisting of the remains of the oblation situated in the vessel;

Because the address is appropriate, there is no fault, as the meaning "I consume whatever belongs to that deity" is established.

"In the Taittirīya recension."

For in that [rite], having recited from "mandrābhibhūtiḥ" up to "varcasaḥ," one says: "O Soma, Lord of the Vasu-group, knower of the mind, of the morning pressing, of the Gāyatrī metre, drunk by Indra, drunk by Narāśaṃsa, drunk by the Pitṛs, full of sweetness, being invited, I, invited, partake; O Soma, Lord of the Rudra-group, knower of the mind, of the midday [pressing]..."
"Of the third pressing, having the *triṣṭubh* metre, drunk by Indra, drunk by Narāśaṃsa, drunk by the Fathers, full of sweetness, being invited, I, invited, partake;

[of that] belonging to the host accompanied by the Ādityas, O Soma-deity, you who know the thought. Of the third pressing, having the *jagatī* metre, drunk by Indra, drunk by Narāśaṃsa, drunk by the Fathers, full of sweetness, being invited, I, invited, partake."
Thus, this reading differs from the reading of the mantra found in another recensional branch (śākhā) as written by the author of the Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya.

In that case, if the three words beginning with "indrāpīta" (drunk by Indra) were intended to refer to Soma alone, then— since the application of those specific words would already be established through their indicative power (liṅga) as part of the common formula (tantra) for the consumption of the remnants of the offerings dedicated to those respective deities— the triple recitation would result in being purposeless.

Since the recitation is meaningful for the purpose of manifesting the specific limbs of the *savana*s— each associated with the Soma drunk by its respective deity according to the distinctions among the *savana*s—
the term "drunk" (*pīta*) is determined in this branch to refer to the connection between the Soma and the *savana* through secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Consequently, it is logical that the same determination applies to the mantra cited in the Bhāṣya, in accordance with the principle of restrictive application (*upasaṃhāranyāya*).

However, this much is the distinction: in the case of the *vasumadgaṇa* and other such mantras, the *Bhāṣya* cites their application to specific *savanas* according to a fixed rule (*vyavasthā*), preceded by a division of the mantras that was not previously established.

In the Taittirīya school, however, because the division according to the *savana*s is already established by its very nature, there is merely a fixed application according to the indicative marks (*liṅga*). Thus, the sense is that the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) here is indeed based on the Tatpuruṣa compound.

And regarding this, because the *siddhānta-sūtra*—"For Aitiśāyana, there is a single mantra for all [the cups], because they are the drinking-portion of the oblation; for there is eligibility for the *savana*"—mentions Aitiśāyana, one might mistakenly think that the view that there is a single mantra for other Ṛṣis is not Jaimini’s, and that his own position is actually the latter alternative set forth in the subsequent sūtra intended to refute the initial prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) beginning with "Or rather, according to the deity, for it shows that to be its archetype. To dispel such a misconception, he says:
In the Kalpasūtra.
The position regarding *ūha* (modification) which was stated by Jaimini in the subsequent Sūtra is presented here as the opinion of the authors of the Kalpasūtras;

whereas the position regarding *aikamantrya* (single mantra), though stated as the view of another, is indeed his own final conclusion (*svasiddhānta*) because it is established by reasoning. Therefore, the meaning is that when there is a conflict with the principles of Mīmāṃsā, the statement of the Kalpasūtra authors lacks authority—characterized by non-observance—because it is based on a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Therefore, at the end of this [section], the author of the Bhāṣya stated: "Thus the teacher Aitiśāyana thought;
this is our view as well.
The mention of the 'teacher' (ācārya) is for the purpose of declaring that [the doctrine] has come down from him."
The purpose has not been stated because it is obvious.
Thus ends the twentieth section, the section on the conclusion of the eleventh topic.
Thus ends the second quarter of the third chapter in the *Bhāṭṭadīpikāprabhāvalī*, composed by Śambhubhaṭṭa, the ornament of the scholarly assembly and disciple of the venerable Khaṇḍadeva.
